en: Preface to the Collated Edition of Verses from the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
As for the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, it is the great axe that cleaves through the [delusions of] self and dharmas, and the essential gateway for opening up cultivation and realization.
Its meaning is profound and far-reaching, while its phrasing is intricate and multifaceted. Without great wisdom, there would be no means to guide its subtleties;

how could those of minor intelligence possibly unravel its threads? Thus, Maitreya versified it, Asaṅga received it, and Vasubandhu inherited it, whereby the teaching was brought to flow throughout the land of India—like the golden sun blazing brilliantly over Fusang.
When its meaning was expounded in the Divine Land (China), it was like the jade hare [of the moon]...
Its radiance floats over the Snowy Peaks. Master Yijing stated that Bodhisattva Asanga formerly received these eighty verses in person from the Venerable Maitreya in Tuṣita Heaven.
He further noted that while there are many commentaries on the *Vajracchedikā* in the West, upon examining its origins, these verses are the earliest;
they constitute the verse version of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. And as for the verses...
That this [work] originated from Maitreya is clearly evidenced.

Nevertheless, since Master Yi (Paramārtha) already knew that these verses were transmitted by Maitreya, the fact that the version he translated attributes them to Asaṅga’s composition is likely a scribal error in the title.
Furthermore, when comparing the verses he translated with those translated by Bodhiruci, they differ by a mere hair's breadth; therefore, let...
The commentators on the commentaries have mostly adopted the translation by Bodhiruci. Now, in composing this new commentary, I likewise employ the version by Bodhiruci;

however, unlike other masters who arbitrarily selected and omitted passages resulting in discrepancies between preceding and succeeding sections, I have striven to ensure that the prose and verses correspond to one another, their alignment as perfect as two halves of a jade disk joined together.

The underlying intent is mutually pervasive; their support is like that of two reeds leaning against one another. As each section is analyzed and explained, the essence of all parts is found to be thus. There are also sections where verses are absent;
the commentary provides the reasons for each case, which may be understood through careful inspection. However, I fear that lecturers might rely solely on the commentary to deliver their discourse.
The listeners held that the scripture contained no verses; consequently, the Master opened both doors so that the disciples might obtain half of the pearl.

Is this not convenient for the lecturer but inconvenient for the listener? For this reason, I have compiled a combined edition and composed a preface to the commentary for circulation, so that future lecturers and listeners may each have something to rely upon.
It is like two mirrors facing each other with a single lamp burning between them; not only do they illuminate one another simultaneously, but...
The likeness is remarkably similar on both sides. As it is about to be carved into woodblocks, I have briefly composed this to express my humble sentiments.
Written on the third day before the full moon of the eleventh month in the year of Yiyou, the thirtieth year of the Qianlong era.
Recorded with reverence by Tongli, a junior disciple of the Venerable School,
regarding the *Combined Edition of Verses on the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*,
translated by Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty.
Verse: Translated by Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, when it was mealtime, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered [the city].
He went on almsround in the great city of Śrāvastī. Having completed his sequential begging within the city, he returned to his original place.
When he had finished his meal, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, arranged a seat, and sat down. At that time, the Elder Subhūti rose from his seat amidst the great assembly;
he bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha.
He said: "It is rare, World-Honored One! The Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas; he well entrusts all bodhisattvas.
World-Honored One, how should sons and daughters of good family who have resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* abide?
How should they subdue their minds?"

One should know that the meaning of "skillful protection" consists in bestowing [the teachings] upon their bodies and causing them to practice together; it is called "entrusting well" because they do not regress from what has been attained and strive to attain what has not yet been attained.
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is as you have said. The Tathāgata skillfully protects and mindfully sustains all bodhisattvas."
[Sā]. I have well entrusted the bodhisattvas to you. Listen attentively now; I shall speak for your sake.
Son of good family, daughter of good family, those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should abide in this manner and thus subdue their minds.
"Yes, World-Honored One," [Subhūti] replied, "I wish and desire to hear it. The Buddha said to Subhūti: "All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas..."

A bodhisattva should subdue the mind in this way: "All classes of sentient beings—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether with form or without form;
whether with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—I shall cause them all to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to liberation. Thus...
He has thus extinguished immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings; yet, in reality, there are no sentient beings who have attained extinction.
Why is this? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva possesses the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of a life-span, then he is not a bodhisattva.
Vast, foremost, and eternal, with a mind free from inversion, dwelling in a profound intention to benefit others,
one whose merit is fulfilled abides in this vehicle.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice giving without dwelling on any phenomenon whatsoever.
The meaning of *dāna* (generosity) is subsumed within six [categories]: material goods, fearlessness, and the Dharma. Among these, one, two, and three are called the "abodes of practice," namely:
giving without dwelling on form; giving without dwelling on sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena.
One does not cling to oneself, nor to gratitude, nor to the karmic fruit; one does not protect oneself, nor does one withhold giving, nor seek after other matters.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should give in this way, not dwelling on signs. Why is this? If a bodhisattva...
Giving while not dwelling on signs—its merit is inconceivable and immeasurable. Subhūti, what do you think?
Can the space in the eastern direction be measured? "No, World-Honored One. Subhūti, can the space in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below be measured?
"No, World-Honored One. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva does not dwell on signs...
Generosity and merit are likewise thus, beyond measure and calculation. Subhūti, a bodhisattva should simply abide as instructed.
Within those matters of subduing [the mind], one should remain far removed from a mind that grasps at signs and sever all various doubts.
Furthermore, Subhūti, to prevent the arising of such thoughts, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of his physical marks? No, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of his physical marks. Why is this? The physical marks spoken of by the Tathāgata are not, in fact, physical marks.
[The Buddha said: "Subhūti, all marks whatsoever are empty and false. If one perceives that all marks are no-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata."
The entity of the conditioned is analyzed; to prevent its attainment through such accomplishment, because the three marks have distinct entities, one is detached from them—this is the Tathāgata.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, is there any sentient being who, upon hearing such spoken words and phrases,"
“Will they give rise to true faith? The Buddha told Subhūti, “Do not speak thus.

After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during the final five hundred years, there will be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit who will be able to give rise to faith in these chapters and verses, regarding them as the truth.”
One who explains the profound meaning of cause and effect during the evil times of the future,
and who is not in vain because they possess the three virtues of a true Bodhisattva—
one should know that such a person has planted roots of goodness not under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas, but has already [done so].
Those who have planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable thousands of myriads of buddhas,
who have cultivated the precepts in the past and planted various roots of goodness,
and who, upon hearing these phrases, give rise to even a single thought of pure faith— Subhūti, the Tathāgata knows them all, and he perceives them all.
[The Buddha] saw that these sentient beings had attained such immeasurable merit.
Regarding the perfection of the precepts among all Buddhas, he also spoke of the fulfillment of their virtues.

Why is this? It is because these sentient beings no longer possess the notion of a self (*ātman*), the notion of a person (*pudgala*), the notion of a sentient being (*sattva*), or the notion of a life-span (*jīva*). They are without [these notions].
There is neither the characteristic of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) nor the characteristic of non-phenomena.
That life-principle (*jīva*) and the phenomena are far removed from grasping at characteristics.

Furthermore, it is taught that one knows those characteristics through eight sets of eight distinct meanings; their differentiated continuity is the essence, which persists without interruption until the end of life.
Furthermore, they resort to divergent paths; these are the four kinds of self-characteristics (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*). All things are empty and devoid of substance;
their true existence cannot be expressed, yet they are spoken of by relying on words and phrases. These are the four kinds of dharma-characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*).
Such persons, relying on faith and generating reverence, give rise to the perception of reality; yet, upon hearing sounds, they do not grasp them correctly.
When one speaks thus of such grasping, the Buddha does not perceive it as a fruit to be known.
Even if one seeks offerings and respect through the manifestation of the power of vows and wisdom, that person cannot explain why this is so.
This is because if these sentient beings grasp at signs with their minds, they immediately become attached to a self, a person, a being, and a life-span.
If one grasps at the characteristics of dharmas, one is attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span. Why is this?

If one grasps at the characteristics of non-dharmas, one is likewise attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span. Therefore, one should not grasp at dharmas, nor should one grasp at non-dharmas.
For this reason, the Tathāgata has constantly said: "O bhikṣus, you should understand my teaching of the Dharma as being like the parable of the raft. The Dharma...
One should abandon even that which is permissible, let alone what is contrary to the Dharma.
One who does not abide in accordance with the realized wisdom within the Dharma is like a person who abandons a boat or raft;
such is the principle regarding the Dharma.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?

Or has the Tathāgata preached any dharma? Subhūti replied, "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no fixed dharma called anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Nor is there any fixed dharma that the Tathāgata could [attain or preach]."
It is said:
"The manifested transformation is not the true Buddha, nor is it the speaker of the Dharma.
Why is this? All that the Tathāgata has taught cannot be grasped and cannot be spoken; it is neither dharma nor non-dharma."
Why is this? Because all noble and holy ones are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Preaching the non-dual Dharma, without grasping, beyond verbal expression—Subhūti, what do you think?
If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and use them...
“Regarding the merit obtained by that person through such giving, would it not be great? Subhūti replied, “It would be very great, World-Honored One.
Why is this? That merit is not the nature of merit; therefore, the Tathāgata says the merit is great.
Furthermore, if there is another person who receives and upholds even as little as a four-line verse from this sutra and explains it to others, their...”
The merit is superior to that. Why is this? Subhūti, all Buddhas and the dharmas of the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas all emerge from this sūtra.
Upholding the Dharma and teaching it are not in vain regarding merit; merit alone does not lead to enlightenment, but these two can lead to enlightenment.
Regarding reality, they are the cause of realization (*pariniṣpatti-hetu*); furthermore, they are the cause for other births.
Only the qualities of a Buddha constitute the supreme essence of merit.
Subhūti, that which is called "Buddha-dharma" is not actually Buddha-dharma;
it cannot be grasped nor can it be described.
Because one does not grasp at one's own fruit, Subhūti, what do you think? Does a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) have the thought, "I have attained the fruit of stream-entry"?
"No," Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? One who is a srotāpanna is called 'one who has entered the stream,' yet there is nothing entered.
They do not enter form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas; therefore they are called a srotāpanna.
Subhūti, what do you think? Does a sakṛdāgāmin have the thought: 'I have attained the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin'? Subhūti [replied, "No"].
He replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? The name 'Sakṛdāgāmin' means 'one who comes back once,' yet in reality there is no coming or going;
it is merely designated as 'Sakṛdāgāmin. Subhūti, what do you think?
Does an Anāgāmin have the thought, 'I have attained the fruit of Anāgāmin'? Subhūti said, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? An Anāgāmin..."
"He is called 'one who does not return' (Anāgāmin), yet in reality there is no such thing as 'not returning. Therefore he is named Anāgāmin.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does an Arhat have the thought: 'I have attained the path of Arhatship'? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Truly, there is no dharma named 'Arhat.
World-Honored One, if an Arhat were to have such a thought as, 'I have attained the path of an Arhat,' he would then be attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
World-Honored One, the Buddha has said that I am foremost among men in attaining the Samādhi of Non-contention; I am the foremost in being free from desire."
"Arhat! World-Honored One, I do not harbor this thought: 'I am an Arhat free from desire.
World-Honored One, if I were to harbor such a thought as 'I have attained the path of Arhatship,' then the World-Honored One would not say that Subhūti is one who delights in the practice of araṇya.
This is because Subhūti, in reality, has nothing to practice; it is for this reason that he is named Subhūti, 'One Who Delights in Araṇya.'"
The practice of Araṇa.
Relying on that Subhūti, [the Buddha] spoke of being free from the two kinds of obstacles.
The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "What do you think? When the Tathāgata was formerly with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, was there any dharma [attained]?"
"Was there anything obtained? "No, World-Honored One. When the Tathāgata was in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he truly obtained nothing regarding the Dharma.
Regarding what the Buddha said to Dīpaṃkara: "He did not grasp at the wisdom of ultimate reality; by means of this true meaning, that teaching of non-grasping is established."
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does a bodhisattva adorn buddha-fields? "No, World-Honored One. Why is this?
That which is called 'adorning a buddha-field' is not actually adorning; it is merely named 'adorning.'"
When wisdom practices the penetration of consciousness-only, one thus takes hold of a pure land. It is not a physical form;
it is the primary essence, not a matter of external adornment.
Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to a pure mind in this way. They should not...
One should not dwell on form when generating the mind; one should not dwell on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena when generating the mind.
One should generate the mind by dwelling nowhere. Subhūti, suppose there were a person whose body was as large as Sumeru, the king of mountains.

What do you think? Would that body be considered large? Subhūti replied, "It would be very large, World-Honored One. Why is this? Because the Buddha has said that what is called 'body' is not a body."
Named "Great Body," like the king of mountains,
it is without grasping; the reception of retribution is likewise so, for it is far removed from all outflows (*āsrava*) and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Subhūti, suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River. What do you think?
Would the grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers be numerous? Subhūti replied: "They would be very numerous, World-Honored One.
Even the Ganges Rivers alone would be countless, let alone their sands. Subhūti, I now tell you this in truth: if...
"Suppose there were good sons or good daughters who, with the seven precious treasures, filled as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers and gave them as a gift.
Would they gain much merit? Subhūti replied, "Very much, World-Honored One.
The Buddha told Subhūti, "If a good son or a good daughter, from within this sutra, were to even receive and uphold four..."
Explaining verses and so forth to others, this merit surpasses the former merit.
By explaining many meanings and distinctions, it also becomes a superior comparison; because the subsequent merit exceeds the former, a superior analogy is stated again.

Furthermore, Subhūti, wherever this sutra is spoken, even as little as a single four-line verse, you should know that this place should be honored by the entire world—including its devas, humans, and asuras—as if it were a stupa or temple of the Buddha.
How much more so for those who are able to fully receive, uphold, read, and recite it? Subhūti, you should know that such persons have accomplished the most supreme and foremost rarity.
The Dharma that exists: wherever this sutra is located, there is a Buddha, as well as honored disciples. One should honor these two places.
At that time, having realized the Great Essence through habitual practice, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what should this sutra be named? How should we uphold it?"
"Uphold it. The Buddha told Subhūti: "This sutra is named the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
By this name, you should uphold it. Why is that? Subhūti, what the Buddha calls *prajñāpāramitā* is not actually *prajñāpāramitā*; it is merely designated as *prajñāpāramitā*."
That [practice] involves the habitual cultivation of afflictions; this [practice] subdues defilements and brings merit.
It surpasses the asceticism of bodily suffering and possesses both rarity and the supreme meaning. That wisdom is an immeasurable shore;
it is unlike other dharmas, for it is firm, solid, and understands the profound meaning. It excels other sūtras in its great cause and its purity.
"Subhūti, among all merits, the merit of this is supreme.
What do you think, Subhūti? Has the Tathāgata preached any dharma? Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has nothing to teach. “Subhūti, what do you think?
Are all the atoms contained within a trichiliocosm many? Subhūti replied, “Very many, World-Honored One.
“Subhūti, those atoms which the Tathāgata speaks of are not atoms; they are called ‘atoms. The world which the Tathāgata speaks of is not a world.”
"This is called a world-system. Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks?
No, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks. Why is this?
The Tathāgata has said that the thirty-two marks are themselves non-marks; they are called the 'thirty-two marks. Subhūti, if..."
If there are sons or daughters of good family who give away their lives as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River in acts of charity, and if there were another person who,
from this sutra, were to receive, uphold, or even recite a four-line verse for others, the latter’s merit would be far greater.
One who is able to endure ascetic practices, for through asceticism there is virtue, their merit is immeasurable.
Such is the supreme meaning: being free from self and malice, truly without suffering, and possessing compassion for shared joy;
such is the fruit of ascetic practice, arising from an undaunted mind.
"Practice and steadfastness constitute the perfection of patience.
At that time, Subhūti, having heard this sutra being preached, deeply understood its meaning and intent; his tears flowed as he wept with grief, and he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is rare, World-Honored One! That the Buddha should preach such a profound sutra as this. From the past until now, the wisdom I have attained..."

“O World-Honored One, I have never before heard such a sutra as this. World-Honored One, if there should be anyone who hears this sutra and their mind of faith becomes pure, they will immediately give rise to the mark of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
You should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and most rare merit.
World-Honored One, this mark of reality is itself a non-mark; therefore, the Tathāgata calls it the ‘mark of reality. World-Honored One, I...”
Now, to hear such a sutra as this and to believe, understand, accept, and uphold it is not difficult.

However, if in a future age, during the final five hundred years, there are sentient beings who hear this sutra and believe, understand, accept, and uphold it, such persons shall be the most rare and extraordinary.
Why is this? Because these people will be without the mark of a self, without the mark of a person, without the mark of a sentient being, and without the mark of a life-span.
...the mark of a self. Why is this? The mark of a self is itself no-mark. The mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, and the mark of a life-span are themselves no-marks.
For what reason? One who is free from all marks is called a Buddha. The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is, so it is.
If there should be anyone who, upon hearing this sutra, is not startled, not terrified, and does not fear, they should..."
Know that this person is most rare. Why is this? Subhūti, what the Tathāgata calls the "foremost pāramitā" is not actually a foremost pāramitā;
it is designated as the "foremost pāramitā. Subhūti, what the Tathāgata calls the "pāramitā of patience" is not actually a pāramitā of patience; it is designated as the "pāramitā of patience. Why?

For this reason, Subhūti, when in the past King Kali severed my limbs and body, at that time I had no perception of a self, no perception of a person, no perception of a sentient being, and no perception of a life-span. Why is this?

If, at the time in the past when my body was cut limb from limb, I had possessed a perception of a self, a perception of a person, a perception of a sentient being, or a perception of a life-span, [anger] would have arisen.
"Subhūti, regarding anger and resentment: furthermore, I recall that in the past, for five hundred lifetimes, I was a rishi practicing patience.
During all those lifetimes, there was no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a sentient being, and no mark of a life-span."
Subhūti, because one must train in that mind capable of learning, a bodhisattva should set out for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi while remaining free from all marks (*nimitta*).
One should not give rise to a mind dwelling on forms; one should not give rise to a mind dwelling on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas. One should...
One gives rise to a mind that dwells nowhere. If the mind has a dwelling, it is not truly dwelling. Therefore, the Buddha said:
"A Bodhisattva’s mind should not dwell upon form when practicing giving. Subhūti, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, a Bodhisattva should practice giving in this manner.
The Tathāgata has said: "All marks are, in truth, no-marks. Furthermore, he has said: "All sentient beings..."
That which is born is not a sentient being;
practicing for the benefit of sentient beings—thus one should understand this.

One should also know that sentient beings and their phenomenal characteristics are far removed; [so too are] conventional designations and the aggregates. The Tathāgata is free from those characteristics.
The Buddhas do not possess those two, because they see the true Dharma. Although the fruit does not abide in the path, the path can serve as its cause.
Subhūti, the Tathāgata is a speaker of truth, a speaker of reality, a speaker of suchness, and a speaker who does not deceive.
Regarding "different words," Subhūti: the Dharma attained by the Tathāgata—this Dharma is neither real nor false.
Because it is the true speech of all Buddhas: That wisdom is of four kinds:
True wisdom, the teachings of the Hīnayāna, The Mahāyāna Dharma, and all predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*); Because they are spoken without falsehood.

In accordance with that true knowledge, it is said to be neither unreal nor false. Subhūti, it is taught as an antidote that one who hears the sound and takes it as a realization should act accordingly:
if a bodhisattva dwells upon dharmas while practicing generosity, they are like a person entering darkness; they have no [vision].

As for what is seen: if a bodhisattva practices giving with a mind that does not dwell on phenomena, it is like a person with eyes who, when the sunlight shines brightly, sees various forms and colors.
Time and place truly exist, yet one does not attain suchness. Through lack of wisdom one dwells in phenomena;
others, possessing wisdom, attain it. As darkness belongs to the ignorant who lack wisdom, so clarity belongs to those with wisdom.
Regarding the Abhidharma and its remedies, the cessation of phenomena is attained in this way: in what dharma should one practice?
"What kind of merit is obtained? Furthermore, what karma is accomplished? Subhūti, in this way it is said regarding practice:

"In a future age, if there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who are able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the Tathāgata, by means of his Buddha-wisdom, fully knows these persons and fully sees these persons. All [of them]...

One shall attain the accomplishment of immeasurable and boundless merit. Subhūti, if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, during the first part of the day, gave as many bodies in charity as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River;
and during the middle part of the day, again gave as many bodies in charity as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River;
and during the latter part of the day, likewise gave as many bodies in charity as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—in this manner, for immeasurable hundreds...

If one were to practice giving away their body as a gift for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, and yet another person were to hear this sutra and have faith without opposition, the latter’s merit would surpass that of the former;
how much more so if they copy it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and explain it to others!
The names consist of three kinds of dharmas: receiving and upholding them, hearing their extensive exposition, and practicing them.

Practice is obtained from others and through internal realization; hearing this constitutes the wisdom of practice. This serves to bring oneself to maturity. As for the rest, it is for transforming sentient beings;
because its activity and timing are vast, it is the most excellent merit among all merits.
Subhūti, to speak in brief, this sutra possesses inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit.
The Tathāgata has taught it for those who have set out upon the Great Vehicle; he has taught it for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle.
If there be anyone who can receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively expound it for others, the Tathāgata knows such a person fully and sees such a person fully. All...
They shall attain the accomplishment of immeasurable, incomparable, boundless, and inconceivable merit.
Such persons as these shall indeed shoulder the burden of the Tathāgata’s *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?
Subhūti, those who delight in inferior dharmas are attached to the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span.
They will be unable to hear, receive, read, recite, or explain this sūtra to others. Subhūti, wherever it may be...
Wherever this sutra exists, it should be honored by all the world—gods, humans, and asuras. You should know that such a place is itself a stupa;
everyone should pay respect, prostrate, circumambulate it, and scatter various flowers and incense upon that spot.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if a son or daughter of good family receives, maintains, reads, and recites this sutra...

They will be treated with contempt by others. Because this person’s karmic offenses from previous lives—which would have caused them to fall into the evil realms—are now extinguished through being treated with contempt by people in the present life, they shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is not the domain of others; it is taught solely for the sake of great beings. By hearing and placing faith in this rare Dharma, one fulfills the unsurpassed realm.
