Kumārajīva’s father was Kumārayāna and his mother’s name was Jīvā; thus, the name was formed by combining these two. His ancestors resided in India, and his family had served as prime ministers for generations. His father...
Renowned for his intelligence and acumen, he abdicated his position to leave the household life and traveled to study in Kucha.

When the King of Kucha heard of him, he compelled his daughter to become his wife, and thus Kumārajīva was born. During the days that Kumārajīva remained in the womb, his mother’s wisdom and eloquence increased, much like the circumstances surrounding Śāriputra’s conception.
Upon Kumārajīva’s birth, his mother immediately left the household life and attained the first fruit of realization. When Kumārajīva was seven years old, she likewise departed.
At home, he received the sūtras from his teacher and recited a thousand verses daily.

At the age of nine, he accompanied his mother to Kaśmīra, where he relied upon the renowned and virtuous Dharma Master Bandhudatta to study the sūtras and śāstras of the Hīnayāna. At twelve years of age, his mother took him back.
Upon reaching the Northern Mountains of the Yuezhi, an arhat beheld him and marveled at him, saying to his mother: "You must guard this child well. As it was said:
He was over thirty-five years old and had not violated his precepts; in converting people, he did not fall short of Kumārajīva.

Had he broken his precepts, he would have been merely a Dharma Master of talent, brilliance, and refined arts. He then proceeded to the kingdom of Śākala, where he beheld the Buddha’s bowl and subsequently carried it upon his head.

Suddenly, he noticed that his alms bowl was heavy; unable to lift it, he let out a cry as he dropped it. His mother asked him the reason for this, and he answered her with the meaning of "mind-only" (cittamātra).
Upon returning to Kucha, his fame eclipsed that of all other nations, reaching even into the four Vedas and the five sciences (pañcavidyāsthāna).
Regarding the arts of yin-yang, astrology, and calculation, there were none whose subtleties he did not fathom or whose profound mysteries he did not exhaust.

Later, he studied the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* under Vimalākṣa and received instruction in the Mahāyāna from Śūryasoma. Only then did he realize that his previous study of the Hīnayāna had been mistaken;
he subsequently devoted himself to the transmission and practice of the Mahāyāna, extensively seeking its essential meanings. After some time, Kumārajīva’s mother foreknew the fate of Kucha.

Fashui took his leave to travel to India, where he advanced to realize the third fruit of the path. As he was about to depart, he said to Kumārajīva, "The profound teachings of the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtras) shall be propagated in the capital of Qin;
however, I fear they may bring some misfortune upon my own person. What can be done? Kumārajīva replied, "The conduct of a Bodhisattva is to benefit others even at the cost of one's life.
If these great transformations can be carried out, I would have no regrets even if I were cast into a cauldron. Thereupon, Fashui remained in Kucha and stayed there.
The King newly established a temple for him. Later, he traveled to Kaśmīra and fully expounded the wondrous meaning of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) for his teacher, Bandhudatta.

Moved by this realization, Bandhudatta returned the courtesy and honored Kumārajīva as his master of the Mahāyāna. From that time on, the Way spread throughout the Western Regions (Sīnyan), and its fame flowed to the Eastern Land of Thunder (Zhèn).
During the ninth year of the Jiànyuán era of Fú Jiān of the Former Qín dynasty in this land, a strange star appeared in the Western Regions.
The Bureau of Astronomy submitted a report, stating: "A man of great virtue and wisdom shall enter to assist the Central Kingdom. Yao Jian asked:
"I have heard that there is Kumārajīva in Kucha and Dao’an in Xiangyang; could it not be these two men?
Thereupon, he first sent for Dao’an, and subsequently dispatched General of the Fierce Cavalry Lü Guang to lead seventy thousand troops to invade Kucha and bring Kumārajīva back.
In Xiliang, when Guang heard that Fu Jian had been assassinated by Yao Chang, he took control of the Liang territory and ascended the throne as the King of the Three Rivers.

Kumārajīva also remained there. When Yao Chang ascended the throne, he too heard of the Master’s reputation and invited him repeatedly; however, Lü Guang did not grant permission. Yao Chang subsequently passed away.
When his son Xing ascended the throne, he again requested [Kumārajīva’s presence], but it was not granted. When Fǎguāng passed away, his son Lóng succeeded him.

Yáo Xīng launched a campaign against Liáng and invited Kumārajīva to Cháng’ān, where he was honored with the rites due to a National Teacher (Guóshī). This was during the third year of the Hóngshǐ era. Thereupon, he examined the previously translated sūtras and śāstras.
For the most part, these did not correspond with the Sanskrit originals.

Consequently, he assembled more than eight hundred śramaṇas and newly translated ninety-eight sūtras and śāstras, totaling three hundred and ninety volumes. Among those translated was this sūtra, titled the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
As Kumārajīva approached his death, he gathered the assembly and said: "Out of my own ignorance, I have mistakenly served as a translator. If [there are errors] in what I have..."
The tradition is unerring. It was said that after his self-immolation, his tongue would remain undestroyed; subsequently, it was indeed so.

Thus we know that the Master’s tongue was no different from the Tathāgata’s mark of the broad and long tongue. This is why, although this sutra has been translated six times, those venerated at various times have all propagated the Qin version.

The present commentary relies upon it. (Having carefully examined the biographies of Master Kumārajīva, the records from antiquity differ. In my previous commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, I pointed out...)

I have followed the *Dacheng* (Great Achievement) as my primary basis. However, upon consulting the *Yijing tuji* (Record of the Translation of Scriptures) and the *Shijiao lu* (Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings), I find that they not only disagree with the *Dacheng*, but even these two works contradict one another. As for the citations in the *Jingangmeng yin* (Introduction to the Diamond Sutra), they are even more difficult to verify.

Since this commentary has been compiled by making selections and adjustments based on the *Tujiji* and the *Jiaolu*, I fear there may be points that are not entirely satisfactory; therefore, I have written this to await the instruction of those of broad learning.
The *Eryuan* (Two Dynasties) was translated by Bodhiruci during the Yuan dynasty of the Later Wei.
The Yuan initially established their capital at Heng’an, then moved south to Luoyang, and later to Ye. There were thirteen emperors in total for a period of one hundred and fifty-five years.
To distinguish this from the earlier Wei of the Cao family, it is called the Yuan Wei. As for Bodhiruci, this... [text continues]
Yun Juexi was a native of Northern India. He was thoroughly versed in the Tripitaka and had attained profound mastery of the dhāraṇīs.
With the resolve to propagate the Dharma and spread its teachings far and wide, he arrived at the capital of Luoyang during the Yongping era of the Wei dynasty.

Emperor Xuanwu issued an imperial decree to welcome him with great courtesy and diligence, lodging him at the Yongning Monastery and providing him with exceptionally generous provisions. Seven hundred Indian monks were likewise supplied with all their needs.

The Emperor decreed that Bodhiruci be the master translator. When he first began translating the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Emperor Xuanwu personally received the oral dictation for the initial chapters;
only thereafter were they entrusted to the śramaṇa Sengbian and others until the entire treatise was completed.

The Buddha-dharma flourished, and eminent scholars gathered in abundance, diligently transmitting the teachings to one another with tireless devotion. From then on, the work of translation continued without interruption until the third year of the Yongxi era.
In the year [of the reign], when the capital was moved from Luoyang to Zhangye, Kumārajīva also arrived in Ye to engage in translation.

This continued for nearly thirty years, beginning from the first year of the Yongping era of Emperor Xuanshu of the Northern Wei (Luoyang) and ending in the second year of the Tianping era of Emperor Xiaojing at the capital of Ye.
The sutras and śāstras he produced during this time total thirty-nine works in one hundred and twenty-seven fascicles. Regarding these translations...
The title of the sutra is the same as the Qin (秦) edition. However, there are five points of difference between them: first, a difference in the introductory questions.

According to the Wei (魏) edition, there are four questions: first, "How does one generate the aspiration for enlightenment? second, "How should one dwell? third, "How does one practice? [and fourth, "What is the fruit of this practice?"]

Regarding the four questions: the Qin edition combines the question on "arousing" with the question on "abiding," while the [other] edition includes the question on "cultivating" within the question on "subduing.
This is because one who is able to abide is able to arouse [the mind], and one who is able to subdue it is able to cultivate it. Second, there is a difference regarding presence or absence;
for in the latter half of the volume of the Wei edition, there is the passage beginning with "At that time, the Venerable Subhūti... and continuing until "sentient beings."
Regarding the phrase "sentient beings," the Tathāgata has said they are not sentient beings; this is what is called "sentient beings.

This passage does not exist in the Qin edition and was later supplemented based on a stone inscription from Xiangyang; it appears to be an omission in Master Kumārajīva’s translation. Third, the answers to the questions differ.
In the latter half of the Qin version, there is a passage where the Buddha asks Subhūti, "Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks?
to which Subhūti replies, "So it is, so it is; the Tathāgata can be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks.
However, in the Wei version, he replies, "He cannot be seen by means of the marks. This was likely because Master Liu merely followed the preceding text.

One does not realize that there are differences between the earlier and later versions of the *Śūnyatā-saptati*. Although this is the case for all four subsequent translations, the original commentary (*Ben-shu*) considers the Qin version to be the correct one.
There are two points where these four versions differ in their degree of detail. The first is in the Wei version’s verse, which says:
"If one views me by form, or seeks me by sound," and so on, up to: "The essence of the Dharma cannot be seen; that consciousness cannot know it."

There are eight lines in total. The Qin version (the *Damingzhou jing*) takes only the first four lines. This is because, within the eight lines, the first four serve as a negative illustration (*pratipakṣa*), while the latter four provide the positive exposition.
The other four translations all follow the Wei version. Master Kumārajīva, however, considered that the negative illustration was sufficient to clarify the meaning;
thus, he omitted the latter portion. The verse in the two Qin versions reads: "All conditioned phenomena are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, and a shadow; they are like dew..."

It is also like lightning; one should contemplate it in this way. There are only six metaphors here, whereas the Wei edition contains nine. The other four versions likewise follow the Wei translation.
Master Kumārajīva considered that although the six metaphors are brief, they can encompass all phenomena in terms of their underlying meaning.

Although the nine metaphors are detailed, in terms of their meaning they do not go beyond these [six]. Furthermore, as the four-line [verse] would be difficult to accommodate, he did not take them all. This is the fifth point established.
Regarding the division into sections (*varga*), there is no agreement on whether to establish such divisions. The Wei version divides this sutra into twelve sections;

however, none of the five earlier translations established such divisions. The current Qin version’s thirty-two sections were actually established by Prince Zhaoming of the Liang dynasty. Apart from these five versions...
There are still some minor differences [between the versions], but the meaning is largely the same; thus, they are not described in detail.
Third, regarding the translation by Paramārtha of the Chen dynasty:
when the Chen family took control of the court, the capital was Jianye. It began from the first year of Emperor Wu’s Yongding era and ended with the reign of Emperor Houzhu’s Zhengming.

The Ming dynasty lasted for three years, under five successive emperors, totaling thirty-three years. There were three monastics and laypersons who translated the scriptures, one of whom was Paramārtha.
His Sanskrit name was Paramārtha. He was originally a native of Ujjayinī in Western India, of Brahmin descent, and his clan name was Bharadvāja.
His conduct was pure and luminous, his bearing was serene and dignified, and his spirit was noble and refined; he lived in a state of tranquil self-possession.

Far-reaching were his concerns for the vast sections of the various *piṭakas*, leaving nothing to which he did not direct his devotion. His resolve was set upon propagating and disseminating [the teachings] to benefit sentient beings according to their respective capacities.

In the second year of the Taiching era of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, he arrived at the capital, where the Emperor personally extended him homage and respect, and he was installed in the Baoyun Hall.

From then on, he devoted himself to transmitting and translating the scriptural teachings; he did not envy those who presented their works to the court, but rather produced new texts that surpassed those of the Qi dynasty.

Before long, however, the Liang dynasty fell into chaos at its end, and his aspirations were not fulfilled. Although he continued to translate scriptures, he lived in a state of restless wandering without a fixed residence.

It was not until the second year of the Yongding era of Emperor Wu of the Chen dynasty that he returned to Yuzhang. He subsequently traveled through the various prefectures of Linchuan and Jin’an; though he continued to transmit the scriptures, [the circumstances remained difficult].
The Treatise states: Because his path was incomplete and his mind detached from worldly affairs, he intended to board a ship and travel to the Kingdom of Laṅkā.
Laypeople and monastics earnestly entreated him, binding themselves by oath to detain him, so that he temporarily remained in Nan Yue.

In the fourth year of the Tianjia era of Emperor Wen, monks such as Sengzong, Fahuai, and Sengren traveled far from Jianye to the region south of the Yangtze River to personally seek an audience with him. Delighted by the sincerity of his purpose, they requested him to translate [the scriptures].
He brought with him treatises such as the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, carrying them from beginning to end. Later, upon reaching An County in the Liang state, he intended to return to the Western Regions;

however, at the request of the Prefect Wang Wansha, he stayed temporarily in this coastal region. Subsequently, as he was sailing westward on a ship, he encountered a gale and was driven back to Guangzhou.
There, he happened to meet the Regional Inspector, Duke Ou-yang Wei, who invited him to reside at Zhizhi Temple and requested that he revise the new translations.

Paramārtha looked back upon his karmic conditions and realized there was no way to return to the West; he then, in the presence of the śramaṇa Huikai and others, translated the *Vipula-artha-dharmaparyāya-sūtra*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, and other works.
Later, when Duke Mu passed away, his son Xi served as a patron (*dānapati*) once again, continuing the translation work.
According to records, the sūtras and śāstras produced by Paramārtha during the Liang dynasty total eleven works. At the end of the Liang, he entered the Chen dynasty, where he further...
Thirty-eight sections were produced. Regarding the translation of this sutra, its title is identical to the Qin (秦) edition. However, there are four points of difference in the text:

first, the differences in the questions posed. While the Qin edition contains only two questions—the first asking how one should abide, and the second asking how to subdue the mind—the Chen (陳) edition contains three questions, adding a third that asks how to generate the bodhicitta and practice as a bodhisattva.
1. How should one abide in the vehicle? 2. How should one practice? 3. How does one give rise to the bodhicitta?

In other versions, the third question is "How does one subdue the mind. It is likely that the *Zhendi* (Paramārtha) school erroneously interpreted "subduing the mind" as "giving rise to the mind," for these two differ.
This occurs in two places: first, within the first half of the Qin version, it says: "From the time of antiquity, regarding me..."
Regarding the passage "The eye of wisdom attained has never before heard such a sutra as this," there is no further explanatory text in the lower [versions].
The Chen edition adds: "For what reason? The World-Honored One speaks of the *prajñāpāramitā*, yet it is not the *prajñāpāramitā*;
therefore it is called *prajñāpāramitā*. These three phrases appear in the Chen edition; the Wei edition contains only the first two phrases, while the other editions contain none at all.
There is no [“no”]. It is suspected that this is a scribal interpolation. In two places, it agrees with the Wei version; this constitutes a difference regarding presence or absence.

Regarding the third point, the answers to the questions differ. This also occurs in two places: one agrees with the Wei version, while the second—found in the Qin version immediately after the verse “If one sees me by means of form”—directly states:
“Subhūti, if you should think that the Tathāgata is attained through the possession of marks...”
In the section on Bodhi, there is no separate text in the middle [of the Sanskrit version]. However, the Chen (Southern Qi) edition adds the passage: "Subhūti, what do you think?
Can a Tathāgata attain Bodhi by means of the marks of perfection? and so forth, up to: "A Tathāgata does not attain Bodhi by means of the marks of perfection.

This was likely because the Tathāgata had previously stated that he cannot be apprehended through form or sought through sound; fearing that [the audience] might still cling to this [notion], [he spoke as follows].

This would fall into the view of nihilism; therefore, it is said that one must urgently sweep this away. As for the passage beginning "If you should have such a thought," etc., [the author] disregards the fact that this refers to the True Dharma (satyadharma) and forcibly attempts to join it with the preceding meaning.
I have set aside this section and instead consider the translation by Kumārajīva to be correct. Regarding the fourth point, the differences in detail and brevity are the same as in the Wei edition.
Beyond these, there are minor variations while the general substance remains largely the same; I shall not detail them all.

"Four: Translated by Dharmagupta of the Sui Dynasty. "Sui" is the dynastic name of the state of Yang. It was the designation for the reign of the Yang family. It began with Emperor Wen and ended with Emperor Yang;

the two rulers together held power for thirty-seven years. Emperor Wen’s surname was Yang and his given name was Jian. He was a native of Huayin County in Hongnong. His father was Yang... [text continues]
Zhong served the Northern Zhou dynasty with merit and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Sui. Upon Zhong’s death, Jian succeeded him to the title.
He later ascended the throne following the Zhou, established his capital at Chang’an, and named his state the Great Sui; thus it is called the Sui Dynasty. *Jītā* is an abbreviated form;
its full name is *Dharmagupta*, which translates as “Dharma-Secret. He was a member of the Kṣatriya caste from the country of Lāḍha in South India, and his clan name was Hu.
He was twenty-three years old when he went to a monastery with yellow-flowered *kārṣika* trees outside the city in Central India and left the household life.
At twenty-five, he finally received full ordination (*upasampadā*). After receiving ordination, he traveled extensively through the various Mahayana and Hinayana countries of the Western Regions.
He was widely learned and possessed vast knowledge; his mastery of the arts and disciplines was fully developed within.

Later, while in the kingdom of Kāpiśī, he encountered merchants from the northern route who spoke of the Great Country of China (Mahācīna), where the Three Jewels flourished. He then entered into an agreement with them to travel there.
After years of arduous travel across many kingdoms, he continued to lecture and expound upon the teachings wherever he went. In the tenth year of the Kaihuang era, he arrived at Guazhou. At first...
His companions shared his resolve; some remained while others perished, leaving him alone with but a solitary shadow. Grief and joy welled up within him simultaneously.

Soon thereafter, by imperial decree, he was invited to the capital and stationed at a renowned monastery, where he was provided with abundant and generous supplies. Initially, he worked together with Kumārajīva to assist in the translation work.
However, toward the end of the Renshou era, Kumārajīva was exiled to Dongyue due to other matters. From that time on, [Daotai] took sole charge of the transmission and translation.
When Emperor Yang established his capital at the Eastern Metropolis (Luoyang), his reverence for him grew even more profound.
He issued an imperial decree to establish a Translation Hall within the Shanglin Garden on the southern bank of the Luo River.

From the beginning of the Daye era until its final year, he translated nine works totaling forty-six fascicles, including the *Mahāvaipulya-suvikrāntavikrami-paripṛcchā-sūtra* and the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

Furthermore, its phrasing and meaning are lucid and pure, and its elegance and substance are clearly expressed. Now, examining the *Shijiao lu* (Record of the Translation of the Teachings), the name of this sutra does not appear among the nine divisions [of the canon].

Only the records of Yancong and Jñānagupta state that, initially, Jñānagupta translated one fascicle of the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and fifteen fascicles of the *Pulue jing* (Universal Joy Sutra);
however, before they could be revised and finalized, they encountered the collapse of the state under the illegitimate Zheng dynasty and were consequently lost.
There was no opportunity for further revision. Based on this, it appears that later generations sought out and transmitted the text;
because they had made errors in their editorial cuts and revisions, they replaced "Nengduan" (Able to Cut) with "Jingang" (Vajra), titling it the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

When translated to match the Sanskrit original, the phrasing was often inverted. Although the meaning did not deviate from the Buddha’s intent, the style became contrary to the needs of the times, and the sentences were moreover difficult [to comprehend].

Upon investigation, the meaning remains largely unintelligible. This is likely because, as Yancong remarked, it had not yet undergone refinement or revision and lacked the opportunity for further editing.
Nevertheless, when compared with other versions, they are all slightly different yet largely identical. These have been preserved in the canon for the sake of comprehensive reference;
should there be doubts regarding other versions that remain unresolved, one may consult them for corroboration. Thus, their merit shall not be forgotten, and this [text] is omitted here.
Postscript: Translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty.
The Great Tang was ruled by the Li clan, with its capital at Chang’an. From the first year of Gaozu’s Wude era until the eighteenth year of Kaiyuan.

Together with the reigns of the Empress Wu, this amounts to one hundred and thirteen years. There were thirty-seven monastics and laypeople who translated scriptures, of whom Xuanzang alone was the most eminent.
Xuanzang’s original name was Huì; his secular surname was Chen, and he was a native of Chenliu. He was a descendant of Chen Zhonggong, the Grand Master of Taqiu during the Han dynasty.
His great-grandfather, Qin, served as the Governor of Shangdang under the Later Wei. His grandfather, Kang, served the State of Northern Qi.
The Master was a *ziduō* (hereditary scholar). His fief was in Zhounan, and his descendants settled there; he was also a native of Guoshi County.

His father, Huì, was brilliant, pure, and possessed refined integrity. During the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, he was appointed Magistrate of Jiangling, but he cast off his official sash and returned home. He had four sons.
I was the youngest. My elder brother, Changjie, entered the monastic order first and resided at Jingtu Monastery in the Eastern Capital (Luoyang).

Because I had suffered extreme hardship at a young age, he took me with him to support and encourage me. At eleven years of age, I received full ordination. Subsequently, the Sui dynasty lost its rule.
The world was in turmoil. Accompanied by his brothers, he arrived at the capital and resided at Zhuangyan Monastery.

By the first year of the Wude era of the Tang dynasty, the foundations of the state were still being laid and military conflict persisted; consequently, there were no lecture halls for Buddhist study in the capital.

Furthermore, as his elder brother had entered Shu, he followed him to attend lectures at various seats of learning. Upon reaching the age of twenty, he received full ordination in Chengdu. Thereafter, he traveled extensively to consult with various masters.
Fang fully exhausted the purport of his teachings. He then reflected to himself: "I have traveled throughout the regions of Wu and Shu, and as far as Zhao and Wei;

I have not yet reached Zhou and Qin. Whenever I encountered a lecture hall, I invariably attended. Although what has already been spoken is spread abroad, that which remains accumulated within my breast—those words not yet uttered—I have no place to unravel their meaning.
If I do not disregard my life and sacrifice my destiny, vowing to go to Huaxu, how could I [attain this]?"
Having fully beheld the perfected words and employed them to penetrate his divine understanding, he then, in the third year of the Zhenguan era, resolved to journey westward.

He traveled far through many kingdoms; his sincerity was profound and his toil slight, traversing perilous terrain as if it were level ground. Upon reaching the land of India, he consulted and deliberated without weariness.
He took Śīlabhadra as his teacher, refuting erroneous views through debate. The scholars of India all looked up to his magnificent virtue, and they engaged in discussion with him for seventeen years.

He traveled through more than one hundred countries. On the twenty-fourth day of the first month in the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era of this land, he returned to the capital and had an audience with the Emperor at the Luoyang Palace.
They discussed matters pertaining to both the ultimate and conventional truths, and his words did not contradict the Emperor’s intentions.
The Emperor said, "Since your departure, I have established Hongfu Monastery in the Western Capital on behalf of Empress Dowager Mu for her future [rebirth]."

Having received the imperial decree that the Sanskrit manuscripts could be translated, he subsequently returned to the Western Capital (Chang’an). He gathered more than fifty eminent and virtuous śramaṇas, including Lingrun, who were renowned for their profound learning.
Beginning in the fifth month of that same year, he commenced the oral exposition of the Sanskrit texts and translated the *Mahābodhisattvapiṭaka* and other sūtras and śāstras.
From then on, the translation work continued without interruption until the first year of the Linde era.
In total, he produced seventy-five works comprising one thousand three hundred and thirty-five fascicles from the sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
Among these, the sūtra translated here is titled *The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā that Cuts Off [Delusion]*; it is similar to the version from the Qin dynasty.
It contains three questions: first, how one should abide; second, how one should practice; and third, how one should collect the mind.

In general, both "comprehending" (*saṃgraha*) and "subduing" (*nigraha*) carry the meaning of taming and subjugating. However, there is one additional question inserted in the middle; furthermore, while the Qin version speaks only of four aspects (*lakṣaṇa*), this version speaks of eight perceptions (*saṃjñā*).

These are: the perception of a sentient being (*sattva-saṃjñā*), the perception of a life-principle (*jīva-saṃjñā*), the perception of a person (*pudgala-saṃjñā*), the perception of an individual (*manuja-saṃjñā*), the perception of a mind-born (*manomaya-saṃjñā*), the perception of a youth (*māṇava-saṃjñā*), the perception of an agent (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*), and the perception of an experiencer (*vedaka-saṃjñā*). In essence, the aspect (*lakṣaṇa*) is that which is perceived (*saṃjñeya*); it is merely a matter of [the number of] aspects.

The four and eight [syllables] differ slightly in their opening and closing. Furthermore, while the Qin version states that "Tathāgata" means the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena, here it says that "Tathāgata" is a synonym for true *tathatā*, and a synonym for the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) which is non-arising.
This is a synonym for the path of eternal severance; it is a synonym for ultimate non-arising.
It differs from the Qin edition’s response and questions, yet it accords with the Wei edition. Furthermore, the verse on "seeing forms and seeking sounds" also consists of eight lines.

The prose added after the verse also differs slightly from the Chen edition. The nine similes in the subsequent verse also accord with the Wei edition. All other parts are largely identical to the Qin edition.
The original [text] contains an excess of flowery and elaborate phrasing; it seems not as direct and straightforward as the version by Kumārajīva, which makes it more pleasant for readers to enjoy.
Sixth, the translation by the Dharma Master Yijing of the Tang dynasty:

Yijing was a native of Qizhou. His secular surname was Zhang, and his courtesy name was Wenming. At the age of seven, he took leave of his parents to enter the monastic life. He traveled extensively...

He consulted renowned masters and extensively explored the various scriptures. Admiring the elegant integrity of Faxian and emulating the lofty character of Xuanzang, he harbored the ambition to travel westward;
yet, he was unable to fulfill this wish. Upon reaching the age of ordination, he vowed that he would certainly go.
Thus, in the second year of the Xianxiang era, at the age of thirty-seven, he first gathered like-minded companions until their number reached ten. Finally, they embarked upon the ship.
The others all withdrew and desisted; only Jingjianxin remained, exerting his will to travel alone. Having endured every hardship and peril, he gradually reached the land of India.

In every region he visited, he was thoroughly proficient in the local languages; wherever he encountered kings or ministers, he was universally honored with respect. He personally beheld the sacred sites of the Buddha’s realm:
Vulture Peak, Cock’s Foot Mountain, the Deer Park, Jetavana Garden, and other holy traces. He rested at Nālandā and paid homage at the Bodhi tree.
Throughout his travels, he visited more than thirty countries, traveling back and forth to seek the Way for over twenty years.
In the second month of summer in the year of Yiwei (665 CE), during the Zhengsheng era of Empress Wu Zetian, he returned to the region of the Yellow River and Luo River.

He brought with him nearly four hundred volumes of Sanskrit scriptures, including the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras, as well as one set of portraits of the Vajrāsana and three hundred grains of śarīra relics. Empress Wu, who revered the Dharma and esteemed worthy men, [received him with great honor].
He was escorted in person outside the Upper East Gate; the monastics and laypeople of Luoyang prepared banners and streamers in full array, while drums and music were set forth to lead the way.
By imperial decree, the Sanskrit manuscripts he brought were to be housed at Foshouji Temple and translated.
Initially, he collaborated with the Khotanese Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda to translate the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. It was only after the Jiushi era that he began translating on his own.
Translated. Commenced in the first year of the Jiushi era of Empress Wu (Gengzi), and concluded in the second year of the Jingyun era of Emperor Ruizong (Xinhsi).

Translated across various locations including Fuxian Monastery, Ximing Monastery, and Jianfu Monastery, a total of fifty-six works comprising two hundred and thirty fascicles were produced from the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras.
This particular sūtra translated here bears the same title as the version by Xuanzang, beginning with the "Inquiry."
The location [of the text] is also the same. That which differs from the Qin version is as follows:
below the passage "Wherever this scripture is located, there is a Buddha and his honored disciples," the Qin version contains a separate section titled "Requesting the Name and Upholding it.
The four versions—the Wei, Chen, Sui, and Xuanzang—are largely identical. This version, however, proceeds directly to the teaching on the non-existence of the world of dust (*rajas*).
The passage beginning with "It is not a realm" and continuing through "the manifestation of signs is not like signs" is intended for the request for the name and its upholding;

however, it has been moved to the section following the weeping upon hearing the sutra and the lamentation over not having heard it before. The underlying intention is likely this: since the preaching of the sutra had not yet long occurred, it would have been inappropriate to suddenly request the name.
It must therefore be that Subhūti himself laments that he has never before heard this sutra, and because he realizes it is extraordinary, he thus makes the request.
Question: Although this may seem reasonable, it contradicts the five translations; I fear it is merely a personal conjecture and not the Buddha’s original intent.

Furthermore, in the Qin version, following the verse on "seeking the sound in form," there is a warning against forming such thoughts—namely, that the Tathāgata does not attain bodhi by means of the marks of perfection—out of fear that [the practitioner] might give rise to the view of annihilationism.
Regarding the "Bodhicitta" [chapter], it is said that all dharmas are subject to cessation.

While this appears to accord with reason as it connects the preceding and following sections, the four versions—the Wei, Chen, Sui, and Xuanzang—each add supplementary text and differ slightly from one another; yet even these agree largely. However, when reaching this particular passage, the current version directly asks:
"For those who have set out on the Bodhisattva vehicle, are their dharmas subject to cessation? Since this does not correspond with Kumārajīva’s translation, [it is clear they are distinct].
Upon examining other editions, it appears they also contain omissions. As for the remaining textual meaning, it is largely identical to Xuanzang’s edition;
however, by excising redundant phrasing, it more fully captures the subtle excellence of Master Kumārajīva. Thus concludes the translation from beginning to end.
Second, regarding the proclamation of the time and place: since the Tathāgata’s Dharma is not bestowed indiscriminately, it is taught according to the capacity of the recipient.
As capacities have degrees of ripeness, there is a sequence in the teaching. Therefore, the holy teachings of the entire life of the Buddha are divided into three periods.

During the first period, at the time when the sun first rises and shines, for the sake of sentient beings of great, sudden, and perfect faculties, he turned the unsurpassed fundamental wheel of Dharma; this is called the "Direct" [Teaching].
The Manifest Teaching causes those of the Shared One Vehicle to transform their shared status into that of the Distinct [Vehicle].
It is like the rising sun, which first illuminates the great high mountains such as Mount Sumeru. The sutras taught therein are the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Brahmajāla*, and others.
On the second day, when the sun rises and shines, it first illuminates in general and then specifically.

As for the general illumination: at this time of shining forth, for the sake of sentient beings of the three categories—lower, middle, and superior—it turns the Dharma-wheel that originates from the fundamental to manifest the derivative;
this is called the teaching of skillful means (*upāya*). It causes those followers of the Three Vehicles to transform the three into one, just as mountains and earth [are transformed by the sun].
There are distinctions of high and low; therefore, there is a sequence of priority in illumination. As for the differentiation:
within this single moment, it is further divided into three turnings, namely, the initial turning, the middle turning, and the final turning.

Regarding the "initial turning": this refers to when the Buddha first turned the wheel of the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) at the Deer Park for sentient beings of dull faculties and inferior class.
This is called the "hidden teaching of reality" (*tirobhūta-satya-dharma*), which causes those ordinary people and non-Buddhists to transform their mundane state into the state of a sage.
It is like the rising sun casting its light upon the Black Mountains. The sūtras spoken at that time are the *Dīrgha Āgama* and others. Regarding the "middle turning"...
This refers to the Buddha’s subsequent turning of the wheel of the Dharma during the middle period for those sentient beings of middling faculties belonging to one class;

this is called the "Teaching of Attraction," which causes those followers of the two vehicles to transform the small [vehicle] into the great. It is, for example, like the rising sun first illuminating the high plateaus.
The sūtras he taught therein are precisely the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, the *Vaipulya*, and so forth. As for the "subsequent turning of the period," it refers to the Buddha...
Subsequently, for the sake of sentient beings of superior faculties and highest capacity, he turned the wheel of the Mahāyāna Dharma, which is called the Teaching of Harmonious Integration.

This caused those of the three vehicles of the provisional teachings to transform their provisional [attainments] into the real. It is like the rising sun, which subsequently shines universally upon the entire earth;
the sūtras he preached therein are precisely the *Sūtra of Sublime Wisdom*, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and so forth.

The third [period], when the sun has set but shines once more, is for sentient beings of the highest of the high faculties. It is the Dharma-wheel that turns to gather the branches back into the root, known as the teaching of the "Opening and Assembly" (*kaikai*).
It causes those people of the five vehicles who followed partial teachings to transform their partiality into perfection.
This is like the setting sun shining again upon the high mountains. The sutras spoken therein are precisely the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (Lotus Sūtra), the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, and others.
However, since this sutra belongs to the Prajñāpāramitā class, it should have been spoken during the latter period of the Buddha’s teaching. Yet, there are eight divisions of the Prajñāpāramitā:

the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* (Large Version), the *Svalpaprajñāpāramitā* (Small Version), the *Prabhāsa* (Emitting Light), the *Prasphulla* (Radiant Praise), the *Mārgacaryā* (Practice of the Path), the *Devarāja-vikrīḍita* (Victorious Heavenly King), the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā* (Inquiry of Mañjuśrī), and the *Vajracchedikā* (Diamond).

The Tang translation consists of six hundred fascicles, spoken across four locations and sixteen assemblies. First, at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha, there were seven assemblies (within the mountain...).
There are four assemblies (the summit of the mountain being three assemblies). Second, seven assemblies at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī;
third, one assembly in the Maṇiratnagarbha Hall in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; fourth, one assembly beside the Śarabhañjaka Pond in the Bamboo Grove Park at Rājagṛha.

This sutra belongs to the ninth assembly of the second location. It consists of five hundred and seventy-seven fascicles and is circulated as a single, separate work, commonly known throughout the world.
This is seen. The text appears in the *Mahāvaipulya* [sūtras], yet there are those who do not know this; therefore, I shall analyze it here to make its origins and details fully clear.
Other sections that circulate separately should also be understood according to this principle. Only the single volume of the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is not included among them.

Nevertheless, since the time and place are already clearly established and the teaching was uttered from the golden mouth [of the Buddha], relying on this for translation makes it especially trustworthy.
Third, regarding the classification of the teachings and vehicles (*śāsana-yāna-vibhāga*), there are two parts: first, the differentiation of the teachings; second, the division of the vehicles.

As for the differentiation of the teachings: among the various schools that propagated and elucidated the sacred teachings throughout the generations within the Western Regions and the Eastern Land (China), some have combined them into a single teaching, while others have divided them into two or three, and further divisions have resulted in four or five.
Including both monastics and laypeople, there are in total eighteen such systems.

Within the [Huayan] school, Master Jia [Fazang] followed the correct path while Master Yi [Huiyuan] deviated from it; thus, it is difficult to exhaustively critique other traditions. In terms of both the refinement of facts and the completeness of principle, none surpasses Xianshou (Fazang).
Therefore, relying upon the various patriarchs of the Xianshou school, I shall briefly describe the five teachings.

The first is the Hīnayāna teaching, also called the "Teaching for the Two Vehicles of Dull Capacity. It is so named because it differs from the Mahāyāna, because it is established according to the capacities of beings, and because it follows the words of others.

It teaches that the categories of all phenomena are exclusively distinct, as it distinguishes between the heterodox and the orthodox, differentiates between the noble and the ordinary, clarifies cause and effect, and divides between what is to be rejoiced in and what is to be loathed.
Nevertheless, the number of dharmas taught therein is only seventy-five; it speaks only of the emptiness of persons, and not...
Regarding the elucidation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*): although the emptiness of phenomena is taught, it is for the most part not clearly explained.

By establishing the roots of defilement and purity solely based on the six consciousnesses and the three poisons, the ultimate source of phenomena is not fully exhausted; therefore, much dispute and contention arise.

Second is the Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna, also called the Partial Teaching (*bheda-śāsana*). It merely clarifies that all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty, yet it does not exhaustively reveal the fundamental principles of the Mahāyāna;
therefore, it is termed "Initial. It merely clarifies the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, asserting that some attain Buddhahood while others do not;

therefore, it is termed "Partial. It discusses the characteristics of phenomena extensively but only slightly touches upon the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); even the "nature" it mentions is merely a category of characteristics, as it teaches [the existence of] things.
The One Hundred Dharmas are decisively determined and clearly distinguished; thus, there is little room for dispute.
Third is the Final Teaching, also called the True Teaching. This refers to the elucidation that dependent origination is without self-nature and that all things are suchness (tathatā).

It maintains that those of fixed nature among the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, as well as the icchantikas who lack the Buddha-nature, shall all eventually attain Buddhahood. Because it exhausts the ultimate discourse of the Mahāyāna, it is so named.

It concludes by conforming to the principle of reality; therefore, it is called "Real. It discusses the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) extensively and touches upon the *dharma-lakṣaṇa* (phenomenal characteristics) only sparingly.
Even the characteristics it mentions ultimately converge back into the nature. Thus, encompassing the entirety of Mahāyāna teachings, it is free from contentious debate.

Fourth is the Sudden Teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). It holds that when not a single thought arises, one is immediately called a Buddha; it does not teach according to the gradual progression of stages (*bhūmi*).

As the *Siyi jing* (Saṃghadeva’s translation of the *Saṃgharakṣita-sūtra*) says: "One who attains the true nature of all phenomena does not proceed from one stage to another. The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* says:
"The first stage is itself the eighth," and so on, up to "what sequence can there be where nothing exists? Since this is not the same [as the gradual teaching], [it is the sudden teaching].
The preceding gradual cultivation is also not the same as the subsequent perfect integration of all virtues; therefore, it is designated as "Sudden.

It does not speak of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) at all, but only discriminates true nature (*tathatā*). All that exists is merely deluded thought (*parikalpita*); the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is beyond words.

The five factors (name, appearance, deluded thought, correct wisdom, and suchness), the three natures (dependent origination, deluded thought, and perfected reality), and the eight consciousnesses and two non-selves are all empty.

I dispatch both [methods]. I reprimand, instruct, and exhort them to depart from [attachment], so that they may destroy the marks [of phenomena] and obliterate the mind. To give rise to a mind is delusion; not giving rise to it is Buddhahood.
Furthermore, there is neither Buddha nor non-Buddha, neither arising nor non-arising—just as Vimalakīrti remained silent, and so forth.

This is for the sake of a specific class of practitioners whose faculties are free from discursive thought, and also to serve as an antidote for those three types of people who cling to marks and maintain both emptiness and existence.
Fifth is the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). It universally encompasses the preceding four teachings, being complete and perfect. A single stage is all stages; all stages are a single stage.
At the fulfillment of the ten levels of faith, one subsumes the five stages to achieve Equal and Right Enlightenment; therefore, it is called "Perfect.

What is taught is exclusively the inexhaustible Dharma-realm, wherein the ocean of nature is perfectly interfused, dependent origination is unimpeded, and phenomena mutually identify with and enter one another, as follows:
Like Indra’s net, it is infinitely layered and boundless; its subtle elements are mutually inclusive, and its primary and attendant aspects are inexhaustible.
Each of the tenfold dharma-gates individually encompasses the entire dharma-realm.

This present sutra primarily belongs to the Initial Teaching (*śāstra*), as the *Prajñāpāramitā* generally pertains to the School of Emptiness (*śūnyatāvāda*). It also concurrently belongs to the Final and Sudden Teachings.
For instance, it says: "This Dharma is equal; there is no high or low. Since there is neither high nor low, all sentient beings shall surely attain Buddhahood;
this is the meaning of the Final Teaching. Furthermore, it says: "To be free from all marks is itself called Buddha. Since...
To be free from marks is itself Buddhahood; thus, it is not taught according to the gradual sequence of stages and positions, but rather represents the meaning of the Sudden Teaching.
If one preaches the Dharma with a single voice, yet beings understand it each according to their own kind, this also pertains to the Perfect Teaching, as it is said:
"One should know that the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable, and its karmic fruit and retribution are likewise inconceivable."

Regarding the classification of vehicles (*yāna*): this refers to the fact that the teachings and their meanings vary from shallow to profound, and the capacities of those to whom they are addressed range from superior to inferior.

When divided with subtle precision, the categories are indeed numerous; however, summarizing them broadly, there are three types of vehicle practice: first, the Śrāvaka-yāna, which relies upon the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
With earnest diligence, they desire to quickly escape the triple world and seek nirvana for themselves; this is like the sheep cart. Second, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle:

relying on the law of causes and conditions, they practice with earnest diligence to seek spontaneous wisdom, delighting in solitary tranquility and deeply understanding the causes and conditions of all phenomena;
this is like the deer cart. Third, the Mahāyāna: spoken in contrast to the two aforementioned "small" vehicles, it is also called the Bodhisattva vehicle.
Relying on the Dharma of the six perfections, one diligently cultivates vigor to seek all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and so forth, benefiting devas and humans and delivering all beings.

This is like the ox-cart. However, there are both the provisional (*upāya*) and the real (*tattva*). If practice dwells upon signs (*nimitta*), such that cause and effect are distinct and separate, it is called the provisional.
If cultivation is without dwelling, such that cause and effect are all-pervasive and thorough, it is called the real. This sutra belongs to the Bodhisattvas.

The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* is subsumed under one portion of the reality [of the Prajñāpāramitā]. This is because the two successive inquiries posed by Ākāśagarbha both arise for the sake of those who have generated the bodhicitta.
Furthermore, throughout the sutra, it fully demonstrates the meaning of subduing the mind and departing from signs, as well as the principle of abiding in the non-abiding of the mind.

Furthermore, beyond the Three Vehicles, by adding the Human and Celestial vehicles at the beginning and appending the Buddha Vehicle at the end, they are called the Five Vehicles. Regarding the Human and Celestial Vehicles:

relying on the methods of precepts, wholesome deeds, and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one seeks the five desires of the lower realms as well as the pure and subtle pleasures of the upper realms.

This is like the smallest vehicle (as the *Fire House Parable* in the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "Even if not a single smallest vehicle were given, it would still not be a falsehood," which is a metaphor for the Human and Celestial vehicles). Regarding the Buddha [Vehicle]...
As for the "vehicle" (*yāna*): it relies upon the flowers of the causes of the ten thousand practices to adorn the fruit of the path of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), like the great white ox-cart.

This sutra belongs to the inclusion of the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*). As the text says: "For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, a bodhisattva should practice giving (*dāna*) in this way"—wherein *dāna* encompasses the ten thousand practices.
It further says: "This sutra is taught for those who have set out in the Supreme Vehicle. If one takes this [the One Vehicle] to subsume that [the Buddha-vehicle], [it is as follows].
Although neither humans nor devas are excluded, because this Dharma is equal and possesses no high or low, all sentient beings shall attain Buddhahood.
Other points may be inferred accordingly. This concludes the section on the classification of the vehicles of teaching.

Fourth, regarding that which is brought about by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*): this refers to the extensive teaching of the profound vehicle (*yāna*), which is sufficient to evoke deep reflection. One re-examines the causes and conditions to support superior understanding (*adhimukti*).

Now, there are two types of causes and conditions: the general and the specific. The general refers to the fact that throughout the Tathāgata’s holy teachings of his entire life, there is nothing that is not for the sake of the one great cause and condition (*ekamahā-kṛtya-hetu-pratyaya*).
That is to say, it is intended to cause sentient beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha-...
Regarding the knowledge and vision: specifically, this sutra briefly sets forth ten kinds of causes and conditions.
The first is to demonstrate the methods for subduing the mind and causing it to abide; for indeed, the power of the awakened mind and the deluded mind is like that of a loyal minister and a rebel.
If the deluded mind is not subdued, the awakened mind is difficult to stabilize; if the awakened mind does not abide, the deluded mind is difficult to subdue.
Therefore, the awakened mind must abide and the deluded mind must be subdued. To this end, both are shown together so that by attaining one, both are accomplished.

It is like when the World-Honored One enters the city at mealtime and returns to his dwelling after begging for food: while he precisely demonstrates that there is not a single dharma in which he abides, his awakened mind remains ever-present. Having finished eating—
He withdrew his focus, washed his feet, and spread out his seat. He directly demonstrated that without giving rise to a single thought, the deluded mind naturally subdues itself.

However, because the realm of the Tathāgata cannot be conceived by those at the initial stage of the path, he preached this sutra to enable them to offer verbal praise [of it]. Second, it is for the purpose of destroying the obstacles of the grasping at a self and the grasping at phenomena;
for these two types of grasping—self and phenomena—are the source of illness for ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle, upon which ordinary people rely.

Thereby, afflictions arise; based on these, the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) establishes the "object of knowledge" (jñeya). This leads to the cycle of birth and death and obstructs right knowledge and vision.
Like one in a dream or intoxicated, they do not realize this for themselves. To destroy this, the Buddha preached this sutra, as it is said:
"There is no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a sentient being, and no mark of a life-span. Such statements are all intended to destroy the notion of a self.
This is attachment. Furthermore, it says: "There is no mark of dharmas, nor is there any mark of non-dharmas. Statements of this kind are all intended to refute attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*).
The third [purpose] is to sever doubts regarding active manifestations (*samudācāra*) and seeds (*bīja*); for indeed, when a film of cataracts is in the eye, illusory flowers arise in the sky;

when even a fragment of doubt enters the mind, ten thousand delusions race through one's nature. Whether referring to what has already arisen or what is yet to arise, these obstruct the present and the future.
Such resolute conviction, or doubt regarding principles and phenomena, ultimately becomes the root of affliction.

Since no one but a Buddha can resolve this through their own wisdom, this sutra was taught to universally block and sever it. As in the sūtras where there are questions from those present according to their capacity and the Tathāgata provides answers, all are intended to sever doubts as they manifest.
When the Tathāgata employs counter-interrogation, asking "What do you think of this?", it is likewise for this purpose.
This is to sever doubts regarding seeds. Furthermore, at that time, they all function as manifest activities (*samudācāra*);

however, because the Buddha’s wisdom perceives their capacities and knows that [the seeds] have already arisen, they are collectively termed "seeds" with reference to future generations. This is done by relying on those empty births to benefit those yet to come.
Fourth, it is for the purpose of transforming heavy karma into light karmic retribution; for even if one were to [commit such acts] for hundreds of thousands of kalpas...
Karmic actions do not perish; when causes and conditions meet, one must personally undergo the retribution. Only through the power of repentance can they be eliminated.
Now, the power of repentance is greatest in this sutra; therefore, it is proclaimed so that people may know how to receive and uphold it. As the sutra says:
"If there is someone who receives, upholds, reads, and recites this sutra, yet is treated with contempt by others, this person..."
"Karmic offenses from previous lives that ought to cause one to fall into the evil realms are immediately extinguished because of being treated with contempt by people in the present life;
one shall thereby attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. According to this, the heavy retribution of the future is transformed and offset by a light retribution in the present.
As for the transformation of the light and its total eradication, although there is no explicit textual passage in the sutra, the principle is necessarily so."

Because heavy karma has already been lightened through its retribution, light karma ought not to be experienced at all. The fifth [point] is intended to demonstrate that practice and understanding must necessarily correspond.

For it is by means of faith and understanding that one transcends the mundane and enters the sacred; from cause to fruit, one attains actual efficacy through the conditions of cultivation and realization.
Therefore, to have understanding without practice inevitably leads to the fallacy of wild wisdom (*ku-hui*); to have practice without understanding is certain [to lead to stagnation].

This falls within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Therefore, following the section on faith and understanding (*adhimukti*), this sutra addresses the specific needs of the audience by again questioning the states of abiding and subduing the mind.

This is because, although one’s own realization of faith and understanding may be accomplished, habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are difficult to eliminate; when confronted with objects, thoughts arise, and one fails to achieve abiding and subduing.

In response, the Tathāgata’s answer regarding the subduing of the mind still concerns the non-deliverance of beings while delivering them, and his answer regarding the abiding of the mind still concerns non-abiding in the merit of giving.
This is intended so that they may practice gradually, ensuring that their conduct accords with their understanding.

The sixth [section] is for the purpose of revealing the meaning of the non-obstruction between emptiness and existence. This is because true emptiness is not empty, and wondrous existence is not existent.

Failing to realize the meaning of true emptiness, those of the Two Vehicles flee from their physical forms beyond the realms; failing to realize the meaning of wondrous existence, ordinary people and outsiders [remain deluded].

Those who remain submerged within the mundane realm each abide in one-sided extremes, all of which deviate from the Middle Way. For this reason, the sutra is preached to reveal the meaning of non-obstruction.
As the sutra says: "The Bodhi attained by the Tathāgata is, therein, neither real nor unreal," and so forth, up to: "..."

What is called "all dharmas" (comprehensively encompassing both emptiness and existence) is, in fact, not all dharmas (because it is taught that emptiness is not empty, and existence is not existent).

This is what is named "all dharmas" (meaning that teaching emptiness as non-empty is true emptiness, and teaching existence as non-existent is wondrous existence; therefore, there is no impediment to provisionally establishing names and calling them "all dharmas").

Passages of this kind all serve to reveal the meaning of the unimpeded nature of emptiness and existence. The seventh [section] is intended to remedy the fault of establishing knowledge based on cognitive views.
Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "To establish a knowing within seeing is to form the root of ignorance; to have no seeing within seeing is itself Nirvāṇa, the untainted and truly pure.
Thus we know that although gold dust is precious, it becomes a speck of dust when it falls into the eye. By establishing an object based on luminosity, the myriad dharmas arise from it.
Relying on delusion to produce further delusion, one accumulates confusion upon confusion. Not only is there no merit, but one instead incurs great error. To save [beings] from this...
This is flawed. It is because of the teaching of this sutra that it says: "The Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye, and so forth," up until:
"The past mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended.

Even for a Buddha’s knowledge and vision, these [distinctions] should not be established, let alone for those who have not yet reached the stage of Buddhahood, such as those with the light of a lamp or a crack of daylight. However—
The eighth is for the purpose of dispelling both the aspect of identity and the aspect of separation. To observe the Buddha through the aspect of identity is certainly a view of permanence;

to observe the Buddha by separating from the aspects is even more a fall into nihilism. Both equally constitute failing to see the Buddha-nature, ultimately resulting in belonging to the lineage of ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhists.
Now, this sutra is preached to cause both to be dispelled. As the sutra says: "If one observes the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks... (the text continues with the refutation).

The Wheel-Turning Sage King refers to the Tathāgata and others; this is intended to dispel the notion of perceiving them through their physical marks. Furthermore, it says: "Subhūti, do not entertain such a thought.
It is not by means of the possession of perfect marks that the Tathāgata attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," and so forth; this is intended to dispel the perception of marks.

The ninth [point] is for the purpose of destroying the perception of the two retributions—the primary and the secondary. Now, in receiving retribution, the sense organs and the body constitute the primary retribution.
The receptacle world serves as the support; the body of the faculties is a provisional aggregation of the four great elements. The receptacle world is an accumulation of myriad subtle particles;
in its entirety, it belongs to dependent origination and is entirely illusory and false. Sentient beings do not know this, yet they regard it as truly existent.
Clinging to a self and clinging to phenomena, they transmigrate within it; they protect and guard it, unable to find a way out. To shatter these appearances, this sutra is therefore preached.
As the Sūtra says: "If anyone were to say that the Tathāgata comes or goes, sits or lies down, that person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught.

From this we know that even the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) of the Tathāgata lacks substantial reality; how much less could the *rūpakāya* (form body) of sentient beings possibly have any basis in reality?
Furthermore, it says: "Good sons and good daughters, by means of the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world..."
The realms can be ground into fine dust; even as it says, "That which is a unified whole is inexpressible," and so forth.

Thus, even the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the world are not truly existent, let alone the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) produced by the retribution of karma, which are as fleeting as a whirling torch.

One should firmly adhere [to this]. The tenth [section] generally demonstrates the contemplation of the emptiness of both self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-śūnyatā*). Regarding the term "generally demonstrating":

because the preceding nine types arise sequentially, and because these two rounds of inquiry in the sutra are both for the purpose of subduing the mind and establishing the mind, there is the first [section].

"Translated by Kumārajīva, the Tripiṭaka Master of the Yaoqin [Dynasty].

however, because the translation occurred during the Qin period, it is recorded according to the Qin dynasty. To distinguish it from the earlier Qin of the Fu clan, it is termed "Yaoqin," referring to the later [dynasty]. Thus it is said.
This was during the reign of Yao Xing of the Qin dynasty. "Tripiṭaka Dharma Master" is a title of honor for a master of translation.

The "Tripiṭaka" refers to the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma. The two characters "Dharma Master" (Fashi) encompass a dual benefit: if one takes the holy Dharma of the Tripiṭaka as one's own teacher, this constitutes self-benefit;
if one uses the holy Dharma of the Tripiṭaka as a model for humans and devas, this constitutes [the benefit of others].
Benefiting others. The Master of Translation (Yi-zhu) fulfills both roles; therefore, he is collectively referred to as the *Tripiṭaka-dharmācārya*.

Regarding Kumārajīva: this is the Master of Translation’s personal name (*miàng*). His life story, including his Chinese and Indic names and deeds, is detailed in the first section. "Translator" (*yìzhě*) means one who changes [words] into another form.
The *Yi* (Chinese) is the translation of the Sanskrit term into the Chinese language. This concludes the general explanation of the title.
Second, the detailed interpretation of the textual meaning has three parts: first, the introductory section (*nidāna*); second, the main body of the teaching (*śarīra*);
and third, the dissemination section (*parīndanā*). This is the classification established by the Dharma Master Dao'an; all Buddhist scriptures, regardless of their length, follow this schema.

Since this accords mysteriously with the Western Regions, it is logically appropriate that it be universally observed throughout both past and present. First and second: first, the *Saddharmapratyaya-nidāna* (Sequence of Testimony); second, the *Utpatti-nidāna* (Sequence of Origination). Regarding the first, the *Saddharmapratyaya-nidāna*:

this refers to the time, place, principal and associates of the teaching and its listeners being clearly defined, thereby testifying that this is the Buddha’s own teaching and causing people to believe.
Because it gives rise to faith, it is also called the "General Preface" (sāmānyanidāna), as it is common to all sūtras.

It is also called the "Postscript" (paścānnidāna), because this preface did not exist at the time the Buddha preached the sūtra; rather, it was established during the compilation after he had already spoken. Thus, this preface was established.
There is a cause and there is an intention. Regarding the establishment of the cause: when the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, Ānanda was distressed with grief.
Aniruddha said to him, "You are the one who upholds the Dharma of the Buddha; you must first restrain yourself.
You should go to the Buddha's presence and inquire about matters for the future. Ānanda asked, "What are these matters for the future? Aniruddha replied, "You..."
Question: When the Buddha was in the world, he took the Buddha as his teacher; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, whom shall one take as teacher?
When the Buddha was in the world, one dwelt relying upon the Buddha; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, relying upon whom shall one dwell?
When the Buddha was in the world, the Buddha himself subdued monks of evil character; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, how shall they be subdued? When the Buddha was in the world...

He preached the Dharma to deliver sentient beings. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the compilation of the Dharma-piṭaka, [the assembly] asked: "What words should be placed at the beginning of all sūtras?
Ānanda received the instruction and inquired about each point one by one. The Buddha told Ānanda:

"After my parinirvāṇa, you should take the precepts as your teacher and abide in the four foundations of mindfulness. As for monks of evil character, you should silently exclude them. At the beginning of all sūtras..."
First, one should place the words "Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was at a certain location, together with a great assembly of such-and-such numbers.

There are three purposes for establishing this introductory statement: first, to eliminate doubt; second, to quell dispute; and third, to distinguish from heterodoxy. Regarding the elimination of doubt:
it refers to when Ānanda ascended the seat during the compilation of the Dharma-piṭaka after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, and his physical marks and signs were manifested.

Regarding the Buddha, the assembly gave rise to three doubts: first, the doubt that the Buddha was rising again to preach the Dharma; second, the doubt that a Buddha from another direction had arrived; and third, the doubt that Ānanda would attain Buddhahood.
Because these three doubts were severed all at once by the utterance of these words, it is called "stopping contention.
This means that Ānanda and the assembly were equal in virtue and status; if he had not deferred to what he heard from the Buddha, then contentious debate would have arisen. Therefore—
By uttering these words, it is revealed that this is the Buddha’s teaching, so that the various disputes may naturally cease. As for "distinguishing from the heterodox":

in the sūtras of the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthikas) of the Western Regions, the two characters "Āyu" are frequently placed at the beginning; the present statement of "Thus have I heard," and so forth, is intended to distinguish [this teaching] from theirs.
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, this section comprises six kinds of accomplishment (*siddhi*).

Because the teaching does not arise if even one of these six conditions is lacking, yet it necessarily arises when they are all complete, they are termed "accomplishments. The opening statement, "Thus" (*evam*), constitutes the accomplishment of faith;
for those who have faith say "thus," whereas those without faith say "not thus. As the *Śāstra* states: "The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma..."

Faith is that which enables entry; therefore, it is placed at the beginning. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Faith is the source of the Path and the mother of merit; it nurtures all wholesome dharmas.
Thus, among the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*), as well as all wholesome dharmas, faith is preeminent.
If one connects this with the following phrase "I have heard" (*evaṃ mayā śrutam*), it serves as a term for designating the Dharma, meaning: "Such a Dharma as this, I have heard from the Buddha."

Furthermore, the subsequent phrase "I have heard" (evam mayā śrutam) refers to the accomplishment of hearing. This is because one who is deaf lacks the capacity for hearing, and thus the Buddha would not preach to them.
The term "I" distinguishes [the speaker] from others, manifesting that this was heard personally by oneself and not like those who privately study or read ancient texts.

"Hearing" means that consciousness arises from the faculty of the ear; when a sound is within the range of audibility and one applies the mind with the desire to hear, one then succeeds in hearing. Now...

The reason it says only "I" and does not mention the ear-consciousness and so forth is that it sets aside the specific to follow the general; for "I" serves as the general designation for the single body.

Furthermore, although it says "I heard," in reality there is no conception of a self, because at this time Ānanda had already realized the four fruits of the path and had attained the realization of the emptiness of the self (*ātman-śūnyatā*). As the sutra says: "He wished and desired to hear, and the Buddha then spoke."
Therefore, it is called "accomplishment. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The true essence of the teaching in this land is pure within sound and hearing.
If one wishes to attain samādhi, one must truly enter through hearing. For this reason, among the seven noble riches (*saptadhanāni*), hearing is also reckoned as a treasure.
The third phrase, "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*), refers to the accomplishment of time. "One" signifies the beginning, the end, and the ultimate; it is time.
This refers to the nature of phenomena that undergo flux and transformation; its essence is that of dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

Whether in decline or in prosperity, both may be termed "time. That it is now called "one" should indicate a time of clarity and tranquility, for if things were in decline, the teaching and listening could not reach completion, and thus it could not be called "one.
As for the omission of years and months, it is because the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma transcends [such temporal limitations].
Regarding "at one time" (ekasmin samaye): after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the teachings were compiled and reached far and wide.

Depending on the length of the era—whether it be long or short—and depending on the distance from the source—whether the chronological records differ—the exact years and months are difficult to verify; therefore, it is simply stated as "one time.

This likely refers to the fact that the teaching was given at a single assembly and the listeners were gathered in a single session, such that both the speaker and the audience reached completion simultaneously. As the ancient masters said: "The seasons..."
If one reaches [this point], its principle will manifest of itself. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Now is precisely that time;

at this time, I shall speak according to reality. Thus, the significance of the timing is truly great indeed. As for the four characters used for "Buddha," they signify the accomplishment of the Master.

In full, it is called *Buddha*, which here means "the Awakened One. This refers to the perfection of awakening through self-awakening, awakening others, and the fulfillment of awakening—distinguishing him from ordinary beings.

Now, as for the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas: because ordinary beings do not awaken by themselves, the followers of the two vehicles do not awaken others, and the bodhisattvas’ awakening is incomplete, they cede this name exclusively to the Tathāgata. If one were to explain the meaning according to this very sutra:
Self-awakening means that there is no fixed dharma; this is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Awakening others means to bring all sentient beings to *parinirvāṇa* while remaining free from any notion of "delivering" them. Full awakening means being detached from all marks (*nimitta*);
this is what is called a Buddha. To identify the person specifically: it is our own teacher, Śākyamuni. This Dharma can only be realized by a Buddha and can only be taught by a Buddha.

The others, however, cannot; therefore, they yield the position of master to the Buddha. Furthermore, were there no Buddha, looking backward, faith would have nowhere to return and hearing would have nowhere to follow;
time would have been spent in vain. Looking forward, the multitude would have had nothing to rely upon and their dwelling place would have remained empty and desolate.
Thus we know that the accomplishment of the other five factors all depends upon the accomplishment of the Master. The fifth [factor] refers to Śrāvastī and so forth.
This refers to the accomplishment of the location. Śrāvastī is also called Śāvatthī; in the new [translation], it is rendered Śrāvastī.
This is likely because the Sanskrit sounds differ across the five regions of India. Here, it means "Abundant Virtue" (Phon-de) or "That Which Is Heard of" (Wen-wu).
It is so named because the country abounds in four virtues and is renowned for them. These four virtues refer to sensual objects, wealth and treasures, extensive learning, and liberation.
The Tripitaka Master Yijing translated [the name] as "City of Great Renown" (Mahāśravaṇa) and also heard its meaning.

This city is located in the kingdom of Kośala in Central India; it is now simply called Śrāvastī because there is also a kingdom of Kośala in South India, and he wished to avoid confusion with that one.
This refers to the general location, whereas the following refers to the specific site. As for Jetavana, "Jeta" refers to...
The tree given by the Crown Prince: Jeta—translated as "Victorious in Battle"—was the son of King Prasenajit.
When he was born, the king returned from a campaign against foreign lands having been victorious in battle; thus he was named accordingly.
The trees within the grove were those he gave as a gift, and for this reason they are called the "Jeta Grove. As for the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden, it is the garden given by the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada.
The elder’s original name was Sudatta; he was a minister of King Prasenajit.

He was also called Sudāna, which means "Good Giver," a name derived from his excellence in performing acts of charity. "Givaka" (or *Kevaddha*) is an honorary title based on his virtue. "Giving" (*giv*) refers to providing for others.
One who has no father while young is called "orphaned" (*gu*), and one who has no son while old is called "solitary" (*du*). This elder was a virtuous giver.
Furthermore, he was uniquely able to provide for these two [categories of people] with complete generosity; the world praised his virtue, and thus it was named after him.
He purchased a grove and built a monastery, serving as its patron (*dānapati*); therefore, it is called the Jetavana (Givaka’s Grove).
According to the *Kanding ji*, it is cited that King Prasenajit had a minister named Sudatta who, having gone in person to Rājagṛha to arrange a marriage for his son, stayed there...
The householder Jeta stopped at the home of Sudatta. In the middle of the night, Jeta rose, adorned his residence, and prepared various delicacies.
Sudatta asked, "Do you wish to invite the king for a wedding feast? He replied:
