This concludes the correct demonstration of the method. Second, the interrogation and explanation of its meaning.
Why is this? If a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling on signs, that merit and virtue is inconceivable and immeasurable.
Subhūti, what do you think? Is the space in the eastern direction conceivable and measurable? "No, World-Honored One. Subhūti, [it is likewise].
"Can the space of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir be measured? No, World-Honored One.
Subhūti, it is the same with the merit of a bodhisattva who practices giving without dwelling on signs; that merit also cannot be measured."
The text is divided into three sections: first, the inquiry and explanation; second, the illustrative analogy; and third, the application to the Dharma. These can be seen in the text itself.
Regarding the first section, the inquiry asks: "For what reason is it said that one should give alms in this manner?
In the explanation, it states that the merit of giving alms without dwelling on signs is inconceivable because it is a cause for the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state. Conversely...
This reveals giving performed while abiding in signs (*nimitta*). Although such merit exists, it is still conceivable because it is a cause with outflows (*sāsrava*).
As Yongjia said: "Giving while abiding in signs produces heavenly blessings; it is like an arrow shot upward into the void.
When its momentum is exhausted, the arrow falls back down, bringing about an unfavorable rebirth in the next life. How can this compare to the gate of the unconditioned true reality (*dharmatā*)?"

This refers to the direct entry into the stage of the Tathāgata in a single leap. Regarding the analogies, the space of the eastern direction is cited first because it is the foremost of the directions.
Non-abiding generosity is a cause for outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*);
like the nature of space, it cannot be destroyed, and thus it is compared to space. It is precisely because space is indestructible that [this analogy is employed].
Transversely pervasive and vertically exhaustive, it is difficult to conceive.
This metaphor illustrates that the cause of the untainted (*anāsrava*) is vast and profound, beyond the reach of mental cognition or deliberation.

To the question, "Can it be deliberated upon?"—intended to lead one to know the Dharma through its causal metaphor—the answer is "No," because emptiness is already known within the metaphor itself. Furthermore, [the text] proceeds with the south...

The analogy of the empty space of the four intermediate directions, the zenith, and the nadir illustrates that emptiness does not abide in any direction, yet receives different names according to those directions;

this serves as a metaphor for the cause of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*), which does not abide in any stage, yet realizes its respective fruits according to each stage. Although it realizes them individually according to the stages, these stages are mutually inclusive;
therefore, all are likened to that which cannot be measured or conceived. This is intended, in short, to demonstrate through a single emptiness.
One knows all things to be empty because one perceives every stage within a single stage. This is consistent with the teaching in the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*:
"The merit of giving without dwelling on signs is likewise," and with the statement that one should see the Tathāgata correctly, namely, "one should give in this manner."
It is not that there is nothing to say; having completed the examination and explanation of its meaning, [the Buddha] offers three exhortations to abide according to the teaching:
"Subhūti, a bodhisattva should simply abide as taught."
What has been taught above is precisely the method for abiding in the mind. A bodhisattva who has generated the aspiration should simply abide according to my instructions;
there is no need to laboriously seek other methods for abiding in the mind. This concludes the section on the method for abiding in the mind.
The third [verse] simultaneously explains and resolves potential doubts.
The verse states: "In those matters of subduing, one remains far removed from the mind that grasps at signs, severs various doubts, and also prevents the arising of the creative mind."
The commentary states: This is a verse that concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one.

"In the matter of disciplining them" means to discipline and gather the awakened mind so that it abides in the practice of giving; to subdue the deluded mind so that it ceases within the practice of saving sentient beings.
Regarding "distancing oneself from a mind that grasps at signs": if one perceives that there are sentient beings to be saved or that there is giving to be performed, [these are all signs].

Regarding the grasping of signs: previously, concerning the saving of sentient beings, it was said that "in reality there are no sentient beings," and regarding the practice of giving, it was said that "one does not dwell on forms, sounds, and so forth.
This indicates that one has already been able to distance oneself from the mind of grasping signs; this concludes the preceding section.

"And severing various doubts" as well as "preventing the arising of a doubting mind" means that one severs these various doubts and also prevents the mind that would give rise to doubt based on what preceded it, as well as the successive development of such a doubting mind.
This section of the sutra is divided into two parts: first, explaining the causes for the arising of doubt; second, preventing the further development of doubt. Regarding the first:
A doubt arises: The single practice of giving (*dāna*) applies to both the superior and the inferior.

While it may be appropriate for the inferior to benefit sentient beings by not dwelling on the mark of birth (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), as this serves to transcend the causes of outflow (*sāsrava-hetu*), how can one who makes offerings to the Buddhas above fail to dwell on the mark of the Buddha?

For the Buddha is without outflow (*anāsrava*); if one does not dwell on the mark of the Buddha, I fear the cause of the state without outflow will not be established. What benefit, then, would there be in such giving?
Because there was this doubt, he thus explained and resolved it:
"Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of physical marks? No, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of physical marks. Why is this? The physical marks spoken of by the Tathāgata are, in fact, not physical marks."
"Regarding the marks: what do you think? This is a phrase used for inquiry. The Tathāgata’s intention is this: "Suppose you doubt whether the Buddha's marks can truly abide;
I shall now ask you: in the depths of your own mind, what do you think? Will [you accept them]?
That is to say: can one perceive the True Tathāgata by means of a golden body endowed with the thirty-two marks?
If it were possible to perceive [the Buddha] through physical characteristics, then one could abide [in that state]. But if it is not so, then it is not the reality.

How then can you wish to abide [therein], while depending upon it to establish the cause for the outflow-free (anāsrava)? It is like reaching out with one's hand to grasp at empty space, wishing to rely upon it.
That this constitutes a cause for non-falling is certainly known to be unattainable. To answer with "No" was to awaken from the inquiry.

That the Buddha cannot be seen by means of the marks of his body (*lakṣaṇa*) was already understood by Śūnyatā-utpanna (Śāriputra); even if one makes the highest offerings to the Buddhas, the marks of the Buddha (*buddha-lakṣaṇa*) likewise cannot be dwelt upon.
This is truly because the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is like water, and the Retribution-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is like the ripples upon the surface of the water.

Light. The response body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is like a reflection manifested by light. If one mistakes the reflection for reality and seeks to rely upon it, one will inevitably encounter the calamity of being submerged;

therefore, this is not permissible. Second, preventing the transformation into doubt, which has two parts: first, preventing the doubt that the retributive marks (*vipākaphala-lakṣaṇa*) may be permanent;
second, preventing the doubt that there is ultimately no Buddha. Regarding the first:
A doubt arises: "The body of transformation (nirmāṇakāya), with its thirty-two marks, certainly cannot be the abiding [reality].

Is it possible that there is another, separate retribution body (vipākakāya) with an ocean of immeasurable marks that constitutes the abiding? To prevent such a doubt from arising, he thus provides this safeguard against it.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Whatever has marks is entirely false and illusory.

The Buddha’s intention is that not only should one not dwell upon the marks of the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body), but even the ocean of immeasurable marks of the *saṃbhogakāya* is likewise not to be dwelled upon.
This is because the *saṃbhogakāya* is like light upon the surface of water; the light is itself the water—how could it be separate from it?
Water possesses light; thus we know that the retributive marks (*vipāka-lakṣaṇa*) are themselves the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). How could the retributive marks exist apart from the Dharma-body?

It is merely because Bodhisattvas of the ten stages have not yet exhausted subtle mental formations (*saṃjñā*) that they falsely perceive a sea of immeasurable marks of the retributive body (*sambhogakāya*).
If one dwells in these marks, one does not see the Dharma-body; therefore, it is said in summary: "Whatever exists..."
These marks are all illusory and false; this is intended to prevent them from dwelling upon the marks of retribution, so that they may directly perceive the Tathāgata’s true Dharma-body.
Second, it prevents the doubt that there is ultimately no Buddha.
A doubt arises: "The retributive and transformational bodies do not abide, and the Dharma-body is formless and thus cannot be seen; will there ultimately be no Buddha to whom one may offer worship?
Fearing that this doubt might arise, he has therefore provided this safeguard to sever it.
If one sees that all marks are not marks, then one sees the Tathāgata. The Buddha’s intention is this:

by abiding in the marks of response (*nirmāṇakāya*), one remains stuck in the outflows (*āsrava*); by abiding in the marks of retribution (*vipākakāya*), one does not see the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

It is like staying with a reflection—one suffers the peril of drowning—or staying with the light—it provides no benefit of obtaining water. If one sees the various [marks of] response and retribution...

Regarding the marks: that which is not the true mark does not arise or abide. It is not only the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body) that is the Buddha, but the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) is also the Buddha.

This is like a reflected image being an illusion; although one realizes the light has no substance, it is not only the entire light and the entire water [that are empty], but the entire reflection is also entirely water.
Therefore, it is said: "To see is to see the Tathāgata," meaning to personally see the Tathāgata’s true *dharmakāya*.

Therefore, it is known that by merely not dwelling on appearances while making offerings to the *nirmāṇakāya* (response-recompense) Buddha, one is in fact making offerings to the *dharmakāya* Tathāgata;
one need not worry about failing to establish the cause for the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*). How could it be that, ultimately, there is no Buddha to whom one may offer?

Verse: "By distinguishing the nature of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), one prevents [the misconception of] its establishment as having three distinct characteristics; therefore, being apart from those, it is the Tathāgata.
Commentary:
This general verse summarizes the meaning within the sections concerning the arising of doubt regarding causes and the transformation of that doubt. It begins with "distinguishing the conditioned."

As for "essence" (*tattva*): "discrimination" (*vikalpa*) refers to the cognizing mind that acts as the subject; "conditioned essence" (*saṃskṛta-tattva*) refers to the Buddha-body (*buddhakāya*) that serves as the object.

The Buddha-body comprises both the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and the *sambhogakāya* (enjoyment body). Discrimination has both coarse and subtle aspects. Although there are coarse and subtle aspects, they are equally not free from the characteristic of conceptualization;
therefore, they are collectively termed "discrimination. Although there are the *nirmāṇakāya* and the *sambhogakāya*, they are all entirely accomplished through the cultivation of causes; therefore—

They share the same designation as "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*). As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) is conditioned and with outflows (*sāsrava*); the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) is conditioned and without outflows (*anāsrava*).
This can be used to substantiate this meaning. The term "prevention" (*vāraṇa*) is not appropriate here. Regarding "preventing that which achieves attainment":
it means that one cannot, by means of these conditioned bodily forms, achieve, establish, or attain the realization of seeing the Tathāgata. [This concludes] the section on the three characteristics.
This fully explains the two meanings of "establishing the lower by means of the upper. Regarding the explanation of the upper:

the statement that the characteristics of the conditioned body (*saṃskṛta-kāya-lakṣaṇa*) cannot be attained through accomplishment is precisely because, once it belongs to the conditioned, it possesses the three marks of arising, abiding, and ceasing, and is therefore not the essence-body (*dharmakāya*).
Regarding the establishment of the lower: it is precisely because the conditioned body belongs to these three marks and is not [the essence-body].
The true essence. Therefore, to be detached from that is precisely the Tathāgata. To speak of being "detached from that" means not dwelling in appearances (*nimitta*).
Not dwelling in appearances means that appearances are entirely the truth; hence it is said, "this is the Tathāgata. This concludes the summary of the teaching on descending and abiding.
Second, the four sections on accomplishing faith: first, revealing the virtues possessed by faith; second, successive inquiry.

Commentary: Section three clarifies and advances the faith; section four provides a layered explanation to resolve lingering doubts. The first two [sections] consist of: (1) the virtue of generating profound, true faith, and (2) the virtue of a single thought-moment of pure faith.
The first of these has three parts: (1) the question on faith posed by the appropriate recipient, (2) the Tathāgata’s response affirming its existence, and (3) the manifestation of its virtues.
The first [of these three]: [End of provided text]
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, are there any sentient beings who, upon hearing such spoken words and phrases, will give rise to true faith?

In the preceding passage, the cause was taken as the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the fruit was taken as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Since both cause and fruit are profound, it is truly difficult to engender faith."
Sentient beings cultivate causes while mostly clinging to outflows (*sāsrava*), and when they anticipate results, they mostly tend toward the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Fearing that those present might lack faith and thereby lose great benefit, he addressed the Buddha to inquire. The word *pō* (頗) means "it may be" or "perhaps";
by asking whether it is "possible for there to be," he expresses the concern that some might lack faith. The two characters for "speech" (*shuō*) signify both the agent and the act.
The Buddha is that which is capable of speaking, and the chapters and phrases are that which is spoken. This refers generally to both the profound causes and the profound fruits.
Within these texts there are chapters and sections, as well as phrases and pauses; hence the term "chapters and phrases" (*zhangju*). Here, only the expressive medium is mentioned.

This refers precisely to that which is expressed. A chapter expresses the broad purport, while a sentence expresses the detailed meaning, because [the latter] can be understood even without being explicitly stated.
A person of true faith does not merely believe in the chapters and sentences, but must necessarily be able to believe in their purport and meaning;

for to believe only in the chapters and sentences is superficial, whereas to believe both the purport and the meaning is genuine. This is like merely hearing that saving sentient beings is signless and practicing giving is non-abiding.

One then believes that this is the cause of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*). Upon merely hearing that one does not perceive by means of marks (*nimitta*), and that being free from marks is the Buddha, one believes that this is the fruit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
One definitively accepts this and gives rise to neither doubt nor fear; this is what it means to give rise to true faith.
"Not so" (*na*) is a term of ambivalence; it should correspond to the character "頗" (*po*), which is used when asking whether something might be the case or not.
[Subhūti] said: "No. I only hope for the Buddha’s clear explanation. The Wei translation says: "Are there perhaps sentient beings in future ages...

This is because [the Wei translator] took the Buddha’s response regarding the period after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa as the basis; thus it was sufficient to translate it in that way, ensuring that the question and answer corresponded.
As for why the present text does not mention "future ages," the intention is that Subhūti feared [the Dharma] might perish even in the present.
There is disbelief. The Tathāgata replied that there will still be those capable of faith in future generations; how much more so now, given the current state of mind?

Alternatively, it may be that this was originally absent from the Sanskrit manuscript, which is why Master Kumārajīva did not translate it. Once the inquiry regarding faith was concluded, the Tathāgata twice answered that there indeed are [those who believe].

The Buddha told Subhūti: "Do not speak thus. After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during the final five hundred years, there will be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit, who will be able to give rise to faith in these chapters and verses, regarding them as true."

The Buddha’s intention was that, just as with lofty mountains and flowing waters, there will naturally be those who understand them; when taught directly from ear to ear and face to face, how could there not be those who believe?
Therefore, he instructed that one must not speak in such a manner. He feared that those of middling or inferior capacity might develop a sense of timidity and fear due to the difficulty of believing.
Furthermore, by instructing that one "must not speak in such a manner," he indicated that one should not speak of the present; thus, he proceeds below to address the future.

To illustrate by analogy: after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, the True Dharma (saddharma) shall endure for one thousand years, the Semblance Dharma (pratirūpakadharma) for another one thousand years, and the Final Dharma (paścimadharma) for ten thousand years.
Within this period, during the first five hundred years, liberation will be firm; during the next five hundred years, meditative concentration (dhyāna) will be firm;
during the third five hundred years, learning (bahuśruta) will be firm; during the fourth five hundred years, stūpas and monasteries will be firm; and during the fifth five hundred years—

"Strife is firm and persistent. When it is now said that it is "the final five hundred years," this refers to the five hundred years of the Dharma-ending age (*mappō*), precisely when strife is firm and persistent;
this reveals the time of an evil world. "Those who uphold the precepts" means they cultivate the three clusters of pure conduct with diligence.

"Those who cultivate merit" means they practice the three kinds of giving simultaneously. These two constitute the conditions for being able to have faith. This reveals that those who break the precepts and lack merit [cannot].
Because they are able to believe. For one who upholds the precepts must necessarily believe in sin and merit; one who cultivates merit must necessarily believe in cause and effect.
Therefore it is said that one can generate faith in these words and phrases and declare them to be true:
taking the untainted cause as the true cause, and taking the unconditioned fruit as the true fruit. This is definitive patience (*niyata-kṣānti*).
It is so. Do not give rise to doubt or fear. That which Śūnyatāputra has asked is indeed true. Within this there are two layers of analogical clarification:

first, if one still believes after [the Buddha's] parinirvāṇa, how much more so during his present lifetime? Second, if one still believes during the final five hundred years, how much more so during the preceding four periods?
Furthermore, one must not allow the difficulty of belief to breed timidity and thereby lose a great benefit.
Verse: It is said that the profound meaning of cause and effect will not be in vain during the evil ages of the future, because there exist Bodhisattvas endowed with the three virtues of reality.
[Combined statement: This single verse summarizes the meaning of this section. "Cause" refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*), and "fruit" refers to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). That is to say:

What was previously explained distinguishes this from that which is contaminated (*sāsrava*) and conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); therefore, it is called the "profound meaning" (*gambhīrārtha*), while the former is considered the "shallow meaning" because it is easy to understand and believe.
"In the future evil age" refers to the period after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, specifically during the final five hundred years.
The two characters "not empty" (*aśūnya*) should be read as a pause; it means that the teaching is not established in vain, for there are three characters signifying reality (*satya*).

Read it continuously with what follows. This means that because there are true Bodhisattvas who possess the three virtues—observing the precepts, cultivating merit, and generating faith—it is by means of the virtue of the precepts and the virtue of merit that they assist in the perfection of the virtue of faith. Third, this reveals their virtues.
It should be known that such a person has not planted roots of goodness under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas;
rather, they have already planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable tens of millions of Buddhas.

It is said that the arising of faith is firmly established through the assistance of the merit of precepts. Furthermore, the merit of precepts is itself produced by past roots of goodness. Therefore, it is said:
"One should know that such a person has not planted roots of goodness under only one Buddha, two Buddhas, three, four, or five Buddhas.

The intention is that if the number of Buddhas seen were few, the offerings made to those Buddhas and the hearing of the Dharma would likewise be few; since the offerings and hearing of the Dharma were few, [the roots of goodness] from past lives...
If one's roots of goodness are not deep, it may not be possible in this present life to maintain the precepts, cultivate merit, and thereby assist in the perfection of faith.

How easily can it be said that faith has arisen? By the phrase "already for immeasurable tens of millions," it is precisely shown that they have seen many Buddhas, made offerings to many Buddhas, and heard the Dharma many times.
Since their roots of goodness are thus deep, they are able, within this present life, to maintain [the precepts].
Observing the precepts and cultivating merit assist in the perfection of faith.
Based on this, those who wish to believe in Prajñāpāramitā should aspire to see the Buddhas, make offerings to the Buddhas, hear the Dharma, and plant roots of goodness in every lifetime.
Verse: "Cultivating precepts in the past and planting various roots of goodness.
This should be understood as a single verse summarizing the meaning of this section.

The intent is that one's observance of precepts in this life is due to having cultivated precepts during the time of past Buddhas, and one's cultivation of merit in this life is likewise due to having planted roots of goodness during the time of past Buddhas.

This is indeed brought about by the thorough cultivation of goodness. Although the sūtras speak only of "planting goodness," this also encompasses the observance of precepts, as the precepts are likewise subsumed within wholesome dharmas.
Having thus deeply generated the virtue of genuine faith, there follows secondly, the virtue of pure faith in every thought-moment.
"Subhūti, as for those who hear these phrases and give rise to even a single thought of pure faith,
the Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees that all such sentient beings shall obtain immeasurable merit."
The Buddha’s intention is this: because they have planted roots of goodness in past lives, those who now give rise to true faith shall obtain immeasurable merit; this goes without saying.

Even if one hears these phrases and maintains them for years, or recites them for months or days—or even if it does not go so far as that—but only for the duration of a single thought-moment, one suddenly empties the four marks [of selfhood]. Regarding this profound meaning of cause and effect:
Those who give rise to pure faith and harbor not the slightest doubt will obtain merit that is by no means insignificant;

therefore, [the Buddha] addresses the recipient again to inform them once more. By stating that "the Tathāgata knows all and sees all," it is made manifest that the attainment of such merit is never in vain.
As Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "If 'seeing' were not mentioned, one might suppose that the Tathāgata knows [this] through inferential cognition."
If it were not stated that [the Tathāgata] knows, one might suppose that the Tathāgata sees with the fleshly eye; therefore, two phrases are required.

This is intended to clarify that wherever the Tathāgata knows, he sees all, and this is known through wisdom rather than through inferential cognition; wherever he sees, he knows all, and this is seen by means of [omniscience] rather than by the fleshly eye.
As for "attaining such immeasurable merit," it means that one also attains the same immeasurable merit as the aforementioned person. Indeed...

Although the sudden and gradual approaches differ, one who can believe in them finds no duality between them. Moreover, it is later stated that when the mind of faith is pure, the true nature (dharmatā) is immediately realized;
how could the merit thus obtained be any less than that of those mentioned previously?
Verse: "The Buddhas also declare that those who possess the precepts are fulfilled in merit.
[Commentary: This should be understood as a verse summarizing the meaning of this section.

Although it says "even a single moment of pure faith," this is also due to the complete observance of the precepts from the time of past Buddhas. As for the phrase "planting roots of goodness," the precepts themselves encompass all that is wholesome.
Because within the three clusters [of precepts] there is the morality of wholesome dharmas, it is also said that the Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees those whose merits are complete;
their merits should naturally be immeasurable, and thus he likewise speaks of the perfection of their merits as he did for the previous person.

This concludes the summary that reveals the possession of merit through faith. Second, the successive interrogation and explanation has three parts: first, receiving the interrogation and receiving...
Commentary: 1) A double inquiry followed by a double explanation; 2) A second inquiry followed by a second explanation. First: Why is this?
Because these sentient beings no longer possess the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of a life-span.
They have no notion of dharmas, nor do they have any notion of non-dharmas.
First, the introduction: as stated above, for what reason do these two types of persons who possess faith obtain immeasurable merit?
"These [persons]" and so forth provide the explanation. "One who has no mark of self" means that they have already realized the emptiness of self.

There is no grasping at a self (*ātman*). The *Zuanyao* states: "To grasp one's own substance as a self is [the view of] a person (*pudgala*). To reckon that this self transmigrates through various realms of existence is [the view of] a human.
To reckon that this self undergoes various transformations—such as prosperity and decline, suffering and pleasure—in continuous succession is [the view of] a sentient being (*sattva*)."

If one calculates that the life-force of this single retribution remains uninterrupted and abides, it constitutes the "self. Of these, the first is the fundamental [self], while the latter three all arise based upon this aforementioned self;
this is the general characteristic of the self. "Without the mark of dharmas" means that one has already realized the emptiness of dharmas and thus lacks attachment to dharmas.
"Without non-dharmas" means that one has already realized the emptiness of emptiness and thus lacks attachment to emptiness. By means of this "non-... [it is established].

Dharmas are themselves emptiness; there is no dharma that is not empty, for even emptiness itself is empty. Since these three kinds of emptiness are all luminously clear, one’s perspective is identical to that of the Buddha.
To have faith in this manner is surely to obtain immeasurable merit.
Verse: That person (jīva) and phenomena (dharma) are far removed from grasping at signs;

it is also taught that knowing those signs depends on the distinct characteristics of the eightfold and eightfold [dependent origination] in their continuous succession, which persists until life ends and one proceeds toward another path—this is the mark of the self (*ātman*).

All four types of this are empty and non-existent; they have no reality and cannot be described, yet they are spoken of by relying upon conventional expressions. This is the mark of phenomena (*dharma*).
That person, relying on faith and reverence, gives rise to the perception of reality; hearing the sound, they do not grasp it incorrectly but correctly comprehend the teaching.

Thus comprehended, the Buddha does not see a fruit [of their effort], for he knows that the power of his vows and wisdom is manifest before them. Such a person, seeking offerings and reverence, cannot describe it.

The combined commentary states: This single verse serves both as a response to the inquiry and an explanation of its meaning. Within it, the first sixteen lines combine to praise the absence of self and the absence of dharmas;
the final four lines separately praise the absence of even "non-dharmas. Among the former, the initial two lines briefly clarify that both characteristics are abandoned.
The word "that" (*tat*) refers to the person who possesses faith; "life-span" (*jīva*) refers to the mark of a self (*ātman*). And...

The Dharma is precisely the characteristic of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Although one does not speak of the "mark of self" (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*), the term "person who clings to life" (*jīvaka*) is used because there are four types of the mark of self, and the mark of the person who clings to life is difficult to shatter.
The Bodhisattva uses the specific to represent the general, causing [beings] to know that life and its duration are impermanent;

thus, the mark of self becomes easy to attack, and the others are likewise easy to shatter. "To remain far removed from grasping at marks" means that regarding both the self and phenomena, [one has already...]
This refers to the ability to remain far removed from a mind that grasps at signs. The phrase "it is also taught below" is a statement by Maitreya granting permission for that [explanation].
He says that it is not only the Buddha who teaches that one can be free from the notions of self and phenomena; he himself also teaches that one knows those two signs of self and phenomena.
How is this known? It is said that from the two characteristics of self and phenomena, eight characteristics arise in mutual dependence, which constitute eight distinct meanings;
these will be seen in the following verse. As for "differentiation," it refers to various transformations such as prosperity and decline, suffering and pleasure.

As for "continuity," it refers to the cessation of the preceding and the arising of the succeeding, which is the characteristic of sentient beings. That which is taken as the basis of reliance and reckoned as the "self" is precisely [this continuity].

The mark of self (*ātman*) is the continuous, uninterrupted succession [of the aggregates] that leads to the calculation that life endures for a long time; this is the mark of a living being (*jīva*).

To calculate that the self transmigrates and proceeds again toward other realms is the mark of a person (*pudgala*). All of these arise based on the grasping at a self; therefore, it is said that there are four kinds of marks of self.
"All" refers collectively to all phenomena (*dharma*), which is precisely the mark of existence (*bhāva*). If one realizes that their nature is empty, they are fundamentally non-existent.
There is a thing, which is precisely the characteristic of emptiness. If one were to claim that both [existence and emptiness] are substantially real, this cannot be asserted.
That is to say, it cannot be asserted that there is the meaning of actual emptiness or the meaning of actual existence; this is the characteristic of "neither.

For the sake of liberating sentient beings by departing from the two extremes, one speaks of existence based on conventional expression, and one speaks of emptiness based on conventional expression; this is the characteristic of "both."
These all arise from the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*); therefore, it is said that there are four kinds of phenomenal characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
"Those people" refers specifically to those capable of faith. "Relying on faith" means relying upon two kinds of faith. "Reverence" means honoring the Dharma.
One respects the Dharma; the mind opens and the intellect is liberated. The principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) becomes manifest, and thus the meaning arises.
Since the true mark has arisen, one hears the Dharma by relying upon that true mark; even when hearing the sound of "self" being spoken, one does not directly grasp at the characteristic of a self.

Although one hears the sound of the Dharma being taught, one does not directly grasp at the characteristics of the phenomena; therefore, it is said that "hearing the sound, one does not grasp it directly.
"Directly" (zhèng) is synonymous with "straightforwardly" (zhí). If one speaks of the emptiness of the self and the emptiness of phenomena, this constitutes correct teaching.
To "grasp in this manner" means to rely upon what the Buddha has taught and thus grasp the meaning of the two kinds of emptiness. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "There is no mark of a self..."
This is the characteristic of the Dharma (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). The Buddha does not descend to [assert] the four propositions; there is nothing that is not the Dharma. As stated above:
"One takes it up in this manner," yet this is also not a definitive grasping of the meaning of emptiness. For what reason is it not a definitive grasping?

Because the Buddha does not perceive through the knowledge of a result (*phala*). A "result" carries the sense of definitiveness; that is to say, the Buddha does not establish the view: "I know with certainty."

This is because of the meaning of the two kinds of emptiness. If that is so, why is emptiness taught? It is solely by means of great vows and the power of great wisdom that, in order to eliminate the two types of grasping, one manifests the teaching on the meaning of the emptiness of self and the emptiness of phenomena. This Dharma can only be taught by a Buddha.

If there were worldly false teachers or those within the Buddha’s teaching who preach for the sake of profit, seeking offerings and seeking honor, such persons would be unable to speak this [teaching].
Thus we know that those capable of faith follow the Buddha’s intention and likewise do not determinately grasp at emptiness.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Nor is there any characteristic of non-dharma. This is the second turn of questioning and the subsequent turn of explanation.
Why is this? If these sentient beings grasp at signs with their minds, they immediately become attached to a self, a person, a being, and a life-span.
If they grasp at the signs of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), they immediately become attached to a self, a person, a being, and a life-span.

The first part raises a challenge: since you have previously granted that all these sentient beings are without self (*anātman*) and without phenomena (*dharman*), as well as without non-phenomena (*adharman*), for what reason is this so?

The section beginning with "These [beings]" provides the subsequent explanation, stating that there is no mark of a self (*ātma-lakṣaṇa*), no mark of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), and no mark of non-phenomena (*adharma-lakṣaṇa*).
However, if there is any grasping at signs within the mind, one immediately becomes attached to the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span.
Because there is a sign that is grasped, there is a self that grasps; and because there is a self that grasps, the three characteristics of "person" and so forth arise in mutual dependence.
Since these four characteristics remain as they are, how could one possibly be free from the causal relationship of signs?
This indeed gives rise to profound true faith and sudden pure faith. If one were to raise an objection from the perspective of the lower vehicle, one might argue:
"The two vehicles have already realized the emptiness of self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and merely apprehend the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*); thus, they should be without self.

Why then do you say that if the mind apprehends characteristics, it is immediately attached to self, person, sentient beings, and so forth? To prevent this, it is said: "If one apprehends the characteristics of phenomena, then..."
They cling to the notions of a self, a person, a being, and a life-span. This is questioned and explained three times.
Why is this? If one grasps at the mark of non-dharmas, one clings to the notions of a self, a person, a being, and a life-span.
Therefore, one should not grasp at dharmas, nor should one grasp at non-dharmas.
Why does the text inquire again? If we take the subsequent explanation as the answer: if one grasps at what is non-dharmic (*adharma*), one still clings to the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*);
how much more so when grasping at dharmas? This need not be stated explicitly; it is self-evident.

In sum, because the subject-object duality has not been forgotten and the self has not yet entered true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the "four marks of deluded wisdom" in the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* can serve as proof for this meaning. (Regarding the "four marks of deluded wisdom": when the mind has something realized, failing to forget the subject and object constitutes the mark of selfhood. Realizing that the self...)

It is not so. This wisdom does not dispel them. To perceive a person is to fail to realize that the person is non-existent; to maintain a sense of what has been realized is to be a sentient being. To awaken to that which was realized causes the karmic wisdom to continue in a latent manner, becoming a life-sustainer (*jīvaka*). The details are found in that [other] text and are not elaborated upon here.

Therefore, the following serves as a summary: because all the aforementioned grasping at what is dharmic and what is non-dharmic is for the purpose of clinging to a self, you disciples, although you do not grasp at a self, must nevertheless understand that you should not grasp at dharmas.
One should not grasp at what is non-Dharma, because the mere capacity to grasp already belongs to the mark of selfhood (*ātman*).

These two preceding sections were not versified by Maitreya because they were explained as being mutually dependent causes and conditions rather than the primary intent. This concludes the summary of the successive inquiries and explanations.
Third, the conclusion indicates the advancement of faith.
For this reason, the Tathāgata has constantly said: "O bhikṣus, you should understand my teaching of the Dharma as being like the simile of the raft.
Even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not the Dharma."

"By this meaning" means that because these three marks—the mark of self (*ātman*), the mark of phenomena (*dharma*), and the mark of non-phenomena (*adharma*)—should all not be grasped, the Tathāgata habitually makes this statement: "O Bhikṣus, you who know my teaching.
This refers to the Tathāgata’s habitual practice of addressing the bhikṣus and instructing them on what they should know.

The intention behind my teaching the Dharma is as follows: just as I first taught the emptiness of the self (*ātman-śūnyatā*) to transcend attachment to a self, I next taught the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) to transcend attachment to phenomena, and finally taught the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*) to transcend attachment to emptiness. Therefore, it is said that the Dharma is like a raft.
It is said that first one constructs a small raft to cross the river and reach the stream; next, one constructs a medium raft to cross the stream and reach the sea;
finally, one constructs a large raft to cross the sea and reach the mountain of jewels. Thus we know that by clinging to the small raft, one cannot cross the stream;
by clinging to the medium raft, one cannot cross the sea; and by clinging to the large raft, one cannot ascend the mountain to gather the jewels.
Although these three rafts differ in their degree of excellence, all must be abandoned when the time comes;

the Buddha-dharma is likewise. Therefore, it is said that "even dharma should be relinquished. Here, the word "dharma" does not refer to the "dharmas" (phenomena) mentioned previously; rather, it refers to the teachings spoken by the Buddha.
The subsequent phrase "non-dharma" (*adharma*) likewise does not refer to the "non-dharmas" mentioned before; rather, it refers to the world...
Regarding all matters such as fame and gain that arise in the interim, it is said that even those taught by the Buddha should be abandoned at this time;
how much more so worldly fame, gain, and the like, which are not the Buddha’s Dharma? One should therefore have no attachment to them whatsoever.
Furthermore, O World-Honored One, this was for the sake of those in future generations who speak of emptiness with their mouths but walk in existence with their feet.
This is merely the method for untying attachments and removing fetters.
The verse says: "He does not abide [in them], but accords with the Dharma; the realized wisdom is like a person abandoning a boat or raft—the meaning within the Dharma is likewise so."
The combined commentary states: This is a verse composed according to its meaning; its literary structure differs slightly from the scriptural text.

While the scriptural text follows the three characteristics by stating that none should be grasped and cites common parlance as an analogy, this [verse] refers specifically to the person capable of faith.

This directly employs the metaphor of abandoning the raft. To explain its meaning: "he" refers to the person capable of faith, who understands that all the teachings spoken by the Buddha are in accordance with the needs of the times and circumstances, and thus gives rise to neither attachment nor grasping.
Therefore, it is said, "he does not abide in accordance. Rather, he realizes the teachings spoken by the Buddha according to his own capacity; therefore, it is said, "he realizes within the Dharma."

"Wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the emptiness of self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), and the wisdom of the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).
Although one realizes the wisdom of these three kinds of emptiness, one does not abide even within those three emptinesses; thus it is said: "Like a person who abandons a boat or raft.

This is used as a metaphor for the method. Since the teaching must accord with its metaphor, it says: "The meaning within the Dharma is likewise so. This concludes the exhortation to advance in faith. Fourth, the rebuttal of potential objections.

There are three parts to the section on Doubt: first, showing the question to prevent doubt; second, providing the response according to the occasion; third, raising an inquiry and explaining the resolution. Regarding the first: the doubt arises as follows.
"As stated above, all things should not be grasped; there should be neither attainment nor teaching.
For what reason, then, has the Tathāgata attained the Way and preached the Dharma? To prevent this doubt, the question is first presented.
Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Or has the Tathāgata preached any Dharma?

The Buddha’s intention is this: from the standpoint of the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), not a single dharma is established; yet at the gateway of manifested transformation, not a single dharma is lacking.
If one were to say that there is attainment or that there is teaching, one would fall into the view of eternalism and would also contradict the previous statement.

If one were to say that there is neither attainment nor teaching, one would again fall into the view of nihilism and would likewise deviate from the gateway of transformation. Therefore, he asks: "Does the Tathāgata attain *bodhi*? As...
"Does the Tathāgata come with something to preach? Observe these two characters "ye" (come). Then the Tathāgata has already assumed the posture of inevitable victory;
if it comes from the left, he captures it on the left; if it comes from the right, he captures it on the right. Now let us see whether Subhūti recognizes this pivot or not. An ancient worthy said:
"Though the words encompass both 'attainment' and 'non-attainment,' the meaning lies in non-attainment. This statement seems not to have been understood.
This is the response of Subhūti. Second, the appropriate reply:
Subhūti said, "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no fixed dharma called 'anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,' nor is there any fixed dharma that the Tathāgata can speak of."
Śūnyatā-utpanna (Subhūti) is also a veteran general skilled in warfare; borrowing that [opponent's] momentum, he turns back to attack him. Therefore it is said:
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught," which refers precisely to the previously stated principle that "all things should not be grasped.
The intent is that although nothing at all should be grasped, this does not mean there is an absolute absence of attainment; it simply means there is no fixed [attainment].

The Dharma is named *anuttara-bodhi*. As for what ordinary people call "attaining bodhi," this belongs entirely to the bodies of transformation and response (*nirmāṇakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*), which appear when there is a capacity [in sentient beings] and remain hidden when there is no such capacity. Thus, it is not that there is never any teaching; rather, it is simply that there is no fixed dharma to be taught.
As for what ordinary people call "preaching the Dharma," this too belongs entirely to skillful means (*upāya*), which are taught when there is a capacity and [remain unspoken when there is none].
Because the pivot [of the mind] is silent, one knows that there is both attainment and speech; yet it is truly impossible to speak of them.
That there is neither attainment nor speech is likewise impossible to speak of. Thus, Kongsheng may be called one who well understands the Middle Way.
Nevertheless, were it not for this being brought forth, one would almost have forgotten it.
Verse: "The transformation body is not the true Buddha, nor is it the speaker of the Dharma. [Combined Explanation]:
The meaning is that because the transformation body appears or disappears according to the capacities of sentient beings, it is not the true Buddha;

this verse illustrates that there is no fixed dharma to be attained. Because the wisdom of skillful means speaks or remains silent according to the capacities of sentient beings, it is not the speaker; this verse illustrates that there is no [fixed speech].
The definitive Dharma can be explained. This is established through three interrogations and explanations.
Why is this? Because all dharmas taught by the Tathāgata are ungraspable and inexpressible; they are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas.
Why is this so? Because all worthy and holy ones are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
The opening phrase承接 (receives and follows) the inquiry; it essentially continues the previous double inquiry, intending to show that there is no fixed attainment and no fixed teaching.

The Tathāgata’s subsequent reliance on the Śākya [lineage] is explained as follows: regarding the statement that there is no fixed teaching, this is because the teaching serves as an illustration for what is attained.

The term "Tathāgata" refers generally to all that was taught in former years. The phrase "none of it is to be grasped" means that there should be no clinging to the grasper (*grāhaka*) or the grasped (*grāhya*).
This refers precisely to being far removed from all intrinsic natures and characteristics; namely, the clinging to grasper and grasped. It is not to be... [continued].
These three characters are to be read in conjunction with what follows, encompassing both "not dharma" and "not non-dharma.
To say that it cannot be said to be "non-dharma" means that one cannot say it is not dharma; this is because it is taught progressively according to what has been personally realized.
To say that it cannot be said to be "non-non-dharma" means that one cannot say it is dharma; for since...
These were taught progressively as skillful means (*upāya*), for they do not constitute the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Therefore, the text shifts its phrasing to pose a challenge:
it cannot be said that they are not dharmas, nor can it be said that they are not non-dharmas. Why is this so?
The subsequent section provides the explanation: "All worthy ones and sages" refers collectively to the three stages of worthiness, the ten stages of sagehood, and the Buddhas.
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the intrinsically pure mind, which is fundamentally complete and not something attained through effort;
therefore, it is called "unconditioned. The noble ones (*ārya*) of the three vehicles have nothing other than this from which to attain realization;

thus it is said, "all [attain] by means of it," meaning that all take the unconditioned dharma as their object of realization. As it is with the noble ones, so it is with the Tathāgata; they all know the Tathāgata [in this way].
Whatever has been taught is entirely based on the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) realized within oneself; how could it be said that these are not the Dharma?

As for the existence of distinctions, this means that although the unconditioned is taken as the realization, the stages of the noble ones (*ārya*) differ, and there are variations in their sequence, depth, and profundity.
Thus, one should know that whatever the Tathāgata has taught is all in accordance with the capacities and dispositions of sentient beings, being a skillful means (*upāya*).
It is not real. How could one say that it is not a non-dharma? Since what is taught is thus, what is attained is likewise so.
Because it is explained according to what is attained, it may be understood by analogy; therefore, it is not explained separately.

Furthermore, the phrase "by what" below explains that there is no fixed teaching, while the phrase "because" below explains that there is no fixed attainment. Since both are expressed in this manner...
Regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*): it cannot be said that there is attainment, because it is inherently complete from the beginning;

yet there are distinctions, so it cannot be said that there is no attainment, because there are clearly distinct stages and positions. If one follows the verse of Maitreya, the former interpretation is correct.
Because that [text] also merely provides an explanation, as will be seen below from the verse itself:
"The teaching of the Dharma is non-dual, ungraspable, unspeakable, and free from the characteristics of language.
To combine these points: the first line of the verse praises its being ungraspable; that is to say, regarding the Dharma taught by the Buddha, there is no agent therein who can grasp it.
Because of the twofold grasping at the grasper and the grasped, the subsequent verse states that it cannot be said to be either non-dharma or not non-dharma;

that is, regarding the Dharma taught by the Buddha, no one can say within it that it is either "not this" or "this. This is because the Dharma is free from verbal characteristics and is thus ineffable.
Once doubt has been suppressed and destroyed, pure faith arises. This concludes the accomplishment of faith. (3)
Comparing the three types of merit from upholding [the Dharma]: first, that which can compare; second, that which is compared; third, resolving doubts. First: "Subhūti, what do you think?

If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would the merit obtained by this person be great? Subhūti replied, "It would be very great, World-Honored One."
Why is this? Because this merit is not the nature of merit; therefore, the Tathāgata says that the merit is great.
As for the opening phrase, "What do you think?"—this is intended to focus the mind, and all subsequent instances follow this pattern.
"If a person" means if there were someone; what follows below consists of hypothetical matters, such as [the gift of] three thousand...
Regarding the "trichiliocosm" (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*): the *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states:

"One thousand sets of the four continents, the sun and moon, Mount Sumeru, the heavens of the desire realm, and the first dhyāna [heavens], each numbering one thousand, and covered above by the second dhyāna—heaven—is called a small chiliocosm (*sāhasracūḍika*).

One thousand times this small chiliocosm, and covered above by the third dhyāna—heaven, is termed a medium chiliocosm (*dvisāhasramadhyama*). One thousand times this medium chiliocosm, and covered above by the fourth dhyāna—heaven, is called a great trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasra*)."
Regarding the *Dhātu* [chapter], the meaning of the verses in the treatise was slightly incomplete; thus, small characters have been written alongside them, which I have now added in this commentary.
The final two lines have also been slightly revised. To explain the intent of the detailed discussion:

it appears that the term "thousand" is stated three times in succession to form a "great trichiliocosm," referring to the "great thousand" of the three-thousandfold world system according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) analysis. As for the seven treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, [and so forth].
Lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, red pearls, and agate (as seen in the *Amitābha Sūtra*).

The Buddha’s intention was that because the ground of a great trichiliocosm is vast and the seven treasures are precious, if one were to fill the entire ground of this great trichiliocosm with these precious seven treasures and offer them as a gift, the merit thereof could indeed be called supreme.
"Is it not so?"—when asked whether this merit might be considered much, [the Buddha] intended to use this merit as a basis for comparison.
The latter two types of merit among those with form and manifestation are explained as being the most excellent. The response that they are "very great" already conveys the Buddha’s intention;

however, fearing the difficulty of inviting an over-extension of this principle, he again raises a further inquiry to distinguish them, stating: "Although these merits are superior, they are merely the results induced by material giving (*āmiṣadāna*);

being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and subject to outflows (*sāsrava*), they are termed the characteristics of 'merit' (*puṇya-lakṣaṇa*), and thus do not constitute the merit of the Dharma-gift (*dharmadāna*)."
That which is felt—unconditioned and untainted—is called the nature of merit (*puṇya-svabhāva*).
These two phrases already demonstrate that this merit cannot compare to the latter two types of merit, because the former is associated with what is destructible while its nature is indestructible;
furthermore, the former has limitations while its nature belongs to the unlimited. Therefore, the four characters for "Tathāgata" are briefly condensed into a single syllable.
"The merit is great" forms a separate clause. It is as if saying:
"Precisely because this is not the nature of merit," it is said before the Tathāgata that the merit is exceedingly great. This is because it possesses limits;
the intent is to reveal that if it were the nature of merit, I would not say it is exceedingly great, for it would lack limits. Thus, the comparison is concluded.
Second, regarding the comparison:
if there were another person who, from this sutra, were to receive, uphold, and even expound for others as little as a four-line verse, their merit would surpass that [of the former].
Why is this? Subhūti, it is because all Buddhas and the unsurpassed... [enlightenment of] all Buddhas... [arise from this].
The Dharma of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* all issues from this sutra.
At the beginning of each section, there should be the words of the Buddha or the name "Subhūti"; everything from this point downward belongs to the Buddha’s speech.
Alternatively, it may be because the translator omitted it. "If there should be another person" means that even if there were yet another person.
"In this sutra" refers to what was previously explained. Since pure faith has already arisen and the meaning is briefly but completely covered, one may refer to it by the name of this sutra.
Thus, we know that what is said from here downward merely expands upon the meaning within this [section]. "To receive and uphold" means to comprehend...
"Upholding through reception" means grasping both the words and the meaning. To speak first in terms of self-benefit: the phrase "up to and including" (*yāvat*) is a term used for abbreviation.
This means that on the extensive side, it includes the complete or partial portions; on the concise side, it extends down to a four-line verse, or even fewer, down to a single line.
Therefore, the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) is employed. Question: Since the preceding section consists only of prose (*gadya*), why does it mention "verses" (*gāthā*)? Answer: This...
There are two explanations. First, it is not necessarily restricted to four, five, or seven syllables;

rather, whenever the meaning is complete in four lines, that constitutes a single verse (*gāthā*). This may be illustrated by the four lines beginning with "All phenomena whatsoever... as pointed out by Guifeng.
Second, because prose (*gadya*) is difficult to memorize, it is often rendered into verse (*gāthā*) for ease of retention, such as when Maitreya composed verses based on the sūtras.
"Explaining it to others" means to speak of what one has personally seen to other people; this refers to the discourse on benefiting others.

"Its merit" refers specifically to the merit of upholding and explaining [the teaching]. "Surpassing that" means exceeding the former person, because the nature of the merit induced by this gift of Dharma is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and untainted (*anāsrava*). Fearing that this may still not be clear, [the author] repeats:
An explanation of the inquiry: "All Buddhas" refers to those who are capable of realization. "Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" refers to the path that is realized.
That they all emerge from this sutra is due to three causes and conditions: first, it is the nature of merit and virtue;
this nature is able to follow conditions, such that one becomes a Buddha by following the conditions of cultivating causes, and realizes the Path by following the conditions of becoming a Buddha.
Second, this sutra is the portion of faith; it can engender pure faith, serving as the source of the Path and the mother of merit.

Third, when the mind of faith is purified, one immediately gives rise to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). The true mark is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); the attainment of Buddhahood and the realization of the Path both rely on the distinctions within the unconditioned.
Verse: Upholding the Dharma and teaching it are not in vain regarding merit; yet merit alone does not lead to Bodhi. These two can lead to Bodhi.

In reality, they are called the "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*), and also serve as the "generating cause" (*janaka-hetu*) for future lives. Only the merit of the Buddha-dharmas accomplishes the supreme essence.

The combined explanation states: The first four lines provide a general summary of that which compares and that by which it is compared—namely, the recipient who upholds the Dharma and the speaker who preaches it.
This refers to upholding this Dharma, even as little as a single four-line verse, and preaching it for others. This possesses two kinds of merit:
first, upholding; second, preaching. "In vain" means to no purpose; "not in vain regarding merit" refers to this very act of upholding and preaching.
It is not merely a matter of speaking of merit; rather, it is because this is the very nature of merit.
This implies that the giving of material wealth is merely spoken of as "merit," yet it is only the characteristic of merit. Regarding "merit does not lead to bodhi":
this means that the merit of material giving does not lead to bodhi, because it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and tainted (*sāsrava*) merit. Second, "that which can lead to bodhi" refers to this...
The two merits of upholding and explaining [the Dharma] can lead to bodhi because they are unconditioned and untainted merits.

Due to the force of the textual comparison, this differs slightly from the sutra. In the sutra, material giving is compared with the gift of Dharma to show that the merit of the gift of Dharma is superior;
here, the gift of Dharma is compared with material giving to show that the merit of material giving is inferior. The underlying intent is the same. The final four lines [are as follows]:
The separate verse raises the inquiry and provides the explanation. Since the verse lacks a term of inquiry, it follows the exposition found in the Sūtra;

if one wishes to include it for completeness, the term of inquiry should be supplemented as follows: "Why does one proceed toward Bodhi? By what causes and conditions? When this is joined to the reading of the root verse, the meaning will be fully clarified.
This reality is precisely the fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), which is also the self-nature of sentient beings, long concealed within their emotional afflictions.
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) can only be understood through its designation; therefore, it is said that regarding reality, names serve as the "revealing cause" (*vyañjanahetu*).

The remainder is initial awakening (*ādikṣānti*), which is also the stages of the Bodhisattva. Since the cultivation of the myriad practices arises solely through their designation, it is also said to be the "generative cause" (*janakahetu*) for the rest.
This, however, has not yet revealed the most supreme [truth]: only the Buddhas and the Dharma are entirely accomplished by means of this merit.
This merit is foremost and most excellent; it possesses a real essence, namely that which leads to enlightenment.
This concludes the calculation. Third, the resolution of doubts.
A doubt arises: "As I previously stated, there may be no fixed attainment and no fixed teaching. Since the Buddha has offered no further words, this must signify his acceptance [of my view].
Yet, the Buddha now says that the Buddha and the Buddha-dharma emerge from this sutra.
If the Buddha-dharma has an emergence, it seems as though bodhi can be attained; if this sutra can bring them forth, it seems as though this dharma can be taught. Might this not be so?"
Does this contradiction between the preceding and following passages render the doctrinal tenets of both sections untenable? The commentary states:
"Subhūti, that which is called 'Buddha-dharma' is itself not Buddha-dharma."
When I speak of the enlightenment of all Buddhas and the Dharma they teach, it is not actually the enlightenment of all Buddhas nor the Dharma they teach.

This is because the Buddha is fundamentally without self; though he has attained Buddhahood, he does not perceive the mark of attainment; though he has realized bodhi, he does not perceive the mark of realization;
though he teaches the Dharma, he does not perceive the mark of teaching. Thus, this does not contradict what was said previously.
On the contrary, what further doubt could there be?
The verse states: "It cannot be grasped nor can it be described, because its own fruit is not grasped.
This should be understood as follows: "Grasping" has the sense of realization. "Cannot be grasped nor can it be described" means that it cannot be said that there is *bodhi*.

That which can be realized and that which can be spoken of as a phenomenon exist; this clarifies that upon attaining *bodhi*, one does not perceive the mark of attainment, and when teaching the Dharma, one does not perceive the mark of teaching.

"One's own fruit is itself the Buddha" means that one accomplishes the fruit of one's own Buddhahood. "Non-appropriation" means that at the time of becoming a Buddha, one does not give rise to grasping or attachment;
this clarifies that in achieving Buddhahood, one does not perceive the mark of achievement. The word "therefore" connects to and supports the three preceding points.
This means that because these three characteristics are all unperceived, it does not contradict the meaning previously explained.
This concludes the summary of the major sections; the brief explanation of the section on "Subduing, Abiding, and Generating Faith" is finished.

Second, the section on expanding [the practice] to bring about settling and understanding. Bringing the mind down and settling the mind are not accomplished by a single means;
therefore, they must be expanded. Having heard briefly, one gives rise to faith according to the words; having heard extensively, one should rely upon the meaning to open up understanding.

This further has three parts: first, expanding the settling and bringing down of the mind; second, accomplishing the wisdom of understanding; third, revealing the merit of the sūtra. Of these, the first has three sub-sections. First:
I. Correctly expanding and promoting [the teaching]. II. Briefly demonstrating its completeness. III. Exhaustively severing remaining doubts.

Regarding the first two [sections], there are four parts: I. Expanding the method for subduing the mind; II. Expanding the method for abiding in the mind. Regarding the first [of these four], there are four parts: I. The detachment from signs of the first fruit; II. The detachment from signs of the second fruit;
III. The detachment from signs of the third fruit; IV. The detachment from signs of the fourth fruit. First [part]: The detachment from signs of the first fruit.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does a srotāpanna (stream-enterer) have this thought: 'I have attained the fruit of stream-entry'?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? A srotāpanna is called one who has entered the stream, yet there is nothing entered.
He does not enter form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas; therefore he is called a srotāpanna."

The Buddha’s intention was this: although he previously demonstrated the subduing of the mind by focusing solely on the salvation of sentient beings, he feared that at the time of realizing the fruit [of enlightenment], one might still be unable to subdue it.
Therefore, he further elaborated upon the method for subduing the mind by means of the four fruits of the Hīnayāna.
*Srotāpanna* is the name for the first fruit of the Hīnayāna; the Sanskrit term *srotāpanna* is translated here as "entering the stream," which means:
Within the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one gives rise to the mind that seeks liberation from the realms and the cessation of grasping.

By means of sixteen moments of mind, one exhausts the afflictions of the three realms associated with the views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). Having for the first time perceived the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one enters the ranks of the noble ones (*ārya*);

therefore, they are called "Stream-enterers" (*srotāpanna*). This means that although they are not yet ultimate saints, they are nonetheless able to participate in their company. Thus, although they have only just glimpsed emptiness—
It is simply that one has already realized *anātman* (non-self). Because one is obscured by [the failure to realize] this principle, mindfulness cannot arise spontaneously.
When the Tathāgata asks whether one is able or not, he clearly knows the inability and asks nonetheless. "The self" (*ahaṃ*) refers to the mark of selfhood (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*).

To know that there is one capable of producing mindfulness is for the grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*) to persist; this contradicts the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Since Kṣemadatta was one who had already passed through [this stage], he...

He answered directly with "No. To speak of a noble one who has entered the stream (*srotāpanna*), it is impossible for them to remain ignorant of this principle and thus give rise to the thought that a self exists;
therefore, they certainly know that the mark of a self (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*) is absent.

Furthermore, although it is said that there is no self, if the notion of "mine" (*mama-kāra*) is not yet forgotten, the mark of a self has not been fully abandoned. Thus, responding to this inquiry, he proceeds to clarify the nature of the self.
There is also nothing that is attained. To speak of a "Srotāpanna" (Stream-enterer) is merely the name for "entering the stream," yet in reality there is no entering.
Because it is empty and devoid of form or characteristics, how could there truly be any trace of entering?

Since there is no trace of entering, that which is called "entering the noble stream by relying on the principle of emptiness" is likewise nothing more than a mere name. Nevertheless, the name does not manifest in vain.
There must be a reason for this; therefore it is said: "Not entering into form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental objects—this is called a Srotāpanna.

To say that one does not enter into form and so forth refers specifically to the severance of views (*dṛṣṭi*), because the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) consist of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) directed toward objects.
Once the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*) have been severed, there is no longer conceptualization of objects; therefore, it is said that one "does not enter form and so forth.

Since form and the rest are all objects of perception, this merely means not entering into them. In meaning, this resembles "entering" something else, and thus one is named "one who has entered the stream" (*srotāpanna*).
How could there truly be anything entered? One who understands this meaning realizes not only the absence of self (*anātman*), but furthermore—
There is no "mine," and when both [self and mine] are absent, this is true non-self. Where there is no self, there is no thought;
where there is no thought, there is no delusion to be extinguished. That the Tathāgata posed this question was for a very good reason. These two fruits are free from characteristics.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does a sakṛdāgāmin have this thought: 'I have attained the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin'?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? A sakṛdāgāmin is so called because he returns once more;
yet in reality there is no coming and going. It is for this reason that he is called a sakṛdāgāmin."
The *sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner) is the name for the second fruit of the Hīnayāna. In Sanskrit it is *sakṛdāgāmin*, which here means "one who comes back once.

This refers to one who, having previously exhausted the afflictions of view (*darśana-heya*) during the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), now, during the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), first abandons the thoughts of desire.

Within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), there are nine grades of these thought-afflictions (*saṃyojana*), namely: the highest-of-the-high (*adhimātrādhimātra*), the middle-of-the-high (*madhyādhimātra*), and so forth.
The grades are: upper-upper, upper-middle, upper-lower; middle-upper, middle-middle, middle-lower; lower-upper, lower-middle, and lower-lower.
The upper-upper grade moistens two births, meaning two births in the heavens and two returns to the human realm.
Only then can they be severed. The upper-middle and upper-lower grades each moisten one lifetime;
these three upper grades together moisten four lifetimes. The middle-upper grade moistens one lifetime; the middle-middle and middle-lower grades together moisten one lifetime;
these three middle grades together moisten two lifetimes. At this point, the first six grades of the desire-realm afflictions have been severed.

One immediately realizes the second fruit (sakṛdāgāmin). Of the remaining [defilements], those of the lower-upper grade moisten half a birth; those of the lower-middle and lower-lower grades together moisten half a birth.
These three lower grades combined moisten one full birth—meaning one goes once to the heavens and returns once to the human realm before they are severed.
Because of this, the second fruit is named "Once-returner" (sakṛdāgāmin). However, since one has already entered deeply into the principle, it is even more impossible [for them to return].
To form a thought while obscuring the principle is likewise a deliberate inquiry. The intent of the answer may be understood by reference to what preceded.
Why? Because this also further refutes the attachment to "mine. It says that a *sakṛdāgāmin* (Once-returner) is merely named "one who goes and returns," yet in reality there is no going or returning.
Within the principle of the emptiness of self (*ātman-śūnyatā*), how could there be any trace of going or returning? Since there are no traces of going or returning...
That which is called "realizing the fruit of once-returner by relying on the principle of emptiness" also refers exclusively to having severed the first six grades of afflictions;

this is termed a *sakṛdāgāmin*. The subduing of the mind and its faculties may be understood according to the above. Thus, the three fruits of the third [stage] are characterized by the absence of marks (*animitta*).
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does an Anāgāmin have this thought: ‘I have attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin’?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One. Why is that? An Anāgāmin is called ‘one who does not return,’ yet in reality there is no such non-returning; it is for this reason he is called an Anāgāmin.”
Anāgāmin is the name for the third fruit. In Sanskrit, *anāgāmin* means "one who does not come.

This refers to one who, having previously been in the stage of the second fruit, further severs the three lower grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). One thus realizes the third fruit.
From this point on, there is no longer any impulse to be reborn in the desire realm; one will never again return to receive birth there. For this reason, it is called "not coming."

"Come. However, since their entry into the principle is profound, they are likewise unable to harbor thoughts that obscure the principle; therefore, both their questions and answers are identical to what was previously stated.
In the section on investigation and explanation, it says that "Anāgāmin" (Non-returner) is merely a name for one who does not come back.
Yet, within the principle of the emptiness of self, there is in reality no characteristic of "not coming back"; it is simply because there are no afflictions to moisten rebirth in the desire realm.

Therefore, the provisional designation "Anāgāmin" is established; this too is fundamentally non-existent within the ultimate principle (*tattva*). This further refutes the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*).
Part Four: The Non-characteristic of the Four Fruits. Two sections: 1. Revealing non-attachment through question and answer;
2. Citing oneself as proof. First [section]:
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does an arhat have the thought, 'I have attained the path of an arhat'?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Because, in reality, there is no dharma that is called 'arhat'."
World-Honored One, if an Arhat should have this thought: "I have attained the path of Arhatship," he would then be attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
"Arhat" is the name for the fruit of the fourth stage; although it possesses three meanings, it is used here to accord with the meanings of "Once-Returner" and "Non-Returner."

To explain this by way of the "non-arising" [fruit]: it refers to one who, having previously exhausted the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) during the stages of the three fruits, is reborn in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
There, among the *anāgāmin* devas, they further sever the seventy-two grades of afflictions of the two upper realms, exhausting all such delusions of volition (*cetanā*).
Having transcended the triple world, he will never again undergo birth in a future existence; therefore, he is named by the title "Non-arising" (*anuppāda*).
Since his realization of the principle is perfect and he has deeply realized non-self (*anātman*), he cannot spontaneously form the notion of a self, nor does he answer out of any ulterior motive.
In the section providing the formal explanation, the statement that "in truth there is no dharma called an Arhat" is made because of the emptiness of self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

In principle, there is truly no dharma that does not arise that can be called an Arhat. Since principle has no form or characteristics, and one does not perceive arising, how could there be the characteristic of "non-arising"? This is what is meant by seeking the reality behind a name:
