if the reality lacks the meaning corresponding to the name, then even the "self" (ātman) is empty. To conceive the thought, "I have attained Arhatship," is itself to be attached to a self.
Because both the grasping at "I" and "mine" are present; since the mark of a self (ātman-lakṣaṇa) exists, the remaining three [marks] can be known, as they all arise based upon the mark of a self.
The section on clarifying detachment through question and answer is concluded. Second, citing one's own experience as proof.
“World-Honored One, the Buddha has declared that I have attained the samādhi of non-contention and am foremost among men;
he has declared me to be a *arhat* free from desire who stands at the pinnacle. World-Honored One, I do not harbor such a thought as: ‘I am an *arhat* free from desire. World-Honored One...”
If I were to have this thought, "I have attained the path of Arhatship," the World-Honored One would not say that Subhūti is one who delights in the practice of araṇā.
It is because Subhūti actually has nothing practiced that he is named Subhūti,
one who delights in the practice of araṇā.

Fearing that it might be thought that mindfulness resides within the mind—asking who it is that perceives what is done or not done—he thus again addressed the World-Honored One, citing his own experience as proof.

When he says "the Buddha taught," he refers to a different occasion; that is, the Buddha had previously made such a statement at another time, though he had simply not yet encountered the scriptural transmission (*śāsana*).
As for the Samādhi of Non-Contention (*araṇā-samādhi*), in principle there is neither subject nor object, and in practice all things are forgotten.
Standing alone like a horn, one does not compete with things; this is called "non-contention. At first, practice requires effort, and samādhi is not achieved;
after a long time, it becomes spontaneous, and then samādhi is perfected. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Subhūti dwells in the realm of empty space."
If there are sentient beings who resent me for standing, I shall remain seated upright all day long without rising.
If they resent me for sitting, I shall remain standing all day long without shifting my place. By thus not competing with things, no thing can prevail over me.
Therefore, he is the foremost among men. Not only is he the foremost among men, but he is also the foremost Arhat free from desire (*vītarāga*).
Because the absence of contention (*araṇā*) arises from freedom from desire, the pinnacle of the absence of contention is the pinnacle of freedom from desire.
Although all Arhats are free from desire, Śūnyatā-janman (Śāriputra) remains the foremost; for this reason, he is so designated.
The departure from desire occurs spontaneously, without relying on deliberate effort; thus, this itself may serve as the standard for subduing the mind.
How much more so since this was spoken by the Buddha—this is sufficient evidence that it is not false. Not to take pride in this is doubly difficult. Subhūti was not like this;
therefore, he again addressed the World-Honored One, saying, "I do not harbor such a thought: 'I am a desire-free Arhat. This is what Subhūti [meant].
By making this statement, his intention was to reveal that even when he had reached this state, he did not form such a thought, let alone other Arhats;
it is certain that they do not form such thoughts. Furthermore, fearing that others might say, "Now you yourself say you do not form such a thought—who will believe you?
he addressed the World-Honored One once more, saying, "If I were to form the thought, 'I have attained Arhatship'..."
In the Way of the Han [the Lesser Vehicle], both the two attachments of "self" and "what belongs to self" persist.

The Buddha, however, did not say, "Subhūti, you are one who delights in the practice of araṇā. *Araṇā* is translated here as "freedom from contention" (*li-yì*) and also as "quiescence" (*jì-jìng*), which carries the meaning of "non-contention" (*araṇa*).
Its intent is that the attachments to "self" and "what belongs to self" constitute the root of contention; thus, they are not quiescent.

"Quietude. If both were present, how could the World-Honored One have granted such a false assurance? This is an indirect demonstration (*paryudāsa*). What follows is the direct explanation (*vidhi*).
It is precisely because I, Subhūti, truly have no thought of practicing that the World-Honored One names me, Subhūti, "one who delights in the practice of araṇā.
Here, "practice" (*caryā*) is synonymous with "action" (*kriyā*), and the name is likewise explained as such; however—

This is merely a brief modification of the phrasing. However, the reason for elaborating on the subduing of the mind by specifically citing the four fruits of the Hīnayāna is to demonstrate that subduing the mind is not difficult;
it is sufficient simply to be free from the marks of "self" and "what belongs to self," as is the case with the four fruits of the Hīnayāna.
Verse: According to that Subhūti, it is said that one is free from the two kinds of obstacles.

Combined, it says: the character "upper" (shàng) in the preceding line should be connected with the word "verse" (shuō) in the following line. This verse generally summarizes the four sections concerning the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path].
Because all four sections are taught based on the discourse of Subhūti, they expound the removal of two kinds of hindrances, which is the intended meaning of what was taught.

Specifically, it is said that the first fruit removes the hindrance of afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), and the latter three fruits remove the hindrance of afflictions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*). This is because these [afflictions] obstruct the principle of selflessness (*anātman*).

Furthermore, the afflictions of view are the conceptual grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha-vikalpa*), while the afflictions of thought are the [afflictions] concomitant with the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha-sahaja*).

Birth. To be free from these two is to be without self (*anātman*). Being without self is the method for subduing the mind. This concludes the summary and expansion of the method for subduing the mind.
Second, the expansion of the method for abiding in the mind has two parts: first, non-abiding in the cultivation of causes;

second, non-abiding in the attainment of the fruit. The first has three parts: first, non-abiding in receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*); second, non-abiding in adorning the lands; third, the general conclusion.
[The Buddha] showed. First:
The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "What do you think? Did the Tathāgata, when he was formerly with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, obtain anything regarding the Dharma?
"No, World-Honored One. When the Tathāgata was with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he truly obtained nothing regarding the Dharma."
The Buddha’s intention was as follows: Previously, he demonstrated the abiding of the mind solely in terms of giving;

however, fearing that [the practitioner] might still be unable to abide securely while cultivating the causes and awaiting the fruit, he now further elaborates on the method for abiding the mind by means of receiving predictions and adorning the buddha-lands.

Dīpaṃkara Buddha was the teacher who bestowed the prophecy upon Śākyamuni during his second asaṃkhyeya-kalpa; thus, he described it himself, saying, "When the Tathāgata was formerly with Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
The word "formerly" (*xi*) here specifically refers to the period of the second asaṃkhyeya-kalpa.
At that time, the Tathāgata had already attained the eighth bhūmi, and it appears that regarding the method of bestowing prophecy, he truly possessed [realization].
[Subhūti] replied, “I have attained it. In reality, this was not so; therefore, the Buddha asked whether he had attained anything.
The Buddha’s intention was that if there is attainment, there is dwelling, and if there is dwelling, the awakened mind cannot abide.

Subhūti answered, “No,” because he already knew that the Tathāgata has no attainment regarding the dharma of bestowing predictions. He spoke simply as “no,” yet fearing it might not be clear, [the Buddha] further questioned him.
Therefore, it is further clarified by means of the Tathāgata’s presence among those such as Dīpaṃkara.
This is because the Dharma that is attained is manifested solely by one's own mind and one's own wisdom; it is not obtained through the conferral of a prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*).
Thus, we know that what is called a "prophecy" is merely the language and names used for the prophecy. Since it is merely language and names, we know [that it has no inherent reality].
One should not abide; when one does not abide, then one does not abide [in anything]. When there is no abiding, the awakened mind is eternally present.
It is for this reason that the Tathāgata posed his inquiry.
The verse says: "The Buddha did not grasp at the words of Dīpaṃkara; through the wisdom of ultimate reality, he established that non-grasping as the true meaning."
It is said.
Taken together, it means: the first phrase refers to the words of the prediction received by the Buddha in the past from the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
"Not grasping" means that regarding those words of prediction, one does not give rise to fixation or grasping; for within the prediction...

Because, in reality, there is no dharma that can be apprehended. If this is so, when one ascends to the eighth stage and realizes the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), what is the nature of that principle of non-arising?
It is because, in ultimate reality, it is manifested solely by one's own wisdom; therefore, it is called "the ultimate reality of wisdom.
That which is the true meaning refers to what is manifested within one’s own mind and one’s own wisdom.
Because it is the ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*), although one is able to accomplish that patience, one likewise does not grasp at what was spoken by Dīpaṃkara;

therefore, it is said that one accomplishes that teaching of non-grasping. This concludes the section on attaining the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) through non-abiding. Second is the non-abiding in the adornment of the land.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does a bodhisattva adorn buddha-fields? "No, World-Honored One. Why is this?
That which is called 'adorning a buddha-field' is not actually adorning; it is merely designated as 'adornment.'"

Although he has received the prediction [of enlightenment], he does not abide therein; yet, fearing that he might still harbor attachments regarding the adornment of the Buddha-land, this section further clarifies non-abiding by means of the adornment of the land.
To "adorn the Buddha-land" means that one practices the Way within it during the causal stage and attains Buddhahood within it during the resultant stage;
thus, the practitioner who cultivates the Way is precisely adorning the reward-land (vipākabhūmi) of the resultant stage. It is based upon this...
[The meaning is as follows: It appears as if there were a land that could be adorned, but in reality this is not so; therefore, he asks whether one adorns the Buddha-land.
The Buddha’s intention is that where there is adornment, there is dwelling; since the awakened mind does not dwell, it is the same as what was explained above.
Subhūti answers "No," for he already knows that there is no land that can be adorned. Why does [the Buddha] then question him with the phrase "Adorn..."? Below...
Explanation: The so-called "adornment of the Buddha-land" refers solely to the adornment of one's own mind;

it does not refer to the adornment of the land of retribution (*vipākabhūmi*). Therefore, it is said that it is "not [an adornment]. This is because the lands of retribution in the state of fruition are all manifested by mind-only and consciousness-only.
To adorn one's own mind is itself to adorn the land of retribution, for when the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.
Because it is pure, one knows that what is called "adornment" is merely a name; therefore, it is said, "this is named adornment.
Since it is an adornment by name only, one should not dwell upon the adornment of the land.
Verse: Through the mastery of consciousness-only by means of wisdom, one thus grasps the pure land; it is not a physical form, for its primary substance is not ornamentation.
The commentary states: The first line indicates that a bodhisattva who wishes to adorn the land of retribution must first rely upon the *prajñā* of contemplative observation to practice.
One practices the meditative concentration on mind-only consciousness. If one realizes that the three realms are mind-only and all phenomena are consciousness-only, this constitutes penetration.

The next phrase states that once one has realized that the three realms are mind-only and all phenomena are consciousness-only, one then takes up a pure land based upon this principle of mind-only and consciousness-only. Thus, that which is adorned is not a land of physical form, but rather—
Regarding the term "essence" (*tattva*) in reference to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*): it is because the ultimate truth is one's own mind, which serves as the essence of all lands.
The final phrase concludes and synthesizes the scriptural text;

when it says "that which is formless," this refers to the meaning of "non-adornment" in the sutra—namely, that the ultimate truth is the essence of all lands. This is because the mind is pure and thus the land is pure.
This is what is called "adorning the mind" in the sutra. The section on adorning the lands without abiding is concluded. Third, the summary and conclusion:
Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to a pure mind in this way.

They should not give rise to a mind by abiding in form; they should not give rise to a mind by abiding in sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas. They should give rise to [a mind] without abiding anywhere.
"Regarding that mind:
'Therefore, etc. means that because both [the subject and object] do not abide as described above, he calls out to Subhūti to summarize and demonstrate this.
The intent is that, generally speaking, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, at all times, one..."
In all circumstances, one should in this manner give rise to a pure mind without dwelling [upon objects]. This "pure mind" refers precisely to the awakened mind (*bodhicitta*).
"One should not dwell upon form to give rise to the mind" means that at the time of perceiving form, one should not give rise to the mind by dwelling with attachment to form;
for to give rise to the mind by dwelling upon form is itself a deluded mind. One should not...
The arising of the mind in dependence on sounds and so forth can be understood by analogy with this. "One should have no place of abiding" means that one should not abide in any phenomena whatsoever;
to give rise to the mind while having no abode at all is precisely the awakened mind (*bodhicitta*). In this way, the awakened mind is eternally abiding.
This concludes the section on the non-abiding cultivation of causes. Second is the non-abiding attainment of the fruit.
Subhūti, suppose there were a person whose body was as large as Sumeru, the king of mountains. What do you think?
Would that body be great? Subhūti replied: It would be very great, World-Honored One. Why is this? Because the Buddha has taught that it is not a body; it is called a "great body" only by name.
Although there is no abiding in the cultivation of causes, one may still fear that at the time of attaining the fruit, one has not yet been able to let go of attachment;
therefore, this further clarifies non-abiding by means of the *vipākakāya* (retribution body).

For example, suppose there is a person whose mind represents a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva whose vows and practices are fully perfected, who manifests at the stage of Akaniṣṭha as the highest and greatest being in all worlds.
[The Buddha spoke of] the body; therefore, he used Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, as a metaphor.
Since Mount Sumeru was used as a metaphor, it might appear to be the highest and largest body, but in reality this is not so. Therefore, he asked, "Is this body large?
The Buddha’s intention was that if one grasps at characteristics, it cannot be called "large," because it possesses measurable dimensions. As for Mount Sumeru, it [surrounds] the four continents.
It is the Great Central Mountain. In the Sanskrit language it is called Sumeru; here it is translated as "Wondrously High" (Miaogao).
Its substance is composed of four jewels, and for this reason it is called "wondrous. It rises eighty-four thousand *yojanas* above the water, and for this reason it is called "high.
It surpasses the seven golden mountains, and for this reason it is called the "King. Now, since it rises only eighty-four thousand *yojanas* above the water...
Although this is large, it has a measurable quantity that can be recorded. In the answer, the text does not merely say "large," but rather says "extremely large.
This is because Subhūti also knows that what the Tathāgata teaches does not involve grasping at signs (*nimitta*).

In the section providing the proof and explanation, the statement "the Buddha says it is not a body" means that although the Buddha speaks of the body as being like Mount Sumeru, he does not do so by grasping at its having signs.
This is the body [of the Buddha]. Therefore, I say it is "extremely great. This is because one contemplates the body by way of its signlessness (*animitta*), as it transcends all measure and number.
If one were to grasp only the body that possesses signs (*sanimitta*), it would merely be called "great" in name; it would not be truly great.
Since it would not be truly great, the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) could have no abiding place.
Verse: Just as the King of Mountains has no grasping or receiving of retribution, so it is with this; for it is far removed from all outflows (*āsrava*) and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Combined explanation: The first line first employs a simile, meaning that although that King of Mountains is high and vast, it does not...
One might think of oneself as high or great; however, because the King of Mountains has no abiding mind, the subsequent phrase applies this by analogy to the Dharma:
it means that although the Buddha receives a body of karmic retribution, he does not grasp at that retribution, because the Buddha possesses no abiding mind.
This can be understood through analogy; therefore, it is said that "it is likewise so. Not abiding in retribution means seeing the Dharmakāya within retribution itself;
hence, it is said to be "far removed from all outflows (āsrava) and conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma)," because the Dharmakāya is by nature unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and free from outflows.
This unconditioned, outflow-free nature is pervasive horizontally and exhaustive vertically. As for that Sambhogakāya, what else...?
It is truly magnificent. This concludes the summary of the correct [teaching] and the expansion [of its meaning]. Part Two: A Brief Demonstration of Completeness, in three sections:

(1) Comparing the Merit of Upholding; (2) Using the Inferior to Illustrate the Superior; (3) Requesting the Title of the Sutra. The first two [sections] consist of: (1) That which can compare; (2) That which is compared.
The first of these two consists of: (1) Fully manifesting the vast number of Ganges sands; (2) Fully manifesting the gift of jewels.
"Much merit, Subhūti.
Suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River. What do you think, Subhūti?
Would the grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers be numerous? Subhūti replied, "Very numerous, World-Honored One. But these...
The Ganges alone is already beyond counting; how much more so its sands?
The sands within the Ganges are as fine as flour; when calculated by number, their count may truly be called vast.

Furthermore, if one were to take such sands and use them to calculate the number of rivers—counting as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand—their number would be equal to that of the sands. As for those rivers...
It may be said that they are many. The number of sands in all these Ganges Rivers is naturally immense.
When asked whether it is indeed many, the Buddha did not answer himself; he wished for Subhūti to provide the response, thereby using this to manifest that the numbers in the lower realms are vast.
Subhūti replied that they are indeed very many, yet he further stated, "But as for those Ganges Rivers," etc., which is precisely—
This is because one sees that the answer given is not false. Second, it clearly demonstrates that the merit of giving precious things is vast.

Subhūti, I now tell you this in truth: if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, with the seven treasures, filled as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers and used them for giving, the merit they would obtain would be great.
"No. Subhūti said, "Very much, World-Honored One.
I now speak these words of truth: although I am here, my intention is to calculate the merit;
for I fear that the merit would be so great as to be difficult to believe, and thus I wish to ensure that it is certainly believed. 'As many as those' refers to all those [Ganges Rivers]."
There is the Ganges River; this refers to the Ganges River mentioned previously when calculating the number of grains of sand.

Regarding the phrase "the number of sands equaling three thousand," etc.: furthermore, by using the sands from these many rivers to calculate the number of worlds, it can be known that the worlds are exceedingly numerous.
Yet, one fills them with the seven treasures and uses them for giving; the merit obtained from such an act is truly immense.
That it is much goes without saying. When asked whether the merit obtained is great or not, the Buddha did not speak for himself;
rather, he desired to have Śūnyatā (Subhūti) provide the answer, so as to establish a standard of comparison for the merit of upholding and reciting [the sutra] that follows.

By answering that it is "very much," [the Buddha] indicates that the merit of upholding and reciting it is still superior even to this. This concludes the section on establishing the standard of comparison.
Second, the comparative measurement.

The Buddha told Subhūti: "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, from within this sutra, were to receive, uphold, and even recite as little as a four-line verse for others, the merit of this would surpass the former merit."
...up to the receiving and upholding [of this sutra], which may be understood by analogy with what precedes. As for why this merit surpasses the previous merit:
the former consists of conditioned and out-flowing (sāsrava) merit, whereas this consists of unconditioned and non-out-flowing (anāsrava) merit. As the *Mengyin* states:

"If one were to give away treasures as numerous as the sands of the Ganges yet fail to understand one's own mind, but upon hearing and reciting this sutra, one perceives one's nature within a single phrase and, through the perception of nature, attains Buddhahood—whose merit is greater?"

It may be compared. Therefore, it is said that this merit surpasses the former. An ancient worthy said: "A single mani-jewel outweighs a thousand varieties of oceanic treasures"—this may serve as a simile.
Although the comparison was not long ago, it is compared once again because the meaning becomes progressively deeper.

Verse: It is said that even a small amount of merit, when differentiated by many meanings, becomes a superior comparison; because the subsequent merit exceeds the former, a further superior analogy is stated.
To synthesize: the first two lines of the verse repeat the comparison. The intention behind the phrase "differentiated by many meanings" refers to the interpretation.

Regarding what has been explained since the section on "Analysis": as shown previously, the section on "Faith" involved many different aspects, such as the subduing of the mind, which was discussed solely in terms of delivering sentient beings;
this [section], however, specifically discusses the causes and effects of the Hīnayāna. As for the previous demonstration of the "Abiding Mind," it was presented in that manner.

This refers exclusively to *dāna* (generosity). This, moreover, is stated specifically in terms of the cause and fruit of the Mahāyāna. The word "also" (*api*) serves as an analogy to the preceding section on faith (*śraddhā*).

Since the excellence of the karma within the section on faith has already been demonstrated through comparative analysis, and since this [section on generosity] possesses many distinct meanings when compared to that preceding section.

This also establishes the meaning of the excellence of merit through comparative evaluation. The following two lines of the verse express the intention of evaluating superiority over the preceding [merit].

The analogy for the "factor of faith" (*śraddhāṅga*) as that which performs the evaluation is restricted solely to the gift of jewels within a single world-system; this, however, is the analogy for what performs the evaluation herein.
This refers to those who give jewels throughout as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.

By means of the merit from upholding and reciting the latter portion [of this sutra], it surpasses the merit from upholding and reciting the former portion. Therefore, within the section on the measurement of merit, the superior analogy that exceeds the previous one is stated again.
For "analogy" (*dṛṣṭānta*) means comparison; here, the gift of jewels serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna-dharma*). This concludes the measurement of the merit of upholding [the sutra].
The section on merit concludes. Second, comparing the inferior with the superior in two parts: first, even merely explaining it is superior; second, how much more so for upholding it in its entirety.
Regarding the first: furthermore, Subhūti, wherever this sutra is explained, even as little as a single four-line verse, you should know that this place—1.
All those in the world—gods, humans, and asuras—should all make offerings to this [teaching] as they would to a stupa or temple of the Buddha.
Fearing that it might be thought that practicing both [retention and exposition] simultaneously benefits oneself and others, with merit surpassing the former, there is no need for further debate.
Even if one lacks the merit of personal retention, if one expounds it for others as the occasion arises, it may not necessarily bring merit; therefore, [this is emphasized].

This is stated to manifest excellence according to the context of the discourse. Furthermore, "Subhūti" refers to the repeated calling of the recipient of the teaching to address him again during the course of this comparative exposition.

"Whoever preaches this sutra" means that regardless of whether the capacity [of the listener] is great or small, whether the text is extensive or concise, whether the location is superior or inferior, or whether the duration is long or short—following these [conditions]...
He then expounded it. Because it was not spoken with insincerity, he spoke of "even a four-line verse," referring to the very minimum of what might be taught.

"In this place" refers to the location where it was preached; since people often neglect such places, he taught that they should recognize its significance, thereby making it clear that one must not treat it with indifference.
"All worlds" encompasses the fourfold assembly by way of their mental inclinations; "gods, humans, and asuras" encompasses the eight classes of beings by way of their mental inclinations.

"All should be honored" means that these people are sent by the Buddha and the Dharma is spoken by the Buddha; because they propagate [the teaching] on behalf of the Buddha, they are identical to the Buddha being present.
"Like a stupa or a temple" refers to the fact that a stupa enshrines the Buddha’s body and a temple contains the Buddha’s likeness;
since the whole world knows to offer them worship, they are used as a metaphor. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "If one can secretly preach the *Lotus Sūtra* for even a single person... and so forth.
A single phrase: such a person is sent by the Tathāgata to perform the work of the Tathāgata. Since this sutra follows that teaching, it should likewise be so;
therefore, its location is most excellent. Furthermore, if even the location is most excellent, the person may be known [to be so].
Having concluded that even following the teaching is superior, how much more so is it to uphold it in its entirety?
How much more so for anyone who is able to fully receive, uphold, read, and recite it.
Subhūti, you should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme, foremost, and rare Dharma. Wherever this sutra is located, there is a Buddha, as well as his honored disciples.
This further has two parts. First, the primary analogy regarding the excellence of the person. Fearing that it might be thought:

"If the honor and supremacy of one who merely recites this sutra are such as this, then what must the status of one be who, though unable to recite it, is able to uphold it entirely?"—therefore, the text takes the person who merely recites it as a basis for comparison to further illustrate the point.
It says that even a person who merely recites it is already so honorable and supreme.
This is so; how much more so for one who is able to fully receive, uphold, read, and recite it? Such a person’s own benefit will naturally be even more supreme.
Therefore, he addresses the intended recipient again to instruct them with the words "you should know," and so forth. As for "accomplishment" (*siddhi*), it means being perfectly complete.
The *prajñā* of the true nature (*dharmatā*) is called "supreme," because it is that which all Buddhas have realized. The *prajñā* of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*) is called...
First, because it awakens the initial resolve for enlightenment, the Prajñā of Words (vyañjana-prajñā) is called rare.
Because it is taught in accordance with the proper time, all three types of Prajñā are contained within this sutra; therefore, those who are able to receive and uphold it in its entirety—
One will then be able to achieve success. If [the location] is inferior, the second [point] additionally clarifies the excellence of the site.

Lest it be thought that the place where the teaching was spoken is as venerable and supreme as the teaching itself, or lest one wonder what should be done regarding the actual location where the sūtra resides, the text therefore demonstrates this by referring to the location where the sūtra is situated.
As for the location of the scripture, it matters not whether it be a caitya, a stūpa, a temple, a pagoda, or an altar.
This refers to any place where offerings such as banners are installed; it is precisely because [the Buddha] exists there that it is considered a site of the Buddha, for it is the Dharmakāya.
Furthermore, if there are disciples who are worthy of veneration, this is because they possess discriminative wisdom (*pratisaṃvid*).

Regarding why disciples are said to be "worthy of veneration," it means they each possess a specific virtue by which they may be honored and esteemed, such as Śāriputra’s wisdom or Maudgalyāyana’s supernormal powers.
Each claimed that it was the foremost of such [miracles]. Furthermore, this scripture is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and is the common reliance of the noble ones and sages;
therefore, it is said that "there is a Buddha" therein. Regarding the passage on "honoring disciples," the *Mengyin* (Cloud of Inspiration) states:

For example, there was one Xun Sheng of Xinfan in Yizhou who pointed at empty space and painted upon it to transcribe the scripture. It immediately became a single expanse of vajra-ground, and even to this day, auspicious clouds occasionally shroud it.
The rain does not moisten it, yet grass does not grow; how could this sutra not be extraordinary?
Is this not so? Verse: One honors the two bases; through causal cultivation, one realizes the Great Essence.
The commentary states: This combines the meaning of the preceding section and this current section. "Veneration" (*guruka*) means to respect and cherish.
"Two locations" refers to the place where the sutra is preached and the place where the sutra resides. Furthermore, "veneration" also encompasses making offerings (*pūjā*).
This means that all sentient beings should respect and cherish [this teaching], making various kinds of offerings and never treating it with negligence.

To explain the reason for this, the text cites the phrase "due to cultivation" (*xi*). This indicates that because there is the sense of "perfuming" (*vāsanā*) through two aspects—namely, being able to hear and being able to uphold—it is capable of realizing the Great Body (*mahā-kāya*).
What is called the "Great Body" is precisely the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which is pervasive horizontally and exhaustive vertically; therefore [it must be honored].

It is called "Great" because it serves as the basis for the *nirmāṇakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*; thus, it is called the "Essence. This concludes the summary that uses the inferior to illustrate the superior.

Part Three: Requesting the Name of the Sūtra and Its Bestowal. This has two sections: First, the request for the name and its commitment to uphold; Second, the Tathāgata’s response to the request by revealing the name. Regarding the first:
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what should this sutra be named?
How should we uphold it?

Since the efficacy of its subduing and stabilizing power has already been manifested, and its excellence through comparison has also been revealed, it seems there should be nothing further to say; therefore—
The assembly requests the name for upholding [the teaching]: "By what name should this sutra be called? This is the request for the title.
As the ancient masters said: "To explain the meaning based solely on the literal text is to be at enmity with the Buddhas of the three periods."
"To deviate from a single word of the sutra is equivalent to the teaching of Māra. To prevent these two [extremes], he asks, "How should it be upheld?
This is the request for its retention. Second, the Tathāgata, in accordance with this request, provides the instruction.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "This sūtra is named the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
By this name, you should uphold it. Why is that? Subhūti, what the Buddha calls *prajñāpāramitā* is not actually *prajñāpāramitā*; it is merely designated as *prajñāpāramitā*."
As for why this sutra is named *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*: it is because the *prajñā* elucidated herein is like a vajra in its hardness and sharpness;
it is the ultimate dharma that enables one to reach the other shore (*pāramitā*), as no other sutra can equal it.
This indicates its name. "By means of this name, you should uphold it" means by means of this [name], "Vajra..."
"Vajra-prajñā-pāramitā" is its name. You all should receive and uphold it by reflecting upon its meaning as derived from its name.
Within the section on the inquiry and explanation, it asks: Why does the Tathāgata instruct them to receive and uphold it by means of its name?

It is because the term "vajra" possesses two meanings: firmness and sharpness. By virtue of the meaning of firmness, one knows that prajñā is indestructible and can truly reach the other shore; therefore—
The Buddha taught the Prajñāpāramitā; one should uphold it according to the words.

Because of its benefit and meaning, one knows that Prajñā does not abide and reaches that which is nowhere to be reached; therefore, it is not "Prajñāpāramitā. One should uphold it by departing from words.
This is what is meant by "merely nominally existent"; hence it is said, "this is called," and so forth.
The verse states: Because he has cultivated those afflictions, this [bodhisattva] subdues defilement; his merit, body, and victory surpass that [of others], being rare and supreme.
His wisdom-realm is immeasurable, and unlike other dharmas, his firm and solid realization of the profound meaning excels the other sūtras.
Regarding the phrase "the cause of great merit and the most excellent merit among pure merits," it should be understood as follows:
the first four lines contrast this with what precedes to manifest its superiority. The word "that" (*tat*) refers to the merit of giving material wealth (*dāna*).

Because that cause is *sāsrava* (with outflows), it possesses the quality of perfuming (*vāsanā*), and thus it can give rise to all afflictions (*kleśa*), such as greed and hatred, which all depend upon the *sāsrava*.
Because it arises from the perfuming of outflows (*āsrava*). This refers to this sutra. "Subduing" (*parājaya*) has the meaning of "counteracting.

The two characters "defiled merit" (*sāsrava-puṇya*) should be connected with the following phrase "body of suffering" (*duḥkha-kāya*). Since defiled merit is merit associated with outflows, it can serve as the cause for a body of suffering;
because this sutra can counteract that [merit], it is superior to it. Thus, this sutra is not... [incomplete].
Because it encompasses all that exists in the world, it is called "rare. Because it is able to transcend the world, it is said to have the meaning of "surpassing.
That wisdom—this refers to the meaning of the verse—is the wisdom of *prajñā*. It is that which "is able to reach," while the "other shore" is *nirvāṇa*, that which is reached.
Since both are profoundly deep, they are called "immeasurable"; furthermore, they are not the same as other dharmas.
The term "this" distinguishes it from the Hīnayāna and from the mere characteristics of phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*), as it is not merely profound.
"Solid" means as solid as a vajra; "explaining the profound meaning" means as sharp as a vajra.

This is not stated in terms of the sharpness that clarifies the destruction of delusions, because it is explained by way of mutual implication with the aforementioned subduing of defiled merit. It surpasses other phrases; this name should be honored accordingly.
It is upheld. When the Buddha speaks of the *prajñāpāramitā*, that which can bring about great causes is not itself the *prajñāpāramitā*;
it is that which can cause purification. One should uphold it in this manner. Among all merits, it is the most supreme merit, meaning that it is also not the same as other dharmas.
This concludes the brief summary showing its complete sufficiency. Part Three: The Exhaustive Severance.

There are three remaining doubts: first, the doubt as to why it is necessary to insist on calling the abandonment [of defilements] "definitive"; second, the doubt as to how the abandonment is included within the realms when there is no mention of them;
third, the doubt as to how the characteristics manifest when the name "realm" is abandoned. First:
"Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata preached any dharma? Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has preached nothing."
He feared that [the interlocutor] might think: "The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma does not establish names and characteristics.
Since it is merely names, why must one insist on explaining them? Therefore, he asked: "What do you think? Do you suppose that the Tathāgata has any dharma to teach? The Buddha’s intention was this:

if one grasps at the words as they are spoken, it appears as though there is a dharma to be taught; however, if one attains the meaning and forgets the words, how could one possibly cling stubbornly to the literal text?
[This is] a word. Therefore, when the Tathāgata was approaching his parinirvāṇa, Mañjuśrī requested the Buddha to turn the Wheel of Dharma once more.
The Buddha said: "I have dwelt in this world for forty-nine years, yet I have never spoken a single word.
Do you suppose that I have ever turned the Wheel of Dharma? The Buddha now poses a question identical to that one; simply observe how Śūnyatā-janman (Subhūti) understands it.
[The Buddha] said, "Empty-born (Subhūti), you too are a clever lad; with a single prompt, you were awakened.

Thus he replied that the Tathāgata has no teaching—what is called "returning home, there is no need to ask about the path," or "reaching the shore, a boat is not required. Second, [the Buddha] severed the doubt as to how the non-existence of speech could encompass the realms of phenomena.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Are all the atoms contained within a trichiliocosm many?
Subhūti replied, "Very many, World-Honored One. "Subhūti, those atoms which the Tathāgata has spoken of are not atoms; they are called 'atoms' by the Tathāgata.
That which the Tathāgata has spoken of as a 'world' is not a world; it is called a 'world' by the Tathāgata."
Although Śūnyatā-utpanna replied that there is no teaching, this does not mean that there is absolutely no teaching.
What is meant is simply that the illness is removed while the medicine is not retained, for one fears that those who cling to the medicine might themselves fall ill.

If it were truly the case that there is absolutely no teaching, how could the Tathāgata gather and transform beings throughout the three thousandfold world-system as the Master of Dharma? For this reason, the Tathāgata calls out to those whose faculties are appropriate.
He addressed him by name and inquired of him. This was because the three-thousandfold world system is formed by the aggregation of minute particles;

therefore, he asked whether the atoms contained within that world-system were many or not. The Buddha’s intention was that since these atoms can be analyzed into emptiness and the world-system is but a provisional existence, [Subhūti should have understood this].
Yet, Subhūti had not yet grasped the Buddha’s meaning and replied that they were "very many. This is what is called "a fine case."
"Venerable sir, you have gone off in such a manner again. Seeing that he did not understand, the Tathāgata called him by name to rescue him, saying:
"As for what are called 'all minute particles,' the Tathāgata says they are not minute particles, because they can be analyzed further and further."
Because they can be made empty, one knows that atoms have no substantial essence; they are merely provisional designations. Therefore it is said, "These are called atoms.
By this one knows that when the Tathāgata speaks of worlds, they are not worlds, for they appear to exist when combined, yet cease to exist when analyzed.
Thus one knows that worlds, too, are merely provisional designations; therefore it is said, "These are called worlds."
Regarding the doubt concerning the manifestation of the marks of the three types of abandonment called "elements," [the Buddha asked]:
"Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks?
"No, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks. Why is this? The Tathāgata has said..."
These two marks are, in fact, non-marks; this is what is called the thirty-two marks.
Fearing that one might think the world consists of nothing but names and has nothing upon which to rely, [the Buddha asks: "How does the Tathāgata manifest these marks based on the elements (dhātu)?
To prevent this doubt, he asks, "What do you think?"—will you say that the Tathāgata can be seen by means of the thirty-two marks?

"Is it not so, Tathāgata? [Subhūti asked. The Buddha’s intention was that since the *dhātu* (element) is not a *dhātu* and the *lakṣaṇa* (mark) is not a *lakṣaṇa*, and both arise from conditions, what obstacle could there be to their mutual dependence?
Knowing the Buddha’s intention, Subhūti, who delighted in emptiness, answered directly: "No, World-Honored One. One cannot see the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.
His meaning was that one sees the true Buddha only by being free from marks. He should have said this himself...
There is only the true realm (*dharmadhātu*) as the basis. In the section of inquiry and explanation, it says that when the Tathāgata speaks of the thirty-two marks, they are "not-marks.
This is because the marks manifest based upon the nature (*prakṛti*); those who cling to the marks will inevitably become deluded regarding the nature.
Therefore, it is said that they are "not [marks]. Thus, one knows that the thirty-two marks exist only as names; hence, it is said, "this is called the thirty-two marks."
Furthermore, one must not cling to characteristics and thereby become deluded regarding their nature. Now, that by which all sentient beings attain liberation is the Buddha.

That upon which all Buddhas rely to manifest their forms is the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). That by which they encompass the realm and deliver sentient beings, relying upon it to accomplish their transformation, is the Dharma.
If there were a fixed dharma that could be expounded, then one would be unable to encompass the realm; for the realm is without [fixed characteristics].
Because it is fixed. If there were a real realm upon which to rely, then one could not manifest signs, for signs follow conditions.
Thus we know that the Tathāgata, following the conditions of sentient beings, manifests the sign of the moon in water; relying on the realm of empty flowers, he teaches the dharma of the valley echo.
One realizes that these three are merely provisional names; their activity arises profusely yet remains non-abiding. Pure, singular awakening does not harbor even the slightest obstruction.
Wisdom is eternally still yet its reflection is all-pervasive. Although it is said that all remaining doubts are severed, it also demonstrates the awakened mind so that one may abide within it.
Regarding these three sections, there are no verses by Maitreya because they arose from the inquiry into the names of the sūtras and are not part of the formal exposition.
This concludes the summary and extension of the section on descending and abiding. Second, the accomplishment of the wisdom of understanding has five parts:

first, evaluating the merit of the sūtra; second, expressing faith, understanding, and admiration; third, clarifying the remaining perfections by analogy; fourth, synthesizing the preceding statements; and fifth, dispelling doubts.
To assist in understanding:
First, Subhūti, if there were good sons or good daughters who were to give away their bodies and lives as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
yet if there were another person who, from within this sutra, were to receive, uphold, or even recite as little as a four-line verse for the sake of others and explain it to them.
The merit thereof is exceedingly great.

Other doubts have been exhausted, and resolute conviction is about to be established. While the gift of external wealth such as jewels cannot be measured, this [merit] is further compared by means of internal wealth—the body and life.
It is said that among all sentient beings, what is most beloved is the body, and what is most precious is life.
Furthermore, the gift of one’s body may be easy, but the gift of one’s life is still difficult. Now, to perform both gifts simultaneously—its merit may indeed be called great.

Moreover, in a single lifetime, there is but one body and one life. When it is said here that [the merit is as vast as] the sands of the Ganges, it demonstrates that this is not limited to one, ten, a hundred, or a thousand lifetimes;
rather, it intends for every birth and every age to offer one's body...

He was commanded to practice giving; the merit thereof may indeed be called great. Yet, though it be described as "great" or "much," if one does not forget the conceptual mark of giving (*dāna-nimitta*), one still remains within the realm of outflows (*sāsrava*).
This is like those in the world who sacrifice their bodies to achieve righteousness or relinquish their lives to dwell in fame—such as Bi Gan and Jizi.
Among them, we have never heard of anyone accomplishing the work of Buddhahood. Although this sutra consists of but a single verse or a single phrase, [it is like...]
A single grain of *vajra* is to be upheld and expounded; it will never be digested, whether consumed by oneself or given to others, yet when brought forth, it is of great utility.
Therefore, it is said that its merit is exceedingly vast, for it cannot be equaled by the gift of as many bodies and lives as there are sands in the Ganges.
Verse: One who is able to endure ascetic practices does so because those practices possess goodness; their merit is immeasurable.
According to this supreme meaning, being free from self and malice, there is truly no suffering; rather, there is joy and compassion. Such is the fruit of ascetic practice:
arising from an undaunted mind, it constitutes cultivation and steadfastness, serving as the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

The combined explanation states: The first three lines of the verse praise the abundance of merit from giving. To give away one’s body and life as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is itself the practice of enduring hardship (*duṣkara*).
For if one were unable to endure, it would be difficult to give away even a single body or a single life, let alone as many as the sands of the Ganges.
As for the goodness inherent in such ascetic practices (*duṣkara*), it means that through those ascetic practices, one achieves that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Regarding "wholesome dharmas": because one has not yet forgotten their signs (*nimitta*), that merit is immeasurable;
this means that although it belongs to wholesome dharmas with outflows (*sāsrava*), when viewed by worldly wisdom, the merit obtained therein is likewise immeasurable.

The next four lines praise the excellence of the merit of upholding and expounding [this teaching]. "Such is the most supreme meaning" refers to that which is elucidated by this sutra; it is indeed supreme.

Because it is the true ultimate nature within the meaning [of reality], one who maintains this does not perceive a self; hence it is said to be "free from self. Being free from self, all oppositions are severed;
therefore, even hatred is abandoned, for hatred arises from opposition. Since hatred is abandoned, suffering and affliction are no longer perceived;
thus it is said that they "truly do not exist. This serves as a counter-illumination, showing that although he [the practitioner] is able to...
Patience. At times, there may still be anger, for one has not yet completely forgotten the marks of suffering and affliction.
If one speaks thus, wishing for others to share in joy and possessing both compassion and mercy, then both this practice and this teaching become untainted (*anāsrava*).
It is clear that the internal merit of such giving is by no means comparable [to external giving]. The final four lines state the reason why it is superior, saying that "one who is thus able..."
Regarding the merit resulting from enduring hardships and practicing asceticism, it does not equal that of one who upholds and expounds [the teachings].

This is because at the time of receiving such merit, there may arise a mind of stinginess or greed that refuses to relinquish [possessions], and there are those who consequently create negative karma on that account.
Furthermore, by thus relying on the teachings to uphold and expound them, one cultivates the two benefits for self and others as well as firm resolve; therefore, it is able to surpass the former.
Regarding the donor: it is because at the time of upholding and expounding [the teaching], they achieve the power of firm endurance;

by means of this, there are those who reach the further shore. Having completed the comparative evaluation of the merit of the sutra, there are three parts concerning the response of faith and understanding and its expression of wonder:

first, the hearing, understanding, and compassionate resonance of those for whom the teaching is intended; second, the praise of the merit of faith and understanding; third, the Tathāgata’s seal of approval and certification.
Commentary: First.
At that time, Subhūti, having heard this sutra being preached, deeply understood its meaning and intent; he wept with tears of sorrow and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare it is, World-Honored One! That the Buddha has preached such a profound sutra as this. From the past until now, the wisdom I have attained..."
The Eye has never before heard such a sutra as this.
"At that time" refers to the period from the beginning of the orthodox teaching until the conclusion of this present comparative analysis.

When first hearing the brief demonstration of descending and abiding, one merely gives rise to faith following the words; subsequently, upon hearing the expanded exposition of descending and abiding, one then awakens.

The thorns in my breast gradually dissolved. When I requested the names of the sutras, I already possessed a slight understanding; now that the three doubts have been completely purified, I am thoroughly enlightened.
Furthermore, I have heard that internal wealth is not as valuable as [the Dharma] by comparison; from this point on, the celestial signs of the principles will shine forth brilliantly.
Therefore it is said: "Upon hearing this sutra being preached, one deeply understands its meaning and intent. Furthermore, "meaning" (*artha*) refers to the distinct characteristics of phenomena;
for example, the analytical methods for subduing and stabilizing the mind are each different according to the specific practice. "Intent" (*tātparya*) refers to the ultimate destination of principle;

for example, the teachings on subduing and stabilizing the mind all converge in the single state of non-conditioned reality (*asaṃskṛta*). If one only understands the literal meaning, it cannot yet be called "deep"; only when one understands both...
This is what is meant by "profound. Furthermore, when one first hears a brief indication, one merely uses one's own mind as a torch to illuminate the subtle purport of the sutra;
thus, only pure faith is established. Subsequently, upon hearing the exposition expanded, one is then able to use the meaning of the sutra to reflect and examine one's own mind.

Thus, the profound understanding achieved through integration culminates in extreme joy, which in turn gives rise to sorrow. This is why he weeps and wails, like one long separated from a compassionate parent who suddenly encounters them;
unable to restrain himself, his heart is moved by a profound melancholy as he laments his long-standing lack of such fortune.

What flows from the nose is called *tei* (nasal mucus); what flows from the eyes is called *rei* (tears); great lamentation is called *hi* (sorrow); and slight pain is called *seki* (weeping). This refers to the beginning.
He shed tears; following this, he wailed loudly; thereafter, he wept softly. As for "weeping softly," it means that having restrained his intense grief, he was about to speak;
thus he addressed the Buddha, saying: "Rare indeed! This has three meanings: first, praising one's own capacity to hear, because those who can hear this Dharma are rare;
second, praising the Buddha’s ability to teach, because those who can teach this Dharma are rare; third...

This also praises the two locations [of teaching], because this Dharma is heard only when the time has arrived and is taught only when the time has arrived; it is not something heard at all times nor taught at all times.
Furthermore, it is only after attaining profound understanding that one realizes that these three are all unalterable, and thus offers praise.

Regarding the term "profound sutra" (*gambhīra-sūtra*): it is called "profound" (*gambhīra*) to distinguish it from the Hīnayāna, and it is called "extremely profound" (*atigambhīra*) to further distinguish it from the *dharmalakṣaṇa* (phenomenal characteristics) teachings.
This clarifies the rarity of what has been taught; that such [teachings] are spoken only by a Buddha means that the speaker, too, is rare.
"Since ancient times" refers to the period from when I first attended upon the Buddha according to the Āgamas until the attainment of the eye of wisdom.
Having already attained the wisdom-eye of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), this sutra not only empties persons but is also able to empty phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*);
therefore, it has never before been heard. This reveals the rarity of being able to hear it; for a sutra such as this alone, that which is heard is likewise rare.
The occasioned listeners have finished hearing and understanding with deep emotion. Second, praising the merit of faith and understanding.
Two: first, the merit of present faith and understanding; second, the merit of future faith and understanding. Regarding the first:

"World-Honored One, if there should be a person who hears this sutra and their mind of faith becomes pure, such that the mark of reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) arises, you should know, World-Honored One, that this person accomplishes the foremost and most rare merit. This mark of reality, World-Honored One, is precisely the absence of marks."
Therefore, the Tathāgata spoke of it as the "True Mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Śūnyatāsaṃjñin thought: "By the power of having heard this sutra, my mind of faith has first become pure, and subsequently, I have given rise to the wondrous understanding of the True Mark.
From this point forward, I shall personally realize that the benefit will be great indeed. Furthermore, if there should be...

As for this one person: just as I have heard this sutra, just as my faith and mind are pure, and just as I have immediately given rise to the wondrous understanding of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), when I compare myself with them, there should be not the slightest difference. Therefore it is said: "One should know that such persons are equal."
"Accomplishment" also carries the sense of being fully endowed with. It is the foremost rarity. This still refers to the two kinds of *prajñā*:
that of contemplative insight and that of words. These two kinds of *prajñā* both take the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as their essence.

Once this person has given rise to the wondrous understanding of the true mark, then these two kinds of *prajñā* will be spontaneously and fully possessed without even being sought. [End of] Refutation.
The delusions of self and others are termed "merit" (*guṇa*); the accomplishment of the practices for the dual benefit [of self and others] is termed "virtue" (*guṇa*).

This is the primary explanation. The passage beginning with "World-Honored One" serves to prevent a secondary attachment; fearing that upon hearing that [delusions] can constitute merit and virtue, one might conversely cling to the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) as being existent.
Therefore it says: "That which is the true mark is precisely the absence of marks. There are two interpretations of this: first, gold dust...
Though noble, it falls from the eye and becomes dust; though one may give rise to a subtle understanding of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), this understanding itself must not be dwelled upon.
Therefore, it is called "non-mark" (*alakṣaṇa*). This simply means that one correctly perceives its non-dwellability.

Second, if there were truly a mark, it would belong to the destructible and be an insubstantial dharma, and thus could not be called the true mark. Therefore, it is called "non-mark. This means that it is not merely that there is no mark of existence.

Nor is it without characteristics (*animitta*). This precisely reveals that it is indestructible. For this reason, when the Tathāgata speaks of it as "true reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), there are two meanings.
First, although the wondrous understanding of true reality cannot be dwelt upon, because there are causes and conditions, it can nonetheless be described.
Therefore, for those who do not understand the meaning of true reality, the Tathāgata speaks of it by name.
The "true mark" (bhūtalakṣaṇa) causes one to contemplate the meaning based on the name. Second, that which exists cannot be made non-existent, and that which does not exist cannot be made existent;

this is a firm and substantial dharma that cannot be destroyed. Therefore, the Tathāgata, wishing to reveal this indestructible meaning, speaks of it as the "true mark," thereby manifesting that all other things are unreal. This concludes the section on the merit of manifest faith and understanding.
Second, the merit of faith and understanding in the future. This has two parts: first, the actual praise; second, the successive interrogation and explanation.
Regarding the first:
"World-Honored One, it would not be difficult for me now to hear such a sutra as this and to have faith, understand, accept, and uphold it. However, if in the future..."
In a future age, during the final five hundred years, if there are sentient beings who hear this sutra, believe and understand it, and accept and uphold it,
such persons shall be the most rare and extraordinary of all.

The phrase "I have now heard" indicates that this was received directly from the Teacher’s instruction. The expression "such a sūtra as this" refers generally to all that has been previously expounded.

Now, since it was received directly from the Teacher’s instruction, even though one possesses pure faith and a sublime understanding of the true nature (*dharmatā*), and thus receives and upholds it, these things are not to be considered difficult;
for the Tathāgata’s three karmas are preeminent. One beholds...
Hearing and rejoicing [in this teaching] can immediately evoke a mind of faith, understanding, and upholding.

As for "the latter five hundred years of the future," this indicates that the time has long passed since the Sage departed. Any sentient beings who manage to hear this sutra will do so only through successive transmission and reception.
Thus, since the time has long passed since the Sage departed and the teaching is subject to successive transmission and reception, faith...
To purify the mind is difficult; to have a profound understanding of the true nature (*dharmatā*) is even more difficult; and to further receive and uphold it is most difficult.
Unless one possesses past causes, this must certainly be sent by the Buddha. Therefore, it is said that such a person is the most rare and extraordinary.
This is because they are able to rely upon the substance of the true nature to give rise to the two functions of *prajñā*: the contemplation of the essence and the observation of the words. Part Two.
This is a further explanation by way of inquiry.
Why is this? Because this person has no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a sentient being, and no mark of a life-span. For what reason?
Because the mark of a self is precisely no-mark; the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, and the mark of a life-span are likewise no-marks.
[The] characteristics. Why is this? Because being free from all characteristics is precisely what is called "all Buddhas.

The text is divided into three sections. First, following the inquiry and providing the explanation: it states that the person who believes, understands, receives, and upholds [this teaching] is called "the most rare and wonderful" for what reason?
It is because this person has long been free from the four characteristics and is secretly regarded by the Tathāgata as...
They have been dispatched to perform the work of the Tathāgata.

Were it not so, how could they suddenly emerge from the constant stream [of saṃsāra] within the turbid and evil world of the final five hundred years, to believe, understand, accept, and uphold this profound Dharma that is free from marks?
To explain why the marks of a self, a person, and so forth must necessarily be non-existent, what is the reason?
It is because these marks of a self, a person, and so forth are all non-marks, as they are dependent phenomena (*paratantra-dharma*).
If one were to further grasp at the marks of a self, a person, and so forth within them, this would be to superimpose a pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) upon the dependent phenomenon.
[This] calculation is truly the most deluded among all delusions; therefore, it must be negated. Why? [The following] provides both a combined inquiry and an explanation.
Even if one realizes that these are not characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and does not cling to their existence, why is this considered the foremost rarity?

It is because one has long been free from the clinging to the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*), has already abandoned the mark of self (*ātma-lakṣaṇa*), and furthermore, has realized that the four marks are non-marks, as well as [the non-existence of] phenomena (*dharma*).

Characteristics are also transcended. Being able to transcend all characteristics, one’s internal faculties and body, as well as the external environment, shall, upon thought, be transformed into supreme awakening.
Therefore it is said that they are immediately named Buddhas; it is truly appropriate to call this "the foremost rarity.
The absence of verses by Maitreya above is because these are words spoken for the specific occasion (*pratyarha*), and were not spoken by the Buddha.
Thus concludes the summary praise of the merit of faith and understanding. Part three: The Tathāgata’s Seal of Approval and Explanatory Verification, which has two sections:
first, the actual granting of the seal of verification; second, raising a question to provide further explanation. First [the actual granting of the seal of verification]:

The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is, so it is. If there should be anyone who, upon hearing this sutra, is not startled, not terrified, and does not fear, you should know that such a person is exceedingly rare."
"Thus it is, thus it is" serves as a seal confirming that both statements are without error. It is said that this sutra is profoundly deep;

to believe and understand it in the present is difficult, and to believe and understand it in the future will be even more difficult. This too was understood by Subhūti only after he had attained realization.
Therefore, what has been taught is free from error, just as a traveler who has already passed through a place points out the path ahead with natural accuracy.
Thus, the Tathāgata confirms both [the past and the future], desiring that those in the present and those yet to come may hear this sutra.
It would be appropriate to seek [the truth] as Subhūti did. If one were to go even lower, it would be to use an inferior realization to certify a superior one;

yet, because one perceives what he says to be non-erroneous, there are those who—regardless of whether they are present or future—whenever the sound of the Dharma reaches their ears, are all included therein.
"Not startled" means believing this to be the Buddha’s teaching and not giving rise to alarm or fear; it is not that it is not true.
This is faith. As for "not being afraid," it means knowing this is the Mahāyāna and not giving rise to fear or dread; this is not true understanding.

As for "not being terrified," it means that when examining the texts and counting the characters, one does not give rise to apprehension or avoidance; this is not truly being able to uphold [the teaching]. Such a person—
It is already extremely rare; how much more so for those who possess true faith, true understanding, and true capacity to receive and uphold it.
Such individuals should naturally be called the most exceptionally rare—this is no exaggeration. Second, the inquiry is raised to provide a further explanation.
Why is this? Subhūti, that which the Tathāgata calls the foremost pāramitā is not, in fact, a foremost pāramitā;
it is designated as the "foremost pāramitā."
To say that one is not startled, not terrified, and not afraid is merely to speak of the ordinary. Why, then, is this called "extremely rare"?

It is because the Tathāgata speaks according to circumstances, clears away according to circumstances, and establishes according to circumstances; his principles are not fixed, and his words may seem contradictory.
To hear this and yet not give rise to alarm, not give rise to dread, and not give rise to fear or avoidance—truly, such a person is hard to find.
When it is said "the foremost pāramitā," this refers specifically to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) elucidated in the present sutra.
As the *Vajrasamādhi-sūtra* states: "Among the six pāramitās, prajñā is the most supreme; for if the six perfections were devoid of prajñā..."
Thus, in the cause, there would be no merit in destroying delusions; in the fruit, there would be no virtue of the Dharma-body.

We know, therefore, that destroying delusions and realizing the truth are not separate from Prajñā; hence it is called "the foremost. Now, this etymological explanation is the same as the words found in the previous inquiry regarding the title of the sutra.
There, it was called "Prajñā," while here it is called "foremost"; although the phrasing has been slightly altered, it is essentially the same.
This refers to taking that [object] as an example; it is merely one aspect of what is easily seen, easily startled by, easily terrified by, and easily feared.

This concludes the summary of faith, understanding, and exclamation. Part Three: Clarifying the Remaining Perfections. This has two sections: first, clarifying the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*); second, summarizing all [perfections].
The first of these has two parts: first, clarifying through categories; second, citing examples to provide proof and explanation. The first [part]:
Subhūti, the perfection of patience that the Tathāgata has preached is not, in fact, a perfection of patience; it is called the perfection of patience.
That this sutra is so easily startling, easily terrifying, and easily feared is not due to a single aspect of the Prajñā alone.

For instance, regarding those who practice the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) based on this sūtra, the Tathāgata also says it is not the perfection of patience because there is no self (*anātman*).
It is merely a provisional designation for those unable to endure, established as an antidote to anger;
thus it is called "practicing the perfection of patience. Those who do not correctly understand this are few.
It is not one who, being unafraid, yet feels dread and avoids [the truth]. This is the meaning of "enduring criticism. The proof for this will be seen below in the citations.
Second, the explanation by citing examples is twofold: first, a detailed citation of recent events; second, a brief citation of distant events.
First. Why is this?

Subhūti, when in the past I was having my body cut to pieces by King Kaliṅga, at that time I had no perception of a self, no perception of a person, no perception of a sentient being, and no perception of a life-span. Why is this? Because at that time...
In the past, when my limbs were being severed joint by joint, if there had been any notion of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span, I would have given rise to anger and resentment.

The text is divided into two parts: first, the response to the inquiry and the subsequent explanation. It says that the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) taught by the Tathāgata is not [a perfection].
Why is this so? In the *Shichao* (Explanatory Commentary), regarding the passage "As I was formerly... and so forth, it cites the meaning of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* from the *Fayuan*:
"I recall that during the Bhadrakalpa, I was born into a Brahmin family in the city of Puṇḍravardhana in Southern India.
For the sake of sentient beings, I practiced dhyāna in the forests and wilds. At that time, there was a king in that country named Karapu."

(The name of this king is translated as Kali; the Chen dynasty translation is Kalinga, and the Tang dynasty translation is Kali. These are minor variations in the Sanskrit pronunciation. Here it is rendered as "Utterly Evil," because that scripture states: "His nature was violent and cruel, for he was arrogant and self-indulgent.

Accompanied by his court ladies, he went out of the city to enjoy himself. When the king grew weary, he rested for a short while. The ladies, having gone to gather flowers and fruit, came to where I was, and I preached the Dharma to them.
When the king awoke from his rest, he did not see the ladies. He took up his sword and followed after them; then, filled with rage—
He rebuked me, saying, "Why do you use illusory arts to seduce my daughters? Are you possessed by lust? I then replied, "I maintain the pure precepts;
truly, I have no defiled heart. The King asked, "What constitutes your precepts? I answered, "Patience is my precept.
The King then used his sword to sever my hands, feet, and both ears and nose, and asked, "Are you patient? I said:
"Even if, Great King, you were to divide my remaining body into fragments as small as motes of dust, I would ultimately endure it and never give rise to a thought of anger.
Although the ministers vied with one another in remonstrating, the king’s wrath did not cease. At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings rained down vajra-sand;
seeing this, the king was struck with terror, turned away from his anger, and offered an apology. I then made a vow: "If it is true that I harbor no thought of anger, may my..."
His body was restored to its former state. Having made this vow, his body immediately returned to normal. He further prayed:
"May I, in a future life, be the first to deliver the Great King. For this reason, when I have now attained Buddhahood, I am the first to deliver Kauṇḍinya.

This is an illustration cited according to the underlying principle; it merely summarizes the event from the current sutra. "Wei" (爲) means "to be covered by" or "to be affected by. [He] cut and dismembered his body.
"Body" refers here to the act of severing hands, feet, ears, and noses. "The absence of the four marks" precisely reveals the absence of anger (*dveṣa*).
Because there is no self (*ātman*), there is no one who receives [the injury]; because there is no person (*pudgala*), one does not calculate retribution;

because there is no sentient being (*sattva*), one does not perceive the aspect of suffering; and because there is no life-principle (*jīva*), one does not protect the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). All of these serve to eliminate thoughts of anger.
Why is this? It is because as one undergoes being cut and severed, one perceives that there are no four marks [of selfhood].

This is because when, in the past, my hands, feet, ears, and nose were cut off and my limbs were dismembered and scattered piece by piece, if there had been any mark of a self or a person, anger and resentment would have arisen. Why is this? Because...
Because one experiences the retribution of volition and does not forget suffering in order to protect the life-faculty, consider this: even in the past, I still wished to deliver others first;

how could there be any anger? Thus, we know that at that time, the four [defiled] characteristics were absent. Having finished the detailed citation of recent events, secondly, here is a brief citation of distant events.
Subhūti, furthermore, I recall that in the past, for five hundred lifetimes, I was a rishi of patience.
During all those lifetimes, there was no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a sentient being, and no mark of a life-span.
Fearing that his body would be cut and mangled, it is already difficult to endure such things; how much more so, then, to remain free from anger? Why was that son of a Brahmin suddenly able to do so?
Therefore, he further cites a distant event to explain and substantiate this. "The past" refers to the period prior to the Bhadrakalpa (the Auspicious Aeon);
it must have been during the Bhadrakalpika Aeon. As for his having been a "Patient Seer" (*kṣānti-ṛṣi*) for five hundred lifetimes, he saw—

That he has practiced patience for such a long time, and that throughout all those worlds there were no [beings subject to] the four marks, demonstrates that his cultivation of emptiness is already matured.

Because he has practiced for so long, he is able to endure; because his cultivation is matured, he is free from anger. One who possesses the resolve to practice patience should likewise seek to become like the Buddha.
Verse: "Cultivating that mind capable of learning.
This commentary states: "This combines the meaning of this section and the preceding section. 'The mind capable of learning' refers specifically to the practice of patience (*kṣānti*)."

Because one can train in the bodhisattva’s aspiration for enlightenment through the practice of patience (*kṣānti*), yet patience alone does not quickly bring accomplishment, it is necessary to cultivate it—meaning to practice that conduct life after life.
This is exemplified by the Buddha’s acts as a patient seer (*ṛṣi*) over five hundred lifetimes.
This concludes the detailed explanation of the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*). Second, the general summary of all [the perfections].
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should set out for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by relinquishing all marks.
One should not give rise to the mind dwelling on forms; one should not give rise to the mind dwelling on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas.
One should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere. If the mind dwells anywhere, it is not dwelling at all.

The text is divided into three sections. First is the formal conclusion. Since giving (*dāna*) stands at the head of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), it is first stated that giving is free from marks (*animitta*).
Since wisdom (*prajñā*) stands at the end of the six perfections, it is next stated that wisdom is free from marks.

Since patience (*kṣānti*) also encompasses diligence (*vīrya*) and occupies the middle position among the six perfections, it is explained by analogy in the middle section that patience is free from marks. This applies to both the beginning and the end.
Since it is so in this intermediate case, other instances may be understood by analogy. For this reason, addressing those who are ready to receive the teaching, he summarizes by saying:

"A bodhisattva should be free from all marks; that is, when observing the precepts, they should be free from the mark of precepts; when practicing dhyāna, they should be free from the mark of dhyāna."
Even as the myriad practices flourish, one remains free from the characteristics of those myriad practices.
When one thus gives rise to the bodhicitta, the awakened mind can abide in peace. It should not be understood through a downward reversal.

Regarding the statement "one should not give rise to a mind dwelling on form," this means that one should not give rise to a defiled mind by dwelling with attachment upon the forms seen by the eye; for form is like a glowing iron ball.

Because grasping them leads to burning. "One should not dwell on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena when generating the mind" means that one should not dwell with attachment upon the sounds heard by the ear, up to and including the mental objects perceived by the mind, thereby giving rise to a defiled mind.
For sound is like a drum smeared with poison; hearing it inevitably brings death. Odor is like the breath of a venomous dragon; smelling it causes illness. Taste is like...
