This is the answer given by Śūnyatājanman. It not only serves to dispel the delusions of the assembly, but also profoundly accords with the Buddha’s mind;
it is especially sufficient to serve as a compass for those seeking to subdue their minds. Second, a detailed explanation.
Subhūti, if there were any dharma that the Tathāgata had attained as anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then Dīpaṃkara would not have bestowed upon me this prediction:
"In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.
Because, in reality, there is no dharma by which one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, therefore Dīpaṃkara...
The Buddha bestowed upon me a prophecy, saying: "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni. This passage has two parts.
First, the indirect demonstration (*pratiṣedha*): if there were any dharma through which one could attain bodhi, then subject and object would not have been forgotten. Dharma...
"I am present in both [body and mind], yet my mind is difficult to subdue; how could I possibly become a Buddha? For this reason, Dīpaṃkara did not grant me a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).
A 'prediction' refers to the conferring of the name one shall have when becoming a Buddha in the future, so that one may clearly remember it and verify it at a later time.
"In a future age," and so forth, are the words of the prediction granted in the past. This is the explanation in the Sanskrit commentary.
*Kāśyapa-muni*. This is translated as "Able Sage" (*Néng-rén*) and "Silent Stillness" (*Jí-mò*). One may understand this as the family name being the former and the personal name the latter.

If one takes their combined meaning, "Able Sage" refers to the universal covering of compassion, while "Silent Stillness" refers to the secret realization of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). If one dwells in signs, one cannot provide universal coverage;
if there is a dharma, one is dependent upon the unconditioned. That the Buddha does not bestow a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) [of his own enlightenment] is nothing to be wondered at.
The passage below explains that, in reality, there is no dharma by which one can attain bodhi; thus, the principle transcends subject and object.
When one clings to emptiness, self, and dharmas, and not even a single thought arises, then the mind itself is the Buddha.

Therefore, when Dīpaṃkara bestowed a prediction upon me, granting that I would become a Buddha in the future and declaring my name to be Śākyamuni—the "Able One" (Śākya) who does not abide in nirvāṇa, and the "Silent One" (Muni)...

If he remains silent, he will not abide in birth-and-death; his name and virtue will correspond. This record may thus be deemed appropriate. The comprehensive conclusion, the seal of verification, and the detailed explanation are finished.
Third, the inquiry is raised to further reveal the meaning.
Why is this? "Tathāgata" has the meaning of the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas.
Subhūti, if someone were to say that the Tathāgata has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, in reality there is no dharma that the Buddha has attained as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

The text has three parts. The first sentence poses the inquiry: for what reason is it that when there is a dharma that attains *bodhi*, no prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) is given, whereas when there is no dharma that attains *bodhi*, a prediction is indeed given?
The passage beginning with "The Tathāgata" below provides the explanation. The Buddha is called the Tathāgata;
"Tathāgata" signifies the meaning of being as-it-is (*tathatā*) and remaining immovable within all dharmas. There is no dharma that can be attained as *bodhi*.
"Subhūti, it is not thus. There is no dharma that can be attained as bodhi; this precisely accords with the meaning of 'thusness' (tathatā).
This is the reason why [the Buddha] sometimes grants a prediction and sometimes does not. If there is a lower-level objection, the objection states:

'Since there is no dharma that can be attained as bodhi, then even the prediction granted by Dīpaṃkara would be empty. Why, then, do people say that the Tathāgata, beneath the Bodhi tree, attained [it]? "
"Bodhi? Therefore, the *Fangguang* [Prajñāpāramitā] says: "Subhūti, if someone should say that the Tathāgata attained bodhi beneath the Bodhi tree, you should say to him:
'In reality, there is no dharma by which the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Based on this, one receives the prediction of enlightenment by being free from marks, and one attains the fruit by being free from marks.
These two meanings accord with one another, both converging upon non-thought (*amanasikāra*). Those who advance toward and cultivate the bodhicitta must not fail to understand this.
The section on "Investigating and Manifesting the Arising" is concluded. Fourth, the summary that demonstrates the Middle Way.
Subhūti, the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* attained by the Tathāgata—in this there is neither reality nor unreality.
Therefore, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are Buddha-dharmas. Subhūti, what is called "all dharmas" is not actually all dharmas; it is therefore called "all dharmas."
The text has three parts. First, it addresses and dispels a prior doubt. Fearing that one might think:

"If there is no dharma for generating the aspiration for enlightenment, no dharma for receiving the prediction of Buddhahood, and no dharma for attaining Buddhahood, then would it not follow that there is exclusively non-existence, leading to eternal sinking into annihilation? To dispel this doubt, it says:
"The *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* attained by the Tathāgata—within this, there is neither reality nor unreality."
Why is it not real? Because it is manifested through skillful means (*upāya*). Why is it not false? Because it brings about benefit according to conditions.

Because it is not real, it does not contradict what was previously stated; because it is not false, it does not sink into nihilism. To hold onto the medicine and thereby incur illness—what concern is that for the physician?
Therefore, the following section serves as the formal conclusion and demonstration. "Therefore" means: by virtue of this non-reality and non-...

It is because it is empty; it is because it lacks substantial reality. Thus, there is no impediment to the Tathāgata’s teaching of all dharmas, for he speaks of existence and non-existence, and of emptiness and non-emptiness.

Because it is not empty, speaking of existence and speaking of emptiness are both the Buddha-dharma, for he teaches that existence which is not existent is wondrous existence, and that emptiness which is not empty is true emptiness. Subhūti [said], "Furthermore... [The text continues with Subhūti’s further inquiry.]

Clarification: Regarding the previous statement that all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma, fearing that [the audience] may still not fully understand, I again address the one present and clarify it by saying:
"That which is called 'all dharmas' is entirely a skillful means for remedial treatment; therefore, it is said to be 'not all dharmas.
This means that teaching emptiness is in contrast to existence, and teaching existence is in contrast to emptiness; they are not the ultimate truth.
This is indeed so. Although it is not ultimate reality, these names are provisionally established in order to reveal the meaning of the wondrous existence of true emptiness;
thus, all phenomena are explained. Furthermore, this serves to reveal the Middle Way of the primary truth within the context of opening and subduing the mind.

Verse: Because the prediction was given at a later time, the practice of Dīpaṃkara was not the supreme enlightenment; those practices and so forth do not truly possess the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
That which is without such characteristics is itself the characteristic, for it is taught as non-false; this is the essential nature of all the Buddha-dharmas.

The combined commentary states: This generally summarizes the meaning of the major section on "Receiving the Prediction and Transcending Characteristics. It should also follow upon the preceding doubt, which asks:

"Since the Bodhisattva neither maintains a self nor dwells in the Path, and there is no dharma to be attained, for what reason was he previously at the time of Dīpaṃkara given the prediction that he would become a Buddha at a later time? Therefore, Maitreya explains this with these verses, saying: "In the past..."
Regarding the time after [meeting] Dīpaṃkara, when he was granted the prediction of Buddhahood:

it was precisely because the Buddha, while practicing the bodhisattva path under Dīpaṃkara Buddha, did not consider himself superior that the Sūtra says, "There is no dharma by which one attains bodhi," and thus Dīpaṃkara granted him the prediction.
It can be understood from this that had it been otherwise, he would not have been predicted; therefore, Maitreya does not include this in his verses. As for bodhi...
Even attaining bodhi beneath the Bodhi tree is not considered supreme; therefore, it is said that his practice is equal to theirs.
This is precisely the meaning in the sutra that there is truly no dharma by which the Buddha attained bodhi. That people speak to the contrary can be understood accordingly.
Therefore, it is not praised in verse, for fear that doubts regarding annihilation might arise. Thus it is said that the marks of conditioned existence are not real;

this is because the *bodhi* attained by the Tathāgata is not real, being a manifestation through skillful means (*upāya*). This does not contradict what was stated previously, namely the meaning of "non-substantiality" (*asat*) in the Sūtra.
Although it is said to be non-real, it nevertheless possesses the characteristic of being something produced through volitional action. This...
Thus, it does not sink into annihilation; this is precisely the meaning of "non-falsity" in the sutra.
As for the phrase "that which is the mark of non-marks," it refers to that which is called "attaining bodhi"—this is establishing marks within the state of non-marks.
Since it is taught by establishing marks within non-marks, and by establishing speech within the ineffable, for this reason the Tathāgata has never been false.
This is not a false teaching, for what is taught must accord with what has been realized.

Teaching the Dharma in this manner—speaking of emptiness and non-emptiness, existence and non-existence—wherein emptiness and non-emptiness are explained as true emptiness (*tathatā-śūnyatā*), and existence and non-existence are explained as wondrous existence (*prajñapti-satya*):
these are all dharmas realized by the Buddhas. Thus, a sutra says: "The Tathāgata teaches that all dharmas are Buddha-dharmas."
Accordingly, all dharmas are not all dharmas; they are called "all dharmas" only to manifest that the Middle Way alone is the true intrinsic nature and characteristic of all dharmas.
This concludes the summary of attaining the prediction of enlightenment through the departure from signs.
Second is the characteristic of being detached from retribution.
Subhūti, it is like a person whose body is tall and large. Subhūti said, "World-Honored One, when the Tathāgata speaks of a person’s body being tall and large, that is precisely not a large body;
it is merely named a 'large body.'"

This also continues from the previous introduction. Fearing that one might claim the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) is not real and can be said to be "without attainment," yet the *vipākakāya* (retribution body), being accomplished through cultivation, must likewise be "without attainment"—in order to prevent this doubt, it says:

"For example, a person's body is large and tall. This reiterates the analogy of the King of Mountains, Sumeru, from the section on the analysis of interpretation, for it says: "Suppose there is a person whose body..."
It is like Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains. It is said that Sumeru spans the ocean and towers above the multitude of peaks;

by using this as a metaphor for the body, one can know that it is both long and large. Therefore, when it is merely stated that the human body is "long and large," it should be understood that this still draws upon the previous metaphor.
Otherwise, why would Śūnyatāprasiddhi attain awakening immediately upon hearing the words "the human body is long and large"?
This was indeed something already known previously; it was merely forgotten for a moment. Upon a single reminder, one immediately awakens.

Thus, without waiting for the Buddha to speak, he explained it himself, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Tathāgata has said that the human body is large and tall, if one were to grasp only at its marks..."
That would then not be a "great body," because it possesses numerical limits; it is merely called "great" in contrast to the small, being a conventional designation established as a "great body.
Indeed, one must contemplate the body by way of its detachment from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) for it to be truly great.
How, then, could there be any room for the arising of a conceptual mind within that?
Verse: It is based on that Dharma-body Buddha that the metaphor of the "great body" is taught.

Because its body is free from all obscurations, because it pervades all objects, and because of its great essence, it is called the "great body. That which is not a body is itself the body; therefore, it is called the "great body."

The combined explanation states: This verse clarifies the meaning of the main text. There are two types of *dharmakāya*: first, the *svabhāva-dharmakāya*, which refers to the fact that self-nature purity is itself the *dharmakāya*;
second, the *vipākaja-dharmakāya* (the *dharmakāya* obtained through retribution), which refers to being constituted by immeasurable meritorious qualities.
The present case is the second, namely the *vipākakāya* (retribution body). Although the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) is vast, it is [limited] because it possesses numerical [attributes].

It can be compared by means of measurement; therefore, based upon this, the analogy of a "vast body" is taught. If it were the *dharmakāya* of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), its principle would transcend number and measure, and there would be nothing with which to compare it;
thus, we know it is not that. Furthermore, there are two types of *saṃbhogakāya*: first, the self-recompense (*sva-saṃbhoga*), and second, the recompense for others (*para-saṃbhoga*).
The verse says, "free from all hindrances," which refers to the self-recompense; this is the meaning of being fully perfected and pure. It pervades the one...
The entire objective realm is precisely his retribution-body; it carries the meaning of "universal illumination. Regarding "merit" and "the great body":
these are explained in terms of both the supported (the qualities) and the support (the physical form). The "supported" refers to the adornment of myriad virtues, hence it is called "merit.

The "support" refers to the golden body ten thousand feet tall, hence it is called the "great body. This is taught specifically to contrast with the small bodies of the mundane world. Therefore, it is said:
To have a "great body" is not to possess true greatness. If one understands that this body is no-body, it is the *dharmakāya* of self-nature;

its principle transcends all measure and number, and thus constitutes true greatness. Therefore, when the Tathāgata in the sutra says, "For example, a human body is large and tall," it is intended to make known the meaning that it is not a great body.
This concludes the section on the retribution of feeling being free from marks. Part Three: Cultivation.

Regarding the two aspects of being free from characteristics: first, following the previous section, they are explained by way of general analogy; second, they are treated individually according to specific phenomena to eliminate conceptual marks. First:
"Subhūti, it is the same for the bodhisattva."
To say that a bodhisattva is not a bodhisattva is what is called being a bodhisattva; it is like the case of a person who is tall and large in stature.

The reason for this analogy is that many sentient beings claim to be bodhisattvas because they can cultivate the causes, yet they do not realize that "I" am the cultivator and the cause is that which is cultivated. Since both aspects remain present, they are not true bodhisattvas; they are merely...
These are merely provisional designations applied to those who are unable to cultivate the causes [of awakening], and are thus called "bodhisattvas.

Second, regarding the specific elimination of signs (*nimitta-parivarjana*), there are two parts: first, the elimination of signs by means of delivering sentient beings; second, the elimination of signs by means of adorning the buddha-fields.
First:
If one were to say, "I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa," one would not be called a bodhisattva. Why is this?
Subhūti, in reality there is no dharma that is named "bodhisattva. Therefore, the Buddha has said: "All dharmas are without self."
There is no person, no sentient being, and no life-span possessor.
This passage has three parts. First, it transcends verbal expression. One who makes such a statement harbors a sense of self-importance;

thinking that since they are a bodhisattva, they ought to take the salvation of beings as their responsibility, they say, "I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa. (The Confucian Classics...)
It says: "To awaken these people by means of this Way—who else but I could awaken them? This is roughly the same intent.
While this intent is certainly good, one must not harbor a sense of self-congratulation.

If one harbors such self-congratulation, it means that in one's mind there is truly a self that acts as the savior and sentient beings who are saved; therefore, such a person is criticized as not being called a Bodhisattva. Question:
Question: The statement "I shall respond" and the statement "I shall do this"—are they the same or different? Answer: In terms of the literal meaning of the words, they appear the same;
in terms of the underlying intention, they are actually different. The former is a recollection of one's essential nature (*tathatā*); the latter is an assertion of one's own capability.

If one observes the text below the former, there is mention of "non-arising" and "nirvāṇa"; whereas below this [latter], there is language that excludes those who are not true bodhisattvas. Thus, their meanings differ.
It can be seen. Why? [The following] interrogates and then explains to establish the point. The intent of the interrogation is clear.

In the explanation, it is said that all phenomena (*dharma*) arise through the convergence of conditions (*pratyaya*). Since they arise through the convergence of conditions, the phenomena that arise are fundamentally non-existent.

Therefore, it is said: "In reality, there is no dharma. If there is no dharma, then there is no self (*ātman*). If there is no self, then all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are exhausted. To understand this exhaustion of all marks is to...
This is the entry into the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); therefore, one is called a "Bodhisattva. Since the former case is the opposite of this, one is not so named.
Thus, the following section concludes by stating that one should be detached from marks (*lakṣaṇa*). "Therefore" refers back to the two preceding meanings:
one is not called a Bodhisattva in that manner, whereas one is called a Bodhisattva in this manner. For this reason, the Buddha, regarding...
For thirty years, I have taught all the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna dharmas, primarily to reveal the principle of the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*).

As for selflessness, the mark of a person (*pudgala-nimitta*), the mark of a sentient being (*sattva-nimitta*), and the mark of a life-span (*jīva-nimitta*)—all these are non-existent. Thus has the Buddha spoken.

One who is a bodhisattva should be free from signs. Having finished the section on dispelling signs by means of saving sentient beings, the second section concerns dispelling signs by means of adorning the buddha-fields.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to say, "I shall adorn the buddha-fields," he would not be called a bodhisattva.
Why is this? The Tathāgata has said that what is called "adorned Buddha-fields" is in fact not adorned; it is merely named "adorned.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva penetrates the non-existence of self and phenomena, the Tathāgata says that such a person is truly a bodhisattva.

The text also has three parts. First, it addresses the transcendence [of the Buddha] through words; the meaning is the same as in the preceding section, though the specific explanations differ according to the particular matter at hand.

Below this, there is an inquiry that introduces the explanation and establishes its validity. Within the explanation, it says: "When the Tathāgata speaks of adorning buddha-lands, the lands are merely manifestations of the mind, and the adornments are likewise born of the mind.
Since this is but the single mind, whom could one call the 'adorned' and whom the 'adorner'? Therefore, it is said: 'it is not so.'"
Adornment. This shows that what is called "adorned Buddha-lands" is merely a provisional designation established within the gateway of transformative manifestation;
therefore, it is said, "this is called adornment. Subhūti [and those below] conclude by responding that one should remain detached from marks.
Since adornment is merely a provisional name, one knows there is no self and no dharmas. If a bodhisattva, at the time of adorning a Buddha-land, penetrates [this truth]...
Those who realize neither self nor dharmas can advance toward Buddhahood; the Tathāgata calls them true Bodhisattvas.
A Bodhisattva who adorns the Buddha-land must not depart from signs.
Verse: To give rise to the intention to deliver sentient beings and the mind of purifying the buddha-field without having realized the true dharma-realm is itself a perversion.
Sentient beings and bodhisattvas know that all phenomena are selfless; it is the non-saintly who lack faith in their own wisdom, whereas the saints possess such wisdom.

The combined commentary states: This verse generally summarizes the meaning of one major section. The One True Dharma-realm is free from subject and object, transcends all opposition, and is without duality of self and other;
the environment and its inhabitants share a single source. Failing to realize this, the intention to deliver sentient beings arises.
And regarding the mind that adorns the Buddha-land: "purifying" is precisely the meaning of "adornment. However, to give rise to such a conceptual intention (*cetanā*) is to generate a state of mind;

since this violates the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it is an inversion. Therefore, the Sūtra rebukes such a person, stating they cannot be called a Bodhisattva. The word "ji" (及) means "even unto" or "as far as.
If these sentient beings were truly able to reach the stage of a Bodhisattva, they would naturally be able to understand the Dharma.
The principle of non-self is free from all marks and accords with the true *dharmadhātu*.

Although one has not yet attained Buddhahood and is not yet a Great Sage, the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*svasaṃviditajñāna*) is trustworthy; in the future, one will certainly reach the state of a Sage.

Because the wisdom of the two-fold emptiness of self and phenomena serves as the successive stages for attaining Buddhahood, the sūtras permit such a person to be truly called a Bodhisattva. In brief:
The section on the completion of cultivating the causes for detachment from signs concludes. Part two: Knowledge and Vision Detached from Signs.
This has two parts: first, seeing that there is no fixed sign;

second, knowing that there is no real sign. Regarding the first: Subhūti, what do you think? Does a Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye? “It is so, World-Honored One; a Tathāgata possesses [the fleshly eye].”
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye? “Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the divine eye.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the wisdom-eye? “Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the wisdom-eye.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Dharma-eye? “Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the Dharma-eye.”
"Yes, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata possesses the Dharma-eye, Subhūti. What do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha-eye?
"Yes, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye."

This also follows from the preceding introduction. One might fear that if, in saving sentient beings, one does not perceive the marks of sentient beings, and in adorning the land, one does not perceive the marks of the land—since the fruit must correspond to the cause—then at the time of attaining Buddhahood, one likewise ought to be neither knowing nor seeing.
To prevent such a doubt, it is shown that knowledge and vision are free from marks.
Now, let us briefly illustrate this based on what is seen. *Vajra-pin* says: Regarding the "fleshly eye" (*māṃsa-cakṣus*), the four sensory objects—form, odor, flavor, and touch—are called "flesh.

The sense-faculty of ultimate purity dwells in dependence upon this flesh and arises in dependence upon this flesh; that which possesses the capacity for illumination and vision is called the fleshly eye.
However, its function is limited to observing forms within its range of obstruction. As for the "divine eye" (*divya-cakṣus*), it refers to that which is produced through meditative cultivation.
Practice. By relying on the scope of the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*), one perceives external objects; because this visualization is perfected, one is then able to see forms beyond obstructions.

The wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*) is the fundamental, ultimate wisdom that illuminates the principle of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*) is the subsequently attained, provisional wisdom that illuminates the phenomena of differentiation.
The Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*) is the perfection of wisdom such that there is nothing it does not reach, and the completeness of illumination such that there is nothing it does not encompass.
Therefore, an ancient worthy sang in verse: "The Celestial Eye is unimpeded, yet the Fleshly Eye is impeded and lacks penetration.

The Dharma Eye can observe the conventional, while the Wisdom Eye perceives the true emptiness. The Buddha Eye is like a thousand suns; it illuminates diverse forms as being ultimately identical. Furthermore, the *Vajra-Comb* states:
"The first two [eyes] are common to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); the latter two are absent in the Śrāvakas; and the Bodhisattvas possess them all, except for the Buddha [Eye]."

The eyes differ from one another in their respective degrees of depth; only the Buddha possesses all four in their full perfection, each being uniquely sublime, and these are all termed the "Buddha-eye.
Just as when the four rivers enter the ocean, the individual rivers can no longer be discerned, so it is with the ordinary person’s physical eye, which sees only what is within its range;
the celestial eye sees what is beyond that range; and the Buddha’s physical eye perceives countless worlds.
The divine eye of those of the Two Vehicles sees only one great trichiliocosm; the divine eye of a Buddha sees as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
The wisdom-eye of those of the Two Vehicles illuminates only the emptiness of the self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*);

while Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*) also partially realize the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), the wisdom-eye of a Buddha perfectly illuminates the three types of emptiness and penetrates through to the true nature (*tathatā*). As for the Dharma-eye of a Bodhisattva, that which is known is not yet exhaustive. Each...
The Buddha’s Dharma-eye has limits in that all that is knowable is exhausted by it; yet, because there is nothing that is not encompassed, it is said to be "each and every one uniquely excellent.
However, as for the Tathāgata’s respective questions regarding "what do you think" and "is there or is there not," there are two intentions:
first, to manifest the vision of non-vision, wherein there is nothing that is not seen, just as a clear mirror manifests objects without a mind.
Thus, there is nothing that does not manifest; this is explained in order to resolve doubts. Second, although one is able to see everything exhaustively, there is no fixed characteristic.
This is because the fundamental nature is but a single seeing, which, following conditions, becomes five types of seeing—just as when a pond is opened, the moon is reflected within it.

Because the ponds differ, one speaks of the moon as being different. If one were to breach a dike and let the water flow through, then by means of the oneness of the pond, one would speak of the oneness of the moon.
One should know that difference is not inherently different, and oneness is not inherently one. By taking the moon as an analogy for what is seen, how could there be any fixed characteristic?
This is explained in terms of the departure from characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Verse: Although he does not perceive phenomena, it is not that he lacks the eye that cognizes objects; the Buddhas truly see those perversions through five kinds [of knowledge].
Commentary:
This verse summarizes the meaning of the preceding prose. "Perceiving" refers to the arising of conceptualizing emotions (*vikalpa*) regarding all phenomena.

[The interlocutor] says: "I see that the Buddha does not have such a thing; therefore, he said 'no. To 'comprehend' (liao) means to encounter an object directly without being separated from [deluded] conceptualization or emotional views.
The Buddha does have this capacity; therefore, he said it is 'not non-existent. The single character 'though' (sui) is used to concede to his doubt while relying upon it.
Although it is said to rely on what was doubted, there is no conceptualized or deluded view; it is not that comprehension is absent."
The objects are truly seen; why then doubt the meaning that the Tathāgata perceives them all? The following two lines explain and establish the meaning of the preceding two lines.
It is said that the reason the Tathāgata is able to comprehend these objects is that the five types [of sensory faculties] of all Buddhas are entirely real.
Because [the mind] arises from this very nature, for what reason do one not see all phenomena?

If one were to see those phenomena, a conceptualizing mind would arise, which is termed "inversion. Having finished examining that there are no fixed characteristics, secondly, one knows that there are no real characteristics.

"Subhūti, what do you think? Are all the grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā truly grains of sand, as the Buddha has said? "Yes, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata has said they are grains of sand. "Subhūti, what do you think? If there were as many rivers Gaṅgā as there are grains of sand in a single river Gaṅgā, and if one were to count all the grains of sand in all those rivers—" [The Buddha] addressed Subhūti:
"Subhūti, what do you think? Could the number of grains of sand in all those rivers be easily calculated by anyone? "No, World-Honored One; it could not be easily calculated.

"Subhūti, know that the number of sentient beings in the world systems as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is even more difficult to calculate than that. "Subhūti, what do you think? Is the number of grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā great? "World-Honored One, it is indeed great. The Tathāgata has said it is great. "Subhūti, if there were as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, and if all those worlds were filled with the seven treasures and given as a gift to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones..."
"Are the realms thus many? "Very many, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Subhūti:
"In all those lands, the various kinds of minds of all sentient beings, the Tathāgata knows them all. Why is this? The Tathāgata says that all minds are 'no-mind';
it is merely called 'mind. And why is this, Subhūti? Because the past mind does not..."
It can be obtained. The present mind cannot be obtained; the future mind cannot be obtained. This passage has four parts.
First, by comparing the river to its sands, it demonstrates the vastness of the *dhātus*.

Whenever the Tathāgata speaks of phenomena involving great numbers, he frequently uses the analogy of the sands of the Ganges; this can be understood through the questions and answers. Second, it asks: "What do you think?"
"Et cetera. This means that by using the number of sands in one of those rivers to calculate the number of Ganges Rivers, it demonstrates the vastness of the Ganges Rivers.
Then, by using the sands of all those many Ganges Rivers, one calculates the number of world-systems.
This not only reveals the vastness of the worlds, but their extreme abundance as well. This can also be understood from the dialogue that follows.

From "The Buddha said" onwards, the passage discusses the arising [of beings] in relation to the realms to demonstrate the multiplicity of the mind. The phrase "as many lands as there are" refers back to the aforementioned worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
As for "all sentient beings," it is as stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "Throughout the oceans of lands in the ten directions..."
There are sentient beings of various distinctions, namely: those born from eggs, those born from wombs, those born from moisture, and those born by transformation.
Some are born and dwell depending on earth, water, fire, or wind; others are born and dwell depending on space or upon various plants and trees.
Among these diverse classes of birth and various physical forms, the differences in their mental activities can be known.

Therefore, it is said: "various kinds of mind. "Various" (*śakana*) means "as many as. The passage beginning with "The Tathāgata" [down to] "below" clarifies that delusion by way of the Buddha’s capacity for knowledge.
Regarding "the Tathāgata knows them all": this is because they possess mentation. The Buddha himself poses the question:
"For what reason is he able to know them all? He then explains it himself: "The Tathāgata says that all minds are, in fact, no-mind."

This means it is not the true mind; it is merely called "mind" because it possesses temporary function, thereby revealing that it is the deluded mind. The *Mengyin* states: Formerly, when Emperor Daizong welcomed National Teacher Zhong of Nanyang to reside at Guangzhai Temple, [the Emperor asked: "What is the mind? The Master replied: "The mind is neither existent nor non-existent. The Emperor asked: "If it is neither existent nor non-existent, why is it called 'mind'? The Master said: "It is called 'mind' precisely because it is neither existent nor non-existent. The Emperor asked: "If it is neither existent nor non-existent, how can it be called 'mind'? The Master said: "Because it is neither existent nor non-existent, it is called 'mind. If it were existent, it would be a fixed entity; if it were non-existent, it would be empty nothingness. Because it is neither existent nor non-existent, it is therefore called 'mind. The Emperor asked: "Is this the true mind? The Master said: "It is not the true mind. It is only because it has temporary function that it is named 'mind,' which reveals that it is the deluded mind. The Emperor asked: "What is the true mind? The Master said: "The true mind is like empty space; it is neither existent nor non-existent, and it transcends all names and forms. The Emperor said: "I have heard that the Buddha-nature is the true mind. Is it not so? The Master said: "Buddha-nature is the true mind, but the true mind is not necessarily Buddha-nature. The Emperor asked: "Why is that? The Master said: "Sentient beings who have not yet severed their afflictions and have not yet attained the Way do not yet realize the Buddha-nature within themselves. Therefore, although they possess the Buddha-nature, they cannot yet call it the true mind. Only those who have severed afflictions and attained the Way realize the Buddha-nature within themselves; for them, the Buddha-nature is the true mind. The Emperor said: "How can one attain the Way? The Master said: "If you wish to attain the Way, you must first sever the root of delusion. What is the root of delusion? It is the mind that discriminates between self and other, right and wrong, gain and loss, praise and blame. If you can cease such discrimination, you will naturally attain the Way. The Emperor said: "I am still confused. Please explain further. The Master said: "The mind is originally empty and tranquil. It is only due to the conditions of external objects that delusions arise. If you can maintain constant mindfulness and do not allow thoughts to follow after external objects, then the mind will naturally become empty and tranquil. This is what is called attaining the Way. At that time, there was the Tripitaka Master Daili from India, who claimed to have attained the supernormal power of knowing others' minds. The Master [Linji] ordered him to undergo a test.
After a short while, the Master asked, "Tell me, where am I right now? The Tripitaka Master replied, "The Master is the preceptor of this entire nation;
you have gone to Xichuan to watch the boat races. After another short while, the Master asked again, "And where are you right now?"
"Where are you? Mazu asked. Baizhang replied, "I am actually watching the monkey performance at Tianjin Bridge. After a brief silence, Mazu asked again. Baizhang was immediately at a loss.
Mazu rebuked him, saying, "Wild fox spirit! Where is your 'penetration of others' minds' (paracittajñāna) now? Baizhang had no reply.
This shows that as soon as the mind of conceptualization stirs, one is already known by the other. If one says it is a single thought-moment—
It does not arise; even the Buddha cannot know its signs. For this reason, [the text] refutes delusion to reveal that even "knowledge" lacks reality.
Thus, the sentence raises a critical inquiry: why is it that the mind of sentient beings is not truly real but is delusion?
It is because the three minds are all unobtainable—meaning they are unobtainable as having already ceased, unobtainable as abiding, and unobtainable as yet to be.
Because birth cannot be apprehended. Yet, the Buddha knows the minds of all beings through a single cognition; in this sense, it seems as though there is a substantial entity.
However, since the minds of beings are illusory and cannot be found across the three periods of time, although he knows them, fundamentally there is nothing known.
How could there be any real characteristic?
Verse: Various inverted cognitions, because they are devoid of true mindfulness and do not abide in that true wisdom, are therefore called "inverted.
Commentary:
This verse explains the meaning of the original text. "Various" (*nānāvidha*) means "many" (*aneka*). It refers to the many [distinctions] of sentient beings.
All such states of mind are inverted consciousnesses, because they arise from false conceptualization apart from true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
The Tathāgata does not abide in those false conceptualizations; this is what is called true wisdom. Therefore, he is able to know them, and thus they are designated as "inverted.
That which is inverted is not truly mind, yet it is given the name "mind" for conventional purposes. Judging by these two sections, the Buddha knows [them].
Even that which the Buddha perceives lacks fixed reality; how much more so for those who have not yet reached the stage of Buddhahood?

Their false knowledge and false views are certainly known to be utterly hollow and illusory, requiring no further subduing. This concludes the section on "Subduing the Mind and Detaching from Characteristics.
Part Two: The Dwelling Mind Without Abiding. Section One: A Brief Explanation. Section Two: A Detailed Demonstration. First [the brief explanation]:
“Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven kinds of precious jewels and give them as a gift, would that person, by reason of this, acquire much merit?
“Indeed, World-Honored One, that person would acquire very much merit by reason of this.
“Subhūti, if merit had any substantial reality, the Tathāgata would not say that it is acquired.”
The merit is great. Because there is no [conceptual] merit, the Tathāgata says that one obtains great merit.

This passage has two parts. First is the question and answer regarding the merit of giving. Previously, it was stated that the merit of giving without dwelling is like empty space and cannot be measured;
yet, fearing that during the time of practice the conduct might not correspond [to this teaching], there may be renewed doubt concerning the merit of giving. Therefore, he again addresses it...
This is a hypothetical case, cited as an illustration. Suppose there were a person—meaning, let us assume such a person existed—who were to give away jewels filling the entire world-system;
while the merit from such an act would seem great, it would not be so if one dwells upon signs (*nimitta*).
To clarify this meaning, he asks: "By this cause and condition, would one obtain much merit or not? Observe how Subhūti reasons through this, and provide the answer.
Regarding the statement that "by these causes and conditions, one obtains exceedingly great merit," this also indicates that the Tathāgata reveals and abides in merit.
Below, Subhūti provides a further clarification. Seeing that his answer was somewhat vague and fearing it might fall into mere semblance, the Tathāgata does not avoid prolixity;
he provides a clear definition, saying: "If one practices giving while abiding in signs, one does not penetrate the nature [of phenomena]."
"Emptiness. As for those who possess real merit, although you say it is much, the Tathāgata does not say it is much, because this is a gift given without abiding.
Since one already knows that its nature is empty and merit is non-existent, it is not only what you say is much;
the Tathāgata also says it is much—provided only that the practice cultivated corresponds to non-abiding. However, this..."
Within the section on cultivation, the taming of the mind is briefly explained by means of saving sentient beings while realizing there are no sentient beings to save;

the abiding of the mind is briefly explained by means of practicing giving while realizing there is no abiding. This is to manifest the correspondence between practice and understanding—that is, to understand in this way and cultivate in this way.
It is like the eyes and feet: seeing in this way and walking in this way. If one’s practice does not accord with this...
[This is] seeing. Fearing it will hinder one’s future progress, practicing while in contradiction to understanding is likewise so.
Verse: Because the root of the Buddha’s wisdom is non-perverted merit, and due to these characteristics of merit, he speaks again by means of analogies.

The commentary states: This verse explains the meaning of the main text. The first two lines state that the previously mentioned "non-abiding" (*apratiṣṭhita*) giving is the root of the Buddha’s wisdom, because it is capable of producing the Buddha’s wisdom.

It is not like "abiding-characteristic" giving, which is called a "perverted merit" because it does not transcend the suffering of saṃsāra. However, there is only the fear that [people] may not understand non-abiding giving.
Regarding the statement that "generosity is the nature of merit," it is because this constitutes the characteristic of merit.

For this reason, the analogy of bestowing jewels filling the entire world is repeated as a metaphor to clarify the meaning of the vastness of merit when one does not dwell [in the fruits thereof]. This concludes the brief explanation.
Second, the detailed demonstration has four parts: first, seeing the Buddha without dwelling; second, hearing the Dharma without dwelling; third, attaining the fruit...
Non-abiding. There are four types of non-abiding in the cultivation of causes. The first two are: first, non-abiding in the view of the body; second, non-abiding in the view of marks.
Regarding the first: Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Buddha be seen by means of his perfected physical body? "No, World-Honored One."
One should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the body of perfect form. Why is this? The Tathāgata has said that the body of perfect form is precisely not a body of perfect form;
it is merely designated as "the body of perfect form."
This and the following section seem to repeat the previous meaning, yet there are two points of difference. First, the difference between "direct inclusion" (*zhèngjiān*) and [the previous];

second, the difference between "transformation" (*huà*) and "retribution" (*bào*). Regarding the difference between direct inclusion: in the section on faith (*xìn*), it is clarified that the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of physical marks (*śarīra-lakṣaṇa*);
whereas in the section on understanding (*jiě*), it is clarified that the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks (*dvātriṃśan-mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*).

The intent of those [previous] passages was entirely to resolve doubts incidentally; they were not texts intended to formally demonstrate the stages of descending and abiding. Now, however, this passage formally demonstrates the mind of abiding, and thus it is different.
Regarding the difference between the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*):

it means that in the former two explanations, the body and its characteristics are described, yet the first lacks any mention of "complete" (or "endowed"), while the second specifies the numbers "four" and "eight. It is therefore clear that these refer to the transformation bodies.
Regarding the statement that "the physical marks of the present body are all fully endowed," this should refer to the body of true recompense (*vipākakāya*).
For it must be adorned with the myriad virtues to be called "fully endowed," as "full endowment" carries the meaning of perfection.

This is because as one's cultivation gradually deepens and one is about to perceive the retributive essence, even the slightest dwelling-place would obstruct the *dharmakāya*; therefore, this is further discussed in relation to this [recompense].

This clarifies non-abiding. It is the most supreme and vast body, of sublime and wondrous color, lacking nothing whatsoever; therefore, it is called the "body of form endowed with all perfections" (*rūpakāya-samanvāgata*).
Regarding the question beginning with "one should," it is because there is a fear that the mind might dwell [on something].

The answer beginning with "one should not" is because dwelling constitutes an obstruction, as one would then fail to perceive the *dharmakāya*. The intent of this inquiry is thus clear. In the commentary, regarding the Tathāgata...

To speak of "possessing a complete physical body" is because it is the result induced by causes cultivated throughout oceans of eons. However, since it belongs to what is induced by causes, it is *pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent origination).
Because *pratītyasamutpāda* is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), it is said that "it is not a complete physical body.
It is merely a provisional designation established to point toward the fruit and encourage the arising of faith; therefore, it is said, "this is called possessing a complete physical body."
Since these are called "names," one should seek their reality; it is clearly understood that they should not be dwelled upon. Second, the non-abiding of the characteristics of views.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can a Tathāgata be seen by means of his possession of the various marks? No, World-Honored One.
World-Honored One, one should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of his possession of the various marks. Why is this?
The Tathāgata has said that the possession of the various marks is itself the non-possession of them; it is merely designated as "the possession of the various marks."
The physical body is the general [category], while the various marks are the particulars. The various marks act as the adornment, and the physical body is that which is adorned.
Since the excellence of what is adorned resides entirely within the power of the adornment, it remains difficult to forget; therefore, this point is again used to clarify non-abiding.
According to the "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks" (*Lakṣaṇasāgara-parivarta*) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, there are briefly explained ninety-seven kinds of marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*).

When explained extensively, there are as many marks of a Great Man as there are atoms in ten oceans of Flower Treasury worlds (*kusumagarbha-lokadhātu-sāgara*), lacking nothing at all; therefore, it is said they are "complete.
This means they are not merely names and so forth, which can be understood from the above.
Verse: The ultimate essence of the Dharma-body is not that body of marks and signs; because it is not accomplished through marks, it is not that Dharma-body.
Yet, since those two are not non-Buddha, it is stated again that they are "accomplished. Furthermore, there is neither duality nor existence.
The combined commentary states: This section combines the meaning of this verse with the preceding section. Within it, there are two parts.

The first seven lines constitute the actual verse, stating that the Buddha’s true *dharmakāya* ultimately possesses a substantial essence, which is not identical to his marks of excellence (*lakṣaṇa*) or physical characteristics (*vyañjana*).
Therefore, the Sūtra says that one cannot see [the Buddha] by means of the form-body (rūpakāya), nor can one see him by means of the various marks (lakṣaṇa).

Within the Sūtra, there is no such thing as "good" form; form necessarily possesses goodness. As for the verse’s exclusion of form while retaining goodness, this is because it serves as a complementary clarification to the Sūtra.
Regarding the phrase "not accomplished by marks," the character "non-" (fei) should be read as "without" (wu); that is to say, the Dharma-body is without marks.
The physical marks are fully accomplished in accordance with conditions. Therefore, when the Sūtra says "it is not a physical mark," it means that it is not [merely] that dharma-body.
Furthermore, when it says "this is a name," it is because the physical marks are not separate from the dharma-body.
Why are the physical marks not separate from the dharma-body? Because both originate from the dharma-body as they manifest; they are not...
This is not the Buddha of the Dharma-body. Therefore, having already stated "it is precisely not," he further reiterates that it is "accomplished through following conditions.

This "accomplishment through following conditions" is precisely the meaning of the name. The final phrase, which "sweeps away attachments," stating "neither two nor existent," means that the Tathāgata, in order to shatter the attachment to existence, speaks of non-duality;
and in order to shatter the attachment to non-existence, he also speaks of existence.
Second: These scriptural statements that "what is known is not that which is named" are all established as skillful means (*upāya*) according to the capacities of sentient beings.

Within the pure *dharmadhātu*, there is not only that which cannot be expressed; even non-existence itself cannot be expressed. This concludes the section on the non-abiding nature of seeing the Buddha.
Second, the non-abiding nature of hearing the Dharma, which has two parts: first, the non-abiding of the speaker; second, the non-abiding of the hearer.
First:
Subhūti, you must not think that the Tathāgata has this thought: "I shall preach some dharma.
Do not have such a thought. Why? If anyone says that the Tathāgata has preached some dharma, they are slandering the Buddha; they do not understand.
"Subhūti, it is because of what I have said: 'One who preaches the Dharma has no dharma to preach; this is called preaching the Dharma.
[This was said] fearing that people might think that since the Buddha cannot be seen by means of physical marks, one must necessarily see the true Buddha as the Dharma-body.

Yet the Dharma-body is formless; how can it respond to the capacities of sentient beings and, through mental attention, preach all dharmas? The Buddha knew that Subhūti had already [conceived such doubts]."
Conceiving this doubt, he did not wait for a question but preempted it, saying: "Do not say that the Tathāgata forms such thoughts," and so forth.

This means that although the Tathāgata has preached the Dharma according to the capacities of beings, he responds through non-conditionality (*anālambana*) and does not actually premeditate, thinking, "I shall now preach such-and-such a Dharma.
Thus, although he preaches the Dharma all day long, [he remains free from such conceptualization].
"In truth, there is no abiding. The *Zuanyao* says: "In the valley there is no person, yet it can produce sound.
This also reveals that the Dharmakāya does not intentionally engage in preaching the Dharma; therefore, the phrase "do not say" (*mowei*) is used as a negation.
Since it negates "do not say" and further states "do not form this thought," it means that not only is it impossible to speak, but even the very thought [of speaking] must not be formed. Why?

The meaning of the phrase can be understood through its inquiry. In the commentary, it is said that if someone were to claim that the Tathāgata has taught any dharma, they would be slandering the Buddha;
this is because their attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*) has not yet been emptied, for to maintain that there is actually something taught is itself an attachment to dharmas.

If one speaks of the Buddha, none dare slander him. Those who do so do not do so intentionally; it is because they cannot understand what I have taught, which—like an echo—is identical with the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
This is an indirect demonstration (*paryudāsa*) that the Dharma should not be clung to. Below, the text provides the direct clarification:
whatever the Tathāgata says when teaching the Dharma is all provisionally established according to the capacities of beings, for the sake of the pure Dharma-realm.

In the middle, there is absolutely no such thing; therefore, it is said that "there is no dharma that can be taught. One should know that the teaching of the Dharma is merely a provisional name, which precisely demonstrates that one should not dwell [upon it].

Verse: As with the Buddha, so it is with the Dharma; the two distinctions thus explained do not depart from the *dharmadhātu*. In explaining the Dharma, there is no intrinsic characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*).

Combined, this verse summarizes the meaning of the main body of the treatise. Following the previous example, since the Buddha cannot be seen by means of physical marks (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), [so it is with the Dharma].

Nor can it be sought through sounds or voices. Therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] is "like a Buddha. The Dharma is also thus. Whether speaking of existence or non-existence, these differ according to the capacities of those to be taught;

hence it is said that there are two distinctions in what is taught. Although there are these distinctions, they do not depart from the *dharmadhātu*, because the Dharma that is taught arises solely as the *paratantra* (dependent nature) and lacks any intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Thus, the speaker has no abiding. Part Two.
Those who hear it have no dwelling place.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, will there be any sentient beings in future ages [who will believe this]?"
"Upon hearing this Dharma, will they give rise to faith? The Buddha said, "Subhūti, they are not sentient beings, yet they are not non-sentient beings.
Why is that? Subhūti, those who are called 'sentient beings' have been described by the Tathāgata as non-sentient beings; it is merely a designation for 'sentient beings.'"
This section exists in the Wei version but is absent from the Qin version; it was later inserted into the Qin version at a recent time.

The *Zuanyao* does not comment on it, while the *Kanding ji* and the *Lüyao xu* provide brief explanations. Since the meaning is now found within Maitreya’s verses, I have explained it here based on the preceding and following context.
Regarding the phrase "named the crown of the life of wisdom" (*huiming*), the Wei translation renders "elder" (*sthavira*) as "wisdom" (*hui*).
[The Buddha] commanded: "Because it is through wisdom that one can continue the Dharma-body, a Buddha cannot be seen by means of physical marks, and the Dharma cannot be sought through sound.
Both meanings are profound; sentient beings of the Final Dharma Age may find them difficult to believe and accept.
Therefore, [the Buddha] asked, 'Is there perhaps any sentient being in future ages...? This was to show that while [such beings] might be rare in the present, they are not non-existent."
As for "faith," it is simply that they are not [ordinary] sentient beings; because one who can believe in this principle is immediately called a Buddha.

Although they are called Buddhas, if they do not give rise to understanding and initiate practice, there will ultimately be no actual realization. Therefore, it is said: "It is not that they are not sentient beings."
This means that they are still, in fact, sentient beings (*sattva*). This implies an intention to encourage cultivation; the underlying purpose can be understood from this.
In the commentary, it says that these sentient beings should be called Buddhas.

The reason they are still called sentient beings is that although they are named sentient beings, because the Tathāgata is able to believe in them, he says they are not sentient beings; furthermore, because they have not yet attained liberation through cultivation.

Names are provisionally established and spoken of as "sentient beings. How could one dwell within the characteristics of sentient beings and yet give rise to a deluded view that severs all distinctions?
Verse: That which is spoken and the speaker are profoundly not non-existent; those who can believe are not [mere] sentient beings, and sentient beings are neither saints nor non-saints.
The Master said: "This also summarizes the meaning of the preceding section. That which is taught is the Dharma; the teacher is the Buddha.
Since the Buddha cannot be seen through physical marks and the Dharma cannot be sought through sound, both are described as 'profound. It is not that there is no capacity [to perceive them]."
Regarding "those who have faith": this expression is used by way of contrast to clarify that there are indeed those who possess faith.
However, such persons are not [ordinary] sentient beings because they are, in their capacity for faith, already Buddhas. Yet, they remain sentient beings because they lack understanding and practice;

since their understanding and practice are not perfected, they ultimately lack actual realization and are therefore not sages. This interpretation maintains the meaning that they are still sentient beings. They are able...
Faith is itself the Buddha; it will ultimately be realized as such, and therefore it is not non-sacred. This explanation does not refer to the meaning of "sentient beings.
This concludes the section on the non-abiding in hearing the Dharma. Part three: Non-abiding in attaining the fruit, which has two sections:
first, Subhūti’s question regarding whether there is attainment; second, the Tathāgata’s seal-response that there is no attainment. First:
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, when the Buddha attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, is it that there is nothing to be attained?
The thought of emptiness arises: as I previously stated, there is no fixed dharma named *anuttara-bodhi* (referring to the section on faith).
Later, the Tathāgata also said: "In truth, there is no dharma by which one attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" (referring to the section on cultivation).
Now, observing those capable of faith, the Tathāgata says they are not "sentient beings" because they are persons who will attain Buddhahood;

however, because their understanding and practice are not yet perfected, they are called "sentient beings" by name. Thus, it is known that if one possesses understanding and practice, [one is certain].
[They] attain Buddhahood. How much more so now, when the Tathāgata has actually attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. These [cases] all contradict what was stated previously. Let me ask the Tathāgata:
Is this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* which the Buddha has now attained something that is "non-attainment"?
This question is intended to verify the previous statement in order to facilitate further cultivation; it is not a matter of the duality of existence and non-existence.
[The interlocutor] doubts. Observe the response below the seal and you will know for yourself. Regarding the two Tathāgata seals, there is nothing to be attained.
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is, Subhūti. As for me, regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi..."
"Up to and including, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended; this is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

This passage has two parts. First is the definitive confirmation. Although Subhūti knows that there is nothing to be attained, he still harbors some doubt; therefore, he asks whether it is "non-existent."
The Tathāgata accepts this with all his might and cuts it off at its very root; therefore, he seals it by saying, "It is so" (*evam etat*), meaning that what you have asked is indeed correct.
He repeats the words to manifest certainty. Subhūti’s response below is an answer that accords with the question, explaining and clarifying its meaning.
He says: "Regarding my [attainment] of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, from the beginning..."
It appears as if there is something to be attained; subsequently, this gradually disappears until finally not even the slightest dharma can be found.

Because not a single thought arises, it is merely when delusion is exhausted and principle is perfected that one provisionally establishes names and designations, calling it "Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Therefore, it says, "This is called... and so forth; one should certainly know that one ought not to dwell therein.
Verse: "In that place, there is not even the slightest dharma by which one knows unsurpassed bodhi.
[Commentary: It should be understood that this merely restates the seal-response regarding the meaning of non-attainment. "In that place" refers to the locus of cultivation and realization.
This refers to the stages of realization (*bhūmi*). If there were even the slightest dharma to be attained, it would mean that delusion has not been exhausted and principle has not been perfected;
thus, it could not be called "unsurpassed. Therefore, one must reach the point where not even the slightest dharma exists before realizing unsurpassed *bodhi*.
This concludes the section on the non-abiding attainment of the fruit. Fourth is the non-abiding cultivation of the cause.
Furthermore, Subhūti, this dharma is equal; it has no high or low. This is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Because it is without self, without person, without sentient being, and without life-span, one cultivates all wholesome dharmas.
He immediately attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti, as for what are called "wholesome dharmas," the Tathāgata has said that they are not wholesome dharmas;
they are merely designated as "wholesome dharmas."

The explanation has three parts. First: Since the principle is fundamentally without cultivation, there may be the fear that if the fruit is ultimately unattainable, the cause must likewise be uncultivated;

for what reason, then, would a bodhisattva resolve their mind and cultivate goodness? Therefore, the Tathāgata first demonstrates to them that the principle is fundamentally without cultivation. This "Dharma" refers to *bodhi*.
Among the three types of *bodhi*, we shall here speak primarily of *svabhāva-bodhi* (intrinsic enlightenment). Regarding "equality": it resides in...
It does not decrease among ordinary beings; it does not increase among the noble ones. Because it does not increase among the noble ones, there is no height;
because it does not decrease among ordinary beings, there is no lowness. Being without height or lowness, it transcends all dualities. This is called *anuttara*, meaning "unsurpassed.
Its nature is fundamentally endowed with all wholesome dharmas; this is called *samyak*, meaning "perfectly equal. Its nature is fundamentally...
Not being obscured by the four marks is called *sambodhi*, which means "perfect enlightenment.

However, this refers only to the inherent nature (*li-jù*) and does not concern phenomenal practice (*shi-zào*). Therefore, it is also merely a provisional designation, indicating that it is not an actual realization.

Even when one reaches the stage of faith and understanding (*xinjie xiangying*), one must not cling to principle at the expense of phenomena. Yongjia said: "To be expansively vacant and to negate cause and effect..."
Vast and boundless, it invites calamity and misfortune. It is precisely to deeply remedy this defect that one must not fall into inferiority; for practice must necessarily be cultivated.
Although it is said that "this Dharma is equal and has no high or low," we nevertheless see in the present world that sentient beings and Buddhas are clearly distinguished.

This is because ordinary beings are obscured by the four marks and thus fail to attain perfect enlightenment; those of the two vehicles do not cultivate wholesome dharmas and thus lose the state of perfect equality;
and bodhisattvas, though they practice, are not yet fully endowed with it and have not yet reached the unsurpassed state.

The Buddha, being without self, without person, without sentient beings, and without life-span, differs from the lack of awakening of ordinary beings and is therefore called "perfect enlightenment. The Buddha, by means of...
Cultivating goodness that differs from the partiality of the Two Vehicles is called "Right Equality" (*samyaksamatā*).

Because the Buddha has fully cultivated all wholesome dharmas, it differs from the "surpassable" state of Bodhisattvas and is thus called "Unsurpassed" (*anuttara*). Therefore, it is said: "One immediately attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Thus, one should know that a Bodhisattva who has resolved their mind must establish cultivation within non-cultivation; and so too does the Tathāgata realize the fruit.
One establishes attainment only within non-attainment; this still does not contradict the meaning of non-attainment.

Subhūti [says] below that one should not dwell [in anything], for he fears that upon hearing that one should fully cultivate wholesome dharmas, one might again give rise to views regarding causes for dwelling. Therefore it is said:

"As for what are called wholesome dharmas, the Tathāgata says they are not wholesome dharmas," because they are devoid of the marks of self, person, and so forth; thus cultivation is identical to non-cultivation.

Therefore, it is merely for the purpose of severing delusion and restoring reality that provisional names and phrases are established and spoken of as "wholesome dharmas. Thus it is said, "This is called [a wholesome dharma].
Knowing this, one should not dwell upon the cultivation of causes.
Verse: The dharma-realm neither increases nor decreases; it is pure, equal, and possesses its own characteristic of existence.
Through unsurpassed skillful means and being free from outflows, that which is not a pure dharma is itself a pure dharma.
The combined explanation states: The first two lines praise the fact that, in principle, there is no cultivation.
"Dharmadhātu" refers to the one true dharmadhātu, which is self-nature bodhi; the Sūtra’s phrase "this dharma" points to this. "Neither increasing nor decreasing" expresses the meaning of equality.
Regarding "purity-equality" (*viśuddhi-samatā*): the term "equality" is established here to signify that purity-equality is free from the defilement of differentiation.

As for the "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is the natural characteristic of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). It is without high or low, transcends all relativity, and is not something acquired through cultivation.
The following two lines of the verse state that practice must necessarily exist; for although it is called purity-equality, this refers only to its inherent presence within principle (*li*). If...
Desire is created; there is also the method of skillful means for unexcelled bodhi. As the sutra says:
"The absence of marks such as self and person" is precisely the method of skillful means. Having attained this method of skillful means, one must still fully cultivate all manner of wholesome deeds;
therefore, it is said, "and being free from outflowing dharmas. Being free from outflowing dharmas refers specifically to untainted (anāsrava) wholesome dharmas. This is...
Because it is that which ought to be cultivated. Therefore, the following verse clarifies that one should not abide [in signs]. "Therefore" means:

by relying on such skillful means as selflessness (*anātman*) and so forth, one cultivates the departure from tainted phenomena (*āsrava-dharma*); thus, one naturally does not abide in signs (*nimitta*).

Therefore, it is not a pure dharma; this is what the Sūtra means when it says, "It is precisely not a wholesome dharma. However, in order to sever delusion and restore reality, provisional names and phrases are established;
thus it is said, "It is precisely a pure dharma," which is what the Sūtra means when it says, "This is called a wholesome dharma.
This concludes the section on abiding in the mind of non-abiding. Third, the comparison of the merit of upholding [the teaching].

Subhūti, if someone were to take all the Sumeru kings of mountains within a trichiliocosm and offer them as a heap of the seven precious treasures as a gift, and if another person were to [offer] this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra...
Even if one were to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain to others even as little as a four-line verse from this sutra, the former merit would not equal a hundredth part of it;
nor a thousandth, ten-thousandth, or hundred-thousandth part; nor even a hundred-thousand-billionth part; nor could it be reached by any calculation, number, or analogy.
The text has three parts. First, it raises the standard for comparison. According to the teachings, within one great trichiliocosm there are ten billion Sumeru mountains;
now, taking such Sumeru mountains made of the seven treasures and piling them together to use as a gift—such a gift may indeed be called great.
Second, it clarifies what is being compared. The sutra uses only this verse up to its four lines, even extending to... [etc.]

Regarding what is inferior: to receive, uphold, recite, and explain [this teaching], its practice may be called subtle. To clarify what is inferior compared to the former, it says "compared to the previous merit.

This means that when one compares the merit of subsequently upholding and explaining it with the previous merit—that is, the merit of giving away jewels—the latter does not equal even a hundredth part of this merit of upholding. Thus, the merit of giving jewels does not equal this merit of upholding.
It is said: "This also [is inferior] because merit does not lead toward Bodhi, whereas this [practice] can lead toward Bodhi.

One hundred thousand million billion [instances] and so forth should be understood according to the preceding. According to the five previous comparisons: first, giving the jewels of one world-system;
second, giving the jewels of immeasurable world-systems; third, giving bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; fourth, giving bodies as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges rivers.

[The first five] are acts of giving. Fifth, by making offerings to the Buddhas during the Tathāgata’s stage of practice, one proceeds from the inferior toward the superior, manifesting that the Dharma becomes progressively deeper;

this is beyond dispute. Now, we shall examine the sixth [type of giving] through comparison: even the gift of jewels equal to ten billion Mount Sumerus is still inferior to the first, let alone the second through the fifth.
Since each subsequent one is inferior to the preceding, how can such a principle be maintained? It is because...

Because the prior cultivation of faith and understanding is difficult, while the subsequent realization through cultivation is easy. As the Great Sutra says: "The initial aspiration and the ultimate goal are not two;

yet between these two minds, the former is more difficult. Since the difficult is to be weighed as superior, whereas the easy may be addressed according to convenience, this concludes the section on cultivation.
I have briefly employed this weighing to demonstrate the excellence of those who undertake the practice.
This is merely the intention of the progression.

The verse states: Although it is said that [the Buddha] is an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomenon, he is taught to be their cause; therefore, this single Jewel of the Dharma excels immeasurable heaps of precious gems.
Its power is incomparable, and its excellence as a cause is likewise incomparable. No worldly phenomena can be found to equal it.
[This is] an analogy.
The commentary states: This is a verse composed according to the meaning.

The first four lines first manifest the excellence of the sutra, stating that those who wish to attain *bodhi* must cultivate wholesome dharmas, and that the cultivation of wholesome dharmas depends primarily upon upholding and expounding this sutra. However, the sutra alone...
The bodies of names, phrases, and syllables are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas. How can they maintain and explain [the teaching] so as to attain *bodhi*?
To refute this objection, it is said: "Although it is called an indeterminate dharma, it is taught as its cause.
This means that although this sūtra is said to be subsumed under the category of indeterminate dharmas, it is nevertheless taught to be the cause of that *bodhi*. Therefore, this one...
The Dharma Jewel surpasses immeasurable worldly treasures. "Immeasurable treasures" refers here to the mass of jewels equal to ten billion Mount Sumerus mentioned in the sutra.
The subsequent four lines next clarify the excellence of upholding [this sutra].

It states that even if one were to exhaust the power of analysis regarding the quantity of such jewel-gifts, none could equal the excellence of this sutra; since nothing can equal it, the sutra is supreme.
This is also the case for holding and expounding [the teachings] as causes; how much more so for all worldly dharmas, which cannot even serve as metaphors.
They are like a heap of jewels equal to Mount Sumeru, yet by their very nature, they should be measured as falling short [of the Dharma].

This concludes the section on the ultimate summary of descending, abiding, and initiating cultivation. Part Four: The Section on the Decisive Attainment of Realization through Descending and Abiding, in three parts. First: Descending...
The mind is free from marks. Second, the mind abides in non-abiding. Third, the summary and the intent of the question. Regarding the first two [points], there is:
first, a brief clarification; second, a detailed exposition.
First: "Subhūti, what do you think? You should not say that the Tathāgata has this thought: 'I shall deliver sentient beings.'"
“Subhūti, do not conceive such a thought. Why is this? In reality, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata has delivered.
If there were any sentient beings whom the Tathāgata had delivered, the Tathāgata would possess a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
Subhūti, when the Tathāgata speaks of a ‘self,’ it is not a self; yet ordinary people imagine there is a self.”
Subhūti, those who are called "ordinary beings" by the Tathāgata are not, in fact, ordinary beings; they are merely designated as "ordinary beings.
[The text is divided into three parts: First, a preliminary refutation of erroneous doubts.

Fearing that it might be thought that the Tathāgata’s successive demonstrations of subduing the mind all imply that while he speaks of saving sentient beings, there is actually no one saved—why then did the Buddha, immediately after his initial attainment of enlightenment, contemplate for twenty-one days with the intention of saving sentient beings? (As the Dharma...)
As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Buddha, knowing that Subhūti had already conceived this doubt, did not wait for his question but preemptively addressed him, saying:
"Subhūti, what do you think? You should not say that the Tathāgata has the thought: 'I shall deliver sentient beings.

The Buddha’s intention was that the thought of delivering sentient beings arose from thirty-seven days of contemplation; such a notion is merely according to the perceptions of those with limited capacities (*hīnayāna* practitioners).
It is not truly so. Since you have already been cautioned against such views, and furthermore taught that one should not entertain such thoughts, this is a definitive prohibition.

Why is this? [The following] interrogates to reveal the absence of degrees. The intent of the interrogation is clear. Within the explanation, there is first a direct clarification, followed by a reductio ad absurdum.
In the direct clarification, it is said: "The Tathāgata realizes the true Dharma-realm; there is no phenomenon that is not integrated. All sentient beings..."
When one attains enlightenment in a single moment, how could one again perceive a "savior" or a "saved"? This is the reverse illumination (*pratiloma*).

If, in fact, one perceives that there are sentient beings who are saved by the Tathāgata, then it follows that the Tathāgata regards himself as the savior; therefore, it is said that there is a self (*ātman*).
Once the mark of self (*ātma-lakṣaṇa*) is established, the marks of person (*pudgala-lakṣaṇa*), sentient being (*sattva-lakṣaṇa*), and life-span (*jīva-lakṣaṇa*) will necessarily arise along with it.

There is [a distinction]. The Tathāgata is not like that; therefore, one knows there is no [substantial] crossing over. From "Subhūti" onwards, [the text] further prevents erroneous objections. It is feared that one might say:
"If the Buddha has no self, for what reason did the Tathāgata, upon his initial attainment of the Way, say, 'I am the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha;
I am the All-Knowing One, the All-Seeing One,' and so forth (as also stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*)? This is to prevent such [misunderstandings].
This is difficult to resolve; therefore, it is said: "When the Tathāgata speaks of a self, it is not a [truly existent] self.

This was because, upon his initial attainment of enlightenment, he sought to distinguish [his teaching] from heterodox schools, as it is not a product of parikalpita (imagined) nature. Yet worldly ordinary beings do not understand this intent.
